Just a short note to explain Laplace's rule of succession. In a Bayesian framework, we start with a uniform prior $Beta(1,1)$ on the fail probability $p$. After observing $0$ failures out of $n$ trials, we update the prior and get $Beta(1+0, 1+n)$ as a posterior. It has expected value $p=1/(n+2)$, which is precisely Laplace's rule of succession. So the expected number of fails in the next $m$ trials is $m/(n+2)$ and the probability of getting at least one failure is $1-(1-1/(n+2))^m \\approx m/(n+2)$, which in this case immediately gives $\\approx 10\\%$.", "creationdate": "2015-01-22T16:49:15.467000", "comments_rownum": "comments_179865"}, "comments_193850": {"id": 294059, "postid": 153949, "userid": 36229, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "userdisplayname": null, "text": "Statistics never ceases to astonish me", "creationdate": "2015-05-27T15:43:29.560000", "comments_rownum": "comments_193850"}, "comments_327654": {"id": 488717, "postid": 255966, "userid": 145151, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "userdisplayname": null, "text": "I have a justification based on the domain the data is coming from. and only the biggest 4 provinces (KISS)\nplot(ca(df))\n\nsummary(ca(df))\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Output</p>\n\n<pre><code>Principal inertias (eigenvalues):\n\n dim    value      %   cum%   scree plot               \n 1      0.002523  99.9  99.9  *************************\n 2      3e-06000   0.1 100.0                           \n 3      00000000   0.0 100.0                           \n        -------- -----                                 \n Total: 0.002526 100.0                                 \n\n\nRows:\n    name   mass  qlt  inr    k=1  cor ctr    k=2 cor ctr  \n1 | Crrn |  265 1000  191 |  -43 1000 191 |    1   0  43 |\n2 | Dlys |  201 1000  351 |  -66 1000 351 |   -1   0  70 |\n3 | Frmr |  470 1000  432 |   48 1000 432 |   -1   0  98 |\n4 | Occs |   65 1000   26 |   31  964  25 |    6  36 789 |\n\nColumns:\n    name   mass  qlt  inr    k=1  cor ctr    k=2 cor ctr  \n1 |   AB |  116 1000  146 |  -56 1000 146 |   -1   0  34 |\n2 |   BC |  142 1000  775 |  118 1000 776 |   -1   0  41 |\n3 |   ON |  434 1000    7 |   -6  909   6 |    2  91 540 |\n4 |   QC |  308 1000   72 |  -24  994  72 |   -2   6 385 |\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Looking at <code>summary(ca(df))</code> I see that nearly 100% of the inertia is described by the row profile for both modalities (Type of smoker and Province, respectively).</p>\n\n<p><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/ygmU7.jpg\" alt=\"CA of Smoker Types in ON, QC, AB, and BC\"></p>\n\n<p>What (I think) should be immediate takeaways are: </p>\n\n<ol>\n<li>You are more likely to be a daily smoker if you live in AB, QC, or ON</li>\n<li>You are more likely to be a former smoker if you live in BC </li>\n<li>You are least likely to be a daily smoker if you live in BC (this fits with Canadian wide understanding of BC's \"active lifestyle\" culture)</li>\n</ol>\n\n<p>What could we say about occasional smokers? What would your analysis tell us through this correspondence plot and it's associated summary?</p>\n\n<p>Data Source: Statistics Canada, Canadian Community Health Survey (CCHS 3.1), 2005. The CANSIM table 105-0427 was an update of CANSIM table <a href=\"http://cansim2.statcan.gc.ca/cgi-win/cnsmcgi.pgm?Lang=E&RootDir=CII/&Array_Pick=1&ArrayId=105-0227&C2DB=PRD&ResultTemplate=CII%2FCII___\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">105-0227</a>. More current data are in CANSIM tables <a href=\"http://cansim2.statcan.gc.ca/cgi-win/cnsmcgi.pgm?Lang=E&RootDir=CII/&Array_Pick=1&ArrayId=105-0501&C2DB=PRD&ResultTemplate=CII%2FCII___\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">105-0501</a> and <a href=\"http://cansim2.statcan.gc.ca/cgi-win/cnsmcgi.pgm?Lang=E&RootDir=CII/&Array_Pick=1&ArrayId=105-0502&C2DB=PRD&ResultTemplate=CII%2FCII___\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">105-0502</a>.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-03T21:24:06.223000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3112"}, "posts_4183": {"id": 4445, "owneruserid": 919, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 4449, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Model for population density estimation", "tags": "<modeling><unbiased-estimator><spatial>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>A database of (population, area, shape) can be used to map population density by assigning a constant value of population/area to each shape (which is a polygon such as a Census block, tract, county, state, whatever).  Populations are usually not uniformly distributed within their polygons, however.  <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dasymetric_map\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Dasymetric mapping</a> is the process of refining these density estimates by means of auxiliary data.  It is an important problem in the social sciences as <a href=\"https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11113-007-9046-5?from=SL\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">this recent review</a> indicates.</p>\n<p>Suppose, then, that we have available an auxiliary map of land cover (or any other discrete factor).  In the simplest case we can use obviously uninhabitable areas like waterbodies to delineate where the population isn't and, accordingly, assign all the population to the remaining areas.  More generally, each Census unit <span class=\"math-container\">$j$</span> is carved into <span class=\"math-container\">$k$</span> portions having surface areas <span class=\"math-container\">$x_{ji}$</span>, <span class=\"math-container\">$i = 1, 2, \\ldots, k$</span>.  Our dataset is thereby augmented to a list of tuples</p>\n<p><span class=\"math-container\">$$(y_{j}, x_{j1}, x_{j2}, \\ldots, x_{jk})$$</span></p>\n<p>where <span class=\"math-container\">$y_{j}$</span> is the population (assumed measured without error) in unit <span class=\"math-container\">$j$</span> and--although this is not strictly the case--we may assume every <span class=\"math-container\">$x_{ji}$</span> is also exactly measured.  In these terms, the objective is to partition each <span class=\"math-container\">$y_{j}$</span> into a sum</p>\n<p><span class=\"math-container\">$$ y_j = z_{j1} + z_{j2} + \\cdots + z_{jk} $$</span></p>\n<p>where each <span class=\"math-container\">$z_{ji} \\ge 0$</span> and <span class=\"math-container\">$z_{ji}$</span> estimates the population within unit <span class=\"math-container\">$j$</span> residing in land cover class <span class=\"math-container\">$i$</span>.  The estimates need to be unbiased.  This partition refines the population density map by assigning the density <span class=\"math-container\">$z_{ji}/x_{ji}$</span> to the intersection of the <span class=\"math-container\">$j^{\\text{th}}$</span> Census polygon and the <span class=\"math-container\">$i^{\\text{th}}$</span> land cover class.</p>\n<p>This problem differs from standard regression settings in salient ways:</p>\n<ol>\n<li>The partitioning of each <span class=\"math-container\">$y_{j}$</span> must be exact.</li>\n<li>The components of every partition must be non-negative.</li>\n<li>There is (by assumption) no error in any of the data: all population counts <span class=\"math-container\">$y_{j}$</span> and all areas <span class=\"math-container\">$x_{ji}$</span> are correct.</li>\n</ol>\n<p>There are many approaches to a solution, such as the "<a href=\"https://web.archive.org/web/20110506133809/http://astro.temple.edu/%7Ejmennis/pubs/mennis_cagis06.pdf\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">intelligent dasymetric mapping</a>" method, but all those I have read about have <em>ad hoc</em> elements and an obvious potential for bias.  I am seeking answers that suggest creative, computationally tractable statistical methods.  The immediate application concerns a collection of <em>c.</em> <span class=\"math-container\">$10^{5}$</span> - <span class=\"math-container\">$10^{6}$</span> Census units averaging 40 people apiece (although a sizable fraction have 0 people) and about a dozen land cover classes.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-11-11T14:38:22.373000", "posts_rownum": "posts_4183"}, "posts_4483": {"id": 4766, "owneruserid": 2078, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Randomized SVD and singular values", "tags": "<matrix-decomposition><svd>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>Randomized SVD decomposes a matrix by extracting the first k singular values/vectors using k+p random projections. This works surprisingly well for large matrices.</p>\n\n<p>My question concerns the singular values that are output from the algorithm. Why aren't the values equal to the first k-singular values if you do the full SVD?</p>\n\n<p>Below I have a simple implementation in R. Any suggestions on improving the performance would be appreciated.</p>\n\n<pre><code> rsvd = function(A, k=10, p=5){\n       n = nrow(A)\n       y = A %*% matrix(rnorm(n * (k+p)), nrow=n)\n       q = qr.Q(qr(y))\n       b = t(q) %*% A\n       svd = svd(b)\n       list(u=q %*% svd$u, d=svd$d, v=svd$v)\n    }\n\n    > set.seed(10)\n\n    > A <- matrix(rnorm(500*500),500,500)\n\n    > svd(A)$d[1:15]\n     [1] 44.94307 44.48235 43.78984 43.44626 43.27146 43.15066 42.79720 42.54440 42.27439 42.21873 41.79763 41.51349 41.48338 41.35024 41.18068\n\n    > rsvd.o(A,10,5)$d\n     [1] 34.83741 33.83411 33.09522 32.65761 32.34326 31.80868 31.38253 30.96395 30.79063 30.34387 30.04538 29.56061 29.24128 29.12612 27.61804\n\n    B <- matrix(rnorm(500*50),500,500)  # rank 50\n\n> rsvd(B,10,5)$d\n [1] 86.48035 83.02114 81.03988 80.04358 77.24979 76.10945 74.47357 74.08382\n [9] 72.85898 72.06897 69.59526 67.70750 66.53867 62.96446 61.50838\n\n> svd(B)$d[1:15]\n [1] 92.44779 91.47689 88.71948 88.08170 87.24533 85.13312 84.14741 83.71757\n [9] 82.80832 81.43005 80.73903 79.92959 78.87421 78.33509 77.38431\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>As Joris pointed out, I have this posted on stackoverflow as well. you can find the revelant conversation here</p>\n\n<p><a href=\"https://stackoverflow.com/questions/4224031/randomized-svd-singular-values\">https://stackoverflow.com/questions/4224031/randomized-svd-singular-values</a></p>\n\n<p>Also see the relevant paper by Martinsson et al: <a href=\"http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.acha.2010.02.003\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">A randomized algorithm for the decomposition of matrices</a></p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-11-21T04:17:20.387000", "posts_rownum": "posts_4483"}, "posts_4597": {"id": 4884, "owneruserid": 264, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 9742, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Aggregation-Level in AB-Tests", "tags": "<hypothesis-testing><aggregation><ab-test>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>Hello fellow number crunchers</p>\n\n<p>I hope this a valid question for this forum. I am a lonesome quarter-statistician and have trouble finding someone to ask.</p>\n\n<p><strong>Introduction:</strong></p>\n\n<ul>\n<li><a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A/B_testing\" rel=\"nofollow\">Wikipedia Explanation of AB-Tests</a></li>\n<li><a href=\"http://www.abtests.com/\" rel=\"nofollow\">A ton of examples for typical use of AB-Tests</a></li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>The AB-Test has become really popular since it is so easy to implement and execute. Additionally the web is floated with blogs explaining how to determine the significance of the results. All in all, it seems that there is less discussion about the control or exclusion of possible \"influential\" variables (on the other hand, controlling such variables is quite hard on the web).</p>\n\n<p>Most AB-Tests comparing the outcomes of both groups by simple counting how many clicks or conversions every group has generated. Than a binomial distribution is assumed for each group and hence statistical tests are performed to see which group got the greater p. </p>\n\n<p><strong>So the question is:</strong> </p>\n\n<p><em>Is it \"better\" to compare the outcome of both groups without any aggregation or it is \"better\" to aggregate e.g. on daily basis ?</em> </p>\n\n<p><strong>Example:</strong>\nThe AB-Test is to check whether a landing page creates more newsletter subscriptions (<- conversions in this case). The AB-Test is deployed/online the whole test-time. In group A the landing page's main color is blue, in group B the main color is red. Assume 2000 visitors per day, i.e. each group gets roughly 1000 visitors. In this case \"without aggregation\" means, that I get 1000 datapoints per group per day meanwhile \"aggregation on daily basis\" means, that I get one (!) datapoint per group per day.</p>\n\n<p><strong>Discussion</strong></p>\n\n<p>The latter (aggregation on daily baiss) would allow the pairing of values, which in turn can capture daily effects like peaks in user behavior and preferences, but it extends the duration of AB-Tests, because it takes longer to collect enough datapoints. On the other hand, the former (no aggregation) seems to the strategy of the majority, because ... I dont know, maybe because a) with enough traffic you can make nearly anything significant within one day b) it is the easiest thing to do.</p>\n\n<p>One (possibly influencing) example to stimulate your thoughts: \nAssume that on one day during the test the \"National Blue Day\" is celebrated, so the color blue together with positive emotions is visible in all the media. This day group A has created a ton of conversions more than group B. </p>\n\n<p>This difference clearly affects the test if aggregated on daily basis (increase of variance) or (if not aggregated at all) it either vanishes in the sea of data (in the case that multiple days are collected without aggregation) or it leads to the wrong results (if the day is the first and only day of the test).</p>\n\n<p>Another example: Assume that the landing page belongs to a vegetable company. One day the \"National Vegetable Day\" is celebrated and now everyone wants to subscribe to the newsletter, no matter what the color is. This short-time effect is captured by aggregation on daily basis and a paired test, but it increases the variance in the case of no aggregation (because no paired test can performed here (is this even correct ?))</p>\n\n<p>All in all: Am I on the right track or do I miss something completely ?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-11-24T16:23:43.947000", "posts_rownum": "posts_4597"}, "posts_5939": {"id": 6308, "owneruserid": 230, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 6310, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Article about misuse of statistical method in NYTimes", "tags": "<hypothesis-testing><bayesian><statistics-in-media>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I am referring to this article: <a href=\"http://www.nytimes.com/2011/01/11/science/11esp.html\">http://www.nytimes.com/2011/01/11/science/11esp.html</a></p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p>Consider the following experiment. Suppose there was reason to believe that a coin was slightly weighted toward heads. In a test, the coin comes up heads 527 times out of 1,000.</p>\n  \n  <p>Is this significant evidence that the\n  coin is weighted?</p>\n  \n  <p>Classical analysis says yes. With a\n  fair coin, the chances of getting 527\n  or more heads in 1,000 flips is less\n  than 1 in 20, or 5 percent, the\n  conventional cutoff. To put it another\n  way: the experiment finds evidence of\n  a weighted coin “with 95 percent\n  confidence.”</p>\n  \n  <p>Yet many statisticians do not buy it.\n  One in 20 is the probability of\n  getting any number of heads above 526\n  in 1,000 throws. That is, it is the\n  sum of the probability of flipping\n  527, the probability of flipping 528,\n  529 and so on.</p>\n  \n  <p>But the experiment did not find all of\n  the numbers in that range; it found\n  just one — 527. It is thus more\n  accurate, these experts say, to\n  calculate the probability of getting\n  that one number — 527 — if the coin is\n  weighted, and compare it with the\n  probability of getting the same number\n  if the coin is fair.</p>\n  \n  <p>Statisticians can show that this ratio\n  cannot be higher than about 4 to 1,\n  according to Paul Speckman, a\n  statistician, who, with Jeff Rouder, a\n  psychologist, provided the example.</p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p><strong>First question:</strong> This is new to me. Has anybody a reference  where I can find the exact calculation and/or can YOU help me by giving me the exact calculation yourself and/or can you point me to some material where I can find similar examples?</p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p>Bayes devised a way to update the\n  probability for a hypothesis as new\n  evidence comes in.</p>\n  \n  <p>So in evaluating the strength of a\n  given finding, Bayesian (pronounced\n  BAYZ-ee-un) analysis incorporates\n  known probabilities, if available,\n  from outside the study.</p>\n  \n  <p>It might be called the “Yeah, right”\n  effect. If a study finds that kumquats\n  reduce the risk of heart disease by 90\n  percent, that a treatment cures\n  alcohol addiction in a week, that\n  sensitive parents are twice as likely\n  to give birth to a girl as to a boy,\n  the Bayesian response matches that of\n  the native skeptic: Yeah, right. The\n  study findings are weighed against\n  what is observable out in the world.</p>\n  \n  <p>In at least one area of medicine —\n  diagnostic screening tests —\n  researchers already use known\n  probabilities to evaluate new\n  findings. For instance, a new\n  lie-detection test may be 90 percent\n  accurate, correctly flagging 9 out of\n  10 liars. But if it is given to a\n  population of 100 people already known\n  to include 10 liars, the test is a lot\n  less impressive.</p>\n  \n  <p>It correctly identifies 9 of the 10\n  liars and misses one; but it\n  incorrectly identifies 9 of the other\n  90 as lying. Dividing the so-called\n  true positives (9) by the total number\n  of people the test flagged (18) gives\n  an accuracy rate of 50 percent. The\n  “false positives” and “false\n  negatives” depend on the known rates\n  in the population.</p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p><strong>Second question:</strong> How do you exactly judge if a new finding is \"real\" or not with this method? And: Isn't this as arbitrary as the 5%-barrier because of the use of some preset prior probability?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-01-17T11:11:10.560000", "posts_rownum": "posts_5939"}, "posts_7298": {"id": 7815, "owneruserid": 3026, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 7933, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What skills are required to perform large scale statistical analyses?", "tags": "<regression><machine-learning><multivariate-analysis><large-data>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>Many statistical jobs ask for experience with large scale data. observation and outcome\nfor(i in 1:n){\n    # Set base risk\n    event_risk <- base_risk$event \n    comp_risk <- base_risk$cmprsk\n\n    for(j in 1:length(risk_factors)){\n        x[i, j] <- risk_factors[[j]]$event\n            comp_risk <- comp_risk + \n                    risk_factors[[j]]$cmprsk\n        }\n    }\n\n    # Time 2 event/risk is 1/rate meaning that higher number -> risk_factors[[i]]$event/base_risk$event+1\n    cmp_rsk <- risk_factors[[i]]$cmprsk/base_risk$cmprsk+1\n    name <- paste(\"Risk factor no: \", i, \"\\n * ev=\", ev_rsk, \" cr=\", cmp_rsk, \" *\", "posts_5457": {"id": 5782, "owneruserid": 1643, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 5790, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Variance of a function of one random variable", "tags": "<variance><random-variable><delta-method>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Lets say we have random variable $X$ with known variance and mean. The question is: what is the variance of $f(X)$ for some given function f. The only general method that I'm aware of is the delta method, but it gives only aproximation. Now I'm interested in $f(x)=\\sqrt{x}$, but it'd be also nice to know some general methods.</p>\n\n<p><strong>Edit 29.12.2010</strong><br>\nI've done some calculations using Taylor series, but I'm not sure whether they are correct, so I'd be glad if someone could <strong>confirm</strong> them.  </p>\n\n<p>First we need to approximate $E[f(X)]$<br>\n$E[f(X)] \\approx E[f(\\mu)+f'(\\mu)(X-\\mu)+\\frac{1}{2}\\cdot f''(\\mu)(X-\\mu)^2]=f(\\mu)+\\frac{1}{2}\\cdot f''(\\mu)\\cdot Var[X]$</p>\n\n<p>Now we can approximate $D^2 [f(X)]$<br>\n$E[(f(X)-E[f(X)])^2] \\approx E[(f(\\mu)+f'(\\mu)(X-\\mu)+\\frac{1}{2}\\cdot f''(\\mu)(X-\\mu)^2 -E[f(X)])^2]$  </p>\n\n<p>Using the approximation of $E[f(X)]$ we know that $f(\\mu)-Ef(x) \\approx -\\frac{1}{2}\\cdot f''(\\mu)\\cdot Var[X]$  </p>\n\n<p>Using this we get:<br>\n$D^2[f(X)] \\approx \\frac{1}{4}\\cdot f''(\\mu)^2\\cdot Var[X]^2-\\frac{1}{2}\\cdot f''(\\mu)^2\\cdot Var[X]^2 + f'(\\mu)^2\\cdot Var[X]+\\frac{1}{4}f''(\\mu)^2\\cdot E[(X-\\mu)^4] +\\frac{1}{2}f'(\\mu)f''(\\mu)E[(X-\\mu)^3]$<br>\n$D^2 [f(X)] \\approx \\frac{1}{4}\\cdot f''(\\mu)^2 \\cdot [D^4 X-(D^2 X)^2]+f'(\\mu)\\cdot D^2 X +\\frac{1}{2}f'(\\mu)f''(\\mu)D^3 X$</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-12-28T14:13:16.227000", "posts_rownum": "posts_5457"}, "posts_3460": {"id": 3653, "owneruserid": 834, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 3657, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Adding coefficients to obtain interaction effects - what to do with SEs?", "tags": "<regression><standard-deviation><standard-error>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I have a multivariate regression, which includes interactions. I face such a situation in the case of studies with a limited sample size and a lot of data gathered through different questionnaires (socio-demographics data, neuropsychological or medical scales -- e.g., mental or physical functioning, depression/anxiety level, symptoms checklist). It happens that EDA helps to highlight some unexpected relationships (\"unexpected\" meaning that they were not included in the initial analysis plan) that translates into additional questions/hypothesis.</p>\n\n<p>As is the case for overfitting, data <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_dredging\">dredging</a> or <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_snooping\">snooping</a> does lead to results that do not generalize. However, when a lot of data is available, it is quite difficult (for the researcher or physician) to postulate a limited set of hypotheses.</p>\n\n<p>I would like to know if there are well-acknowledged methods, recommendations, or rules of thumb that may help to delineate EDA in the case of small-sample studies.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-01T21:52:02.977000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3075"}, "posts_2647": {"id": 2777, "owneruserid": 183, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2781, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Modelling longitudinal data where the effect of time varies in functional form between individuals", "tags": "<repeated-measures><random-effects-model><latent-class>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p><strong>Context</strong>:</p>\n\n<p>Imagine you had a longitudinal study which measured a dependent variable (DV) once a week for 20 weeks on 200 participants. I went through the docs on the package's CRAN website, but i feel working on a practical example (second practical, considering convolve3) would be more helpfull . </p>\n\n<p>I propose the following code, from the the <strong>robustbase</strong> package because it's neither too long nor too short, uses a combination of R types and R functions and has one of those small arithmetic iterations that are too slow in R. How would you go about Rcpp-ing it ?</p>\n\n<pre><code>scaleTau2<-function (x, c1 = 4.5, c2 = 3, consistency = TRUE, mu.too = FALSE){\nn <- length(x)\nmedx <- median(x)\nx. <- abs(x - medx)\nsigma0 <- median(x.)\nmu <- if (c1 > 0) {\n    x. <- x./(sigma0 * c1)\n    w <- 1 - x. * x.\n    w <- ((abs(w) + w)/2)^2\n    sum(x * w)/sum(w)\n}\nelse medx\nx <- (x - mu)/sigma0\nrho <- x^2\nrho[rho > c2^2] <- c2^2\nif (!identical(consistency, FALSE)) {\n    Erho <- function(b) 2*((1-b^2)*pnorm(b)-b*dnorm(b)+b^2)-1\n    Es2 <- function(c2) Erho(c2*qnorm(3/4))\n    nEs2 <-ifelse(consistency == \"finiteSample\",n-2,n)*Es2(c2)\n}\nelse nEs2 <- n\nc(if (mu.too) mu, sigma0 * sqrt(sum(rho)/nEs2))\n}\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Please explain as much as you can. </p>\n\n<p><strong>EDIT</strong> It's really the idea of a step by step explanation of how you would go about converting a well written (and documented) R code (so at least the foundations are okay) unto an efficient implementation. For example <a href=\"http://www.mdpi.org/entropy/papers/e3020058.pdf\">this</a> paper suggest, assuming that i got it right, that you just get a ML estimator under a suitable reformulation of the problem; MacKey, in his book, says that MaxEnt can give you weird things, and you should't use it even for a starting estimate in a Bayesian inference; etc.. </p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-11-28T13:12:18.827000", "posts_rownum": "posts_4690"}, "posts_1163": {"id": 1207, "owneruserid": 667, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Period detection of a generic time series", "tags": "<time-series><algorithms><frequency><real-time>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>This post is the continuation of another post related to a <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/1142/simple-algorithm-for-online-outlier-detection-of-a-generic-time-series\">generic method for outlier detection in time series</a>.\nBasically, at this point I'm interested in a robust way to discover the periodicity/seasonality of a generic time series affected by a lot of noise.\nFrom a developer point of view, I would like a simple interface such as:</p>\n\n<p><code>unsigned int discover_period(vector<double> v);</code></p>\n\n<p>Where <code>v</code> is the array containing the samples, and the return value is the period of the signal.\nThe main point is that, again, I can't make any assumption regarding the analyzed signal.\nI already tried an approach based on the signal autocorrelation (detecting the peaks of a correlogram), but it's not robust as I would like.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-04T00:32:13.360000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1163"}, "posts_1121": {"id": 1164, "owneruserid": 438, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1170, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Why haven't robust (and resistant) statistics replaced classical techniques?", "tags": "<model-selection><nonparametric><outliers><robust><philosophical>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>When solving business problems using data, it's common that at least one key assumption that under-pins classical statistics is invalid. Most of the time, no one bothers to check those assumptions so you never actually know.</p>\n<p>For instance, that so many of the common web metrics are "long-tailed" (relative to the normal distribution) is, by now, so well documented that we take it for granted. Another example, online communities--even in communities with thousands of members, it's well-documented that by far the largest share of contribution to/participation in many of these community is attributable to a minuscule group of 'super-contributors.' (E.g., a few months ago, just after the SO API was made available in beta, a <em>StackOverflow</em> member published a brief analysis from data he collected through the API; his conclusion--<em>less than one percent of the SO members account for most of the activity on SO</em> (presumably asking questions, and answering them), another 1-2% accounted for the rest, and the overwhelming majority of the members do nothing).</p>\n<p>Distributions of that sort--again more often the rule rather than the exception--are often best modeled with a <em>power law</em> density function. For these type of distributions, even the central limit theorem is problematic to apply.</p>\n<p>So given the abundance of populations like this of interest to analysts, and given that classical models perform demonstrably poorly on these data, and given that robust and resistant methods have been around for a while (at least 20 years, I believe)--why are they not used more often? (I am also wondering why <em>I</em> don't use them more often, but that's not really a question for <em>CrossValidated</em>.)</p>\n<p>Yes I know that there are textbook chapters devoted entirely to robust statistics and I know there are (a few) R Packages (<em>robustbase</em> is the one I am familiar with and use), etc.</p>\n<p>And yet given the obvious advantages of these techniques, they are often clearly the better tools for the job--<em><strong>why are they not used much more often</strong></em>? Shouldn't we expect to see robust (and resistant) statistics used far more often (perhaps even presumptively) compared with the classical analogs?</p>\n<p>The only substantive (i.e., technical) explanation I have heard is that robust techniques (likewise for resistant methods) lack the power/sensitivity of classical techniques. I don't know if this is indeed true in some cases, but I do know it is not true in many cases.</p>\n<p>A final word of preemption: yes I know this question does not have a single demonstrably correct answer; very few questions on this Site do. Moreover, this question is a genuine inquiry; it's not a pretext to advance a point of view--I don't have a point of view here, just a question for which i am hoping for some insightful answers.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-03T07:49:34.003000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1121"}, "posts_8496": {"id": 9131, "owneruserid": 253, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 9144, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Obtaining a formula for prediction limits in a linear model (i.e.: prediction intervals)", "tags": "<r><regression><predictive-models><prediction-interval>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>Let's take the following example:</p>\n\n<pre><code>set.seed(342)\nx1 <- runif(100)\nx2 <- runif(100)\ny <- x1+x2 + 2*x1*x2 + rnorm(100)\nfit <- lm(y~x1*x2)\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>This creates a model of y based on x1 and x2, using a OLS regression. k, \\lambda, \\theta) = \\frac{k}{\\lambda} \\left( \\frac{x-\\theta}{\\lambda} \\right)^{k-1} \\exp\\left( - \\left(\\frac{x-\\theta}{\\lambda} \\right)^k \\right) \\chi_{x \\ge \\theta}(x)\r\n$$</p>\n\n<p>Consider $ \\mathbb{E}\\left( -\\partial_\\theta^2 \\log f(x; Even better, can someone suggest a simple example code for how to run and analyse this in R (e.g: \"non-parametric repeated measures multiway anova\") ?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-04T20:01:07.787000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1216"}, "posts_1217": {"id": 1268, "owneruserid": 170, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1393, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "SVD dimensionality reduction for time series of different length", "tags": "<time-series><machine-learning><pca><data-transformation><multivariate-analysis>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I am using Singular Value Decomposition as a dimensionality reduction technique.</p>\n\n<p>Given <code>N</code> vectors of dimension <code>D</code>, the idea is to represent the features in a transformed space of uncorrelated dimensions, which condenses most of the information of the data in the eigenvectors of this space in a decreasing order of importance.</p>\n\n<p>Now I am trying to apply this procedure to time series data. My first thought was to pad the matrix with zeros by building a <code>num-by-maxDim</code> matrix and filling the empty spaces with zeros, but I'm not so sure if that is the correct way.</p>\n\n<p>My question is how do you the SVD approach of dimensionality reduction to time series of different length? Alternatively are there any other similar methods of eigenspace representation usually used with time series?</p>\n\n<p>Below is a piece of MATLAB code to illustrate the idea:</p>\n\n<pre><code>X = randn(100,4);                       % data matrix of size N-by-dim\n\nX0 = bsxfun(@minus, X, mean(X));        % standarize\n[U S V] = svd(X0,0);                    % SVD\nvariances = diag(S).^2 / (size(X,1)-1); % variances along eigenvectors\n\nKEEP = 2;                               % number of dimensions to keep\nnewX = U(:,1:KEEP)*S(1:KEEP,1:KEEP);    % reduced and transformed data\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>(I am coding mostly in MATLAB, but I'm comfortable enough to read R/Python/.. as well)</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-04T20:51:04.053000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1217"}, "posts_1507": {"id": 1576, "owneruserid": 776, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1579, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What are the differences between Factor Analysis and Principal Component Analysis?", "tags": "<pca><factor-analysis>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>It seems that a number of the statistical packages that I use wrap these two concepts together. A real example would be incredibly useful. </p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-12T03:46:05.987000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1507"}, "posts_1565": {"id": 1637, "owneruserid": 199, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1639, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "If the t-test and the ANOVA for two groups are equivalent, why aren't their assumptions equivalent?", "tags": "<distributions><regression><normality-assumption><t-test><anova>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I'm sure I've got this completely wrapped round my head, but I just can't figure it out.</p>\n\n<p>The t-test compares two normal distributions using the Z distribution. How can they be equivalent if they don't even assume the same things about the data?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-13T09:41:13.160000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1565"}, "posts_1633": {"id": 1709, "owneruserid": 198, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1717, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to draw a probable outcome from a distribution?", "tags": "<distributions><data-visualization>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I have collected positional data. To visualize the data, I'd like to draw a 'typical' outcome of an experiment. </p>\n\n<p>The data comes from a few hundred experiments, where I identify a variable number of objects at different positions relative to the origin in 2D. Thus, I can calculate the average number of objects, as well as estimate the empirical distribution of the objects. A plot of the 'typical' outcome would then have the average (or possibly mode) number of objects, say, 5. What I'm not sure about is where to position these 5 objects.</p>\n\n<p>To simplify the problem, assume that the data follows a 2D normal distribution. If I were just to randomly draw 5 points from the distribution, I might get one point at [3,3], which would be a very rare outcome, and would thus not reflect the 'typical', or 'average' outcome. However, just drawing 5 points at [0,0] would also not make sense - even though [0,0] is the average position of the objects, 5 overlapping points are not an 'average' outcome of the process, either.</p>\n\n<p>In other words, how can I get a 'likely' draw from a distribution?</p>\n\n<hr>\n\n<p><strong>EDIT</strong> </p>\n\n<p>It looks like I should mention <em>why</em> I don't want to use the usual methods (like a 2D smoothed histogram, or plotting all the many points) to look at the 2D distribution. </p>\n\n<ol>\n<li>The objects (which are vesicles (i.e. little spheres) inside cells) vary in number, size and position (distribution of the distance from the cell center, amount of clustering). I would like to display all these features in one graph. Since there are several hundred cells containing many vesicles each, it is not very useful to combine them all in a single plot. I am well aware that I could use a multipanel graph showing the distributions of all parameters, but this would be a lot less intuitive. </li>\n<li>I would like to show a 'typical' cell that shows all the salient features that characterize a specific phenotype. This way, if I want to image a particular phenotype in a mixed population, I know what kind of cell I'm looking for.</li>\n<li>I think such a plot would be a cool way to display a lot of information at once, and I just want to try.</li>\n</ol>\n\n<p>Maybe it would be clearer If I said that I want to simulate a likely experimental result based on my measurements?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-15T14:30:23.597000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1633"}, "posts_1799": {"id": 1881, "owneruserid": 582, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1901, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Analysis of cross correlation between point-processes", "tags": "<point-process><cross-correlation>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I would like an advice on a analysis method I am using, to know if it it statistically sound.</p>\n<p>I have measured two point processes <span class=\"math-container\">$T^1 = t^1_1, t^1_2, \\ldots, t^1_n$</span> and <span class=\"math-container\">$T^2 = t^2_1, t^2_2, \\ldots, t^2_m$</span> and I want to determine if the events in <span class=\"math-container\">$T^1$</span> are somehow correlated to the events in <span class=\"math-container\">$T^2$</span>.</p>\n<p>One of the methods that I have found in the literature is that of constructing a cross-correlation histogram: for each <span class=\"math-container\">$t^1_n$</span> we find the delay to all the events of <span class=\"math-container\">$T^2$</span> that fall in a given window of time (before and after <span class=\"math-container\">$t^1_n$</span>), and then we construct an histogram of all these delays.</p>\n<p>If the two processes are not correlated I would expect a flat histogram, as the probability of having an event in <span class=\"math-container\">$T^2$</span> after (or before) an event in <span class=\"math-container\">$T^1$</span> is equal at all delays. On the other hand if there is a peak in the histogram, this suggests that the two point process are somehow influencing each other (or, at least, have some common input).</p>\n<p>Now, this is nice and good, but how do I determine whether the histograms do have a peak (I have to say that for my particular set of data they're clearly flat, but still it would be nice to have a statistical way of confirming that)?</p>\n<p>So, here what I've done: I've repeated the process of generating the histogram for several (1000) times keeping <span class=\"math-container\">$T^1$</span> as it is and using a "shuffled" version of <span class=\"math-container\">$T^2$</span>.\nTo shuffle <span class=\"math-container\">$T^2$</span> I calculate the intervals between all the events, shuffle them and sum them to reconstitute a new point process. In R I simply do this with:</p>\n<pre><code>times2.swp <- cumsum(sample(diff(times2)))\n</code></pre>\n<p>So, I end up with 1000 new histogram, that show me the density of events in <span class=\"math-container\">$T^{2*}$</span> compared to <span class=\"math-container\">$T^1$</span>.</p>\n<p>For each bin of these histogram (they're all binned in the same way) I calculate the density of 95% of the histogram. In other words I'm saying, for instance: at time delay 5 ms, in 95% of the shuffled point processes there is a probability x of finding an event in <span class=\"math-container\">$T^{2*}$</span> after an event in <span class=\"math-container\">$T^1$</span>.</p>\n<p>I would then take this 95% value for all of the time delays and use it as some "confidence limit" (probably this is not the correct term) so that anything that goes over this limit in the original histogram can be considered a "true peak".</p>\n<p><strong>Question 1</strong>: is this method statistically correct? If not how would you tackle this problem?</p>\n<p><strong>Question 2</strong>: another thing that I want to see is whether there is a "longer" type of correlation of my data. For instance there may be similar changes in the rate of events in the two point processes (note that they may have quite different rates), but I'm not sure how to do that. I thought of creating an "envelope" of each point process using some sort of smoothing kernel and then performing a cross-correlation analysis of the two envelopes. Could you suggest any other possible type of analysis?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-19T06:42:15.767000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1799"}, "posts_1801": {"id": 1883, "owneruserid": 273, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Revolutions in statistics for the last 50 years?", "tags": "<history>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>What areas of statistics have been substantially revolutionised in the last 50 years? About 10 years ago, Hyndman with colleagues revolutionised the area of exponential smoothing. About XX years ago, ... </p>\n\n<p>How do I possibly continue the list, with years and names please? By statistics I mean its all four types from Bartholomew's 1995 presidential address, Chambers's greater and lesser statistics together, as featuring in Hand's recent presidential address on 'Modern statistics' and so on - anything professionally relevant.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-19T07:00:53.840000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1801"}, "posts_2268": {"id": 2356, "owneruserid": 887, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Are there any examples where Bayesian credible intervals are obviously inferior to frequentist confidence intervals", "tags": "<bayesian><confidence-interval>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>A recent question on the difference between confidence and credible intervals led me to start re-reading Edwin Jaynes' article on that topic:</p>\n\n<p>Jaynes, E. T., 1976. `Confidence Intervals vs Bayesian Intervals,' in Foundations of Probability Theory, Statistical Inference, and Statistical Theories of Science, W. L. Harper and C. A. Hooker (eds.), D. Reidel, Dordrecht, p. 175; (<a href=\"http://bayes.wustl.edu/etj/articles/confidence.pdf\">pdf</a>)</p>\n\n<p>In the abstract, Jaynes writes:</p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p>...we exhibit the Bayesian and orthodox solutions to six common statistical problems involving confidence intervals (including significance tests based on the same reasoning). The idea is to provide a LR for each effect that is analogous to the test of that effect that the ANOVA achieves. For example, the LR for main effect represents the comparison of a null model to a model that includes the main effect, the LR for an interaction represents the comparison of a model that includes both component main effects versus a model that includes both main effects <em>and</em> their interaction, etc.</p>\n\n<p>Now, my understanding of LR computation comes from <a href=\"http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15732688\" rel=\"noreferrer\">Glover & Dixon</a> (<a href=\"http://www.thinkingaboutthinking.org/wp-content/uploads/2010/09/Glover-Dixon-2004-Likelihood-ratios-a-simple-and-flexible-statistic-for-empirical-psychologists.pdf\" rel=\"noreferrer\">PDF</a>), which covers basic computations as well as corrections for complexity, and the appendix to <a href=\"http://rads.stackoverflow.com/amzn/click/0521009138\" rel=\"noreferrer\">Bortolussi & Dixon</a> (<a href=\"http://www.thinkingaboutthinking.org/wp-content/uploads/2010/09/Dixon-Unknown-Evaluating-Evidence-Appendix-to-Psychonarratology.pdf\" rel=\"noreferrer\">appendix PDF</a>), which covers computations involving repeated-measures variables. To test my understanding, I developed <a href=\"https://spreadsheets.google.com/ccc?key=0Ap2N_aeyRMGHdHJxUnVNeEl5VGtvY1RVLVc5UjU4Vmc&hl=en\" rel=\"noreferrer\">this spreadsheet</a>, which takes the dfs & SSs from an example ANOVA (generated from a 2*2*3*4 design using fake data) and steps through the computation of the LR for each effect.</p>\n\n<p>I would really appreciate it if someone with a little more confidence with such computation could take a look and make sure I did everything correctly. For those that prefer abstract code, <a href=\"http://gist.github.com/590789\" rel=\"noreferrer\">here is the R code</a> implementing the update to ezANOVA() (see esp. lines 15-95).</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-21T23:40:39.317000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2805"}, "posts_2814": {"id": 2966, "owneruserid": 183, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2967, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Estimating latent performance potential based on a sequence of observations", "tags": "<time-series><bayesian><latent-variable><isotonic>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p><strong>Context</strong></p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>you have 200 observations of an individual's running time for the 100 metres measured once a day for 200 days.</li>\n<li>Assume the individual was not a runner before commencement of practice</li>\n<li>Based on the observed data and the 199 other observations, you want to estimate the latent time it would take the individual to run if they (a) applied maximal effort; and (b) had a reasonably good run for them (i.e., no major problems with the run; but still a typical run). Let's call this <strong>latent potential</strong>.</li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>Of course, the actual data would not measure latent potential directly. The data would be noisy:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>Times would vary from run to run</li>\n<li>On some days the individual would be particularly slow because of one or more possible problems (e.g., tripping at the start, getting a cramp half way through, not putting in much effort). Such problems would result in  massive outliers</li>\n<li>On some days the individual would be slower than you'd expect, perhaps because of more minor issues.</li>\n<li>In general, with practice the runner would be expected to get faster in latent potential.</li>\n<li>In rare cases, it is possible for the runner to get slower in latent potential (e.g., injury)</li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>The implications of this:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>The occasional slow time might provide minimal information on what the individual is capable of. </li>\n<li>A fast time for the individual suggests that the individual is capable of such a fast time, but a small amount of this fast time might be good fortune on the day (e.g., the right wind, a little luck on the start).</li>\n</ul>\n\n<p><strong>The question:</strong>\nThus, how could one estimate  latent potential at each of the 200 time points based on the available data and a few assumptions about the nature of running times?</p>\n\n<p><strong>Initial Thoughts:</strong> I imagine there would be some form of Bayesian approach that combined the available information and assumptions to form an estimate, but I'm not sure where to look for such models. I'm also not quite clear how the effectiveness of such a model would be evaluated.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-22T10:32:51.633000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2814"}, "posts_3967": {"id": 4211, "owneruserid": null, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 4213, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": "user88", "title": "How to visualize 3D contingency matrix?", "tags": "<data-visualization><contingency-tables>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I have a data like this:</p>\n\n<pre><code>> table(A,B,C)\n, , C = FALSE\n\n       B\nA       FALSE TRUE\n  FALSE   177   42\n  TRUE      6    8\n\n, , C = TRUE\n\n       B\nA       FALSE TRUE\n  FALSE     5   31\n  TRUE      4   10\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>How can I plot this on a single graph, possibly without imposing any hierarchy?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-11-04T16:11:48.220000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3967"}, "posts_4783": {"id": 5081, "owneruserid": 264, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Java library for Bayesian Networks", "tags": "<bayesian><bayesian-network><software><java>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>As the headline suggest, I am looking for a java library for learning and inference of Bayesian Networks. Sometimes the parameter of interest is the inverse of the data or the ratio of two variables.    </p>\n\n<p><strong>Examples:</strong> </p>\n\n<ol>\n<li>the ratio of two normally distributed variables:\n<ul>\n<li>data: mean and sd for percent nitrogen and percent carbon </li>\n<li>parameter: ratio of carbon to nitrogen.</li>\n</ul></li>\n<li>the inverse of a normally distributed variable:\n<ul>\n<li>data: mass/area</li>\n<li>parameter: area/mass</li>\n</ul></li>\n</ol>\n\n<p>My current approach is to use simulation:</p>\n\n<p>e.g. for a set of percent carbon and nitrogen data with means: xbar.n,c, variance: se.n,c, and sample size: n.n, n.c:</p>\n\n<pre><code>set.seed(1)\nper.c <- rnorm(100000, xbar.c, se.c*n.c) # percent C\nper.n <- rnorm(100000, xbar.n, se.n*n.n) # percent N\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>I want to parameterize ratio.cn = perc.c/perc.n</p>\n\n<pre><code># parameter of interest\nratio.cn <- perc.c / perc.n\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Then choose the best fit distributions with range $0 \\rightarrow \\infty$ for my prior </p>\n\n<pre><code>library(MASS)\ndist.fig <- list()\nfor(dist.i in c('gamma', 'lognormal', 'weibull')) {\n    dist.fit[[dist.i]] <- fitdist(ratio.cn, dist.i)\n}\n</code></pre>\n\n<p><strong>Question:</strong>\nIs this a valid approach? "title": "Yates' continuity correction in confidence interval returned by prop.test", "tags": "<r><confidence-interval><yates-correction>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>This is the 0.4196787 0.5008409 \n</code></pre>\n\n<p>I tried to reproduce it, reading the code under prop.test. Here is a simplified way to get those two limits</p>\n\n<pre><code>ESTIMATE <- x/n\nYATES <- 0.5\nconf.level <- 0.95\nz <- qnorm((1 + conf.level)/2)\nYATES <- min(YATES, abs(x - n * p)) \nz22n <- z^2/(2 * n)\np.c <- ESTIMATE + YATES/n\n(p.c + z22n + z * sqrt(p.c * (1 - p.c)/n + z22n/(2 * n)))/(1 + 2 * z22n)\n[1] 0.5008409\np.c <- ESTIMATE - YATES/n\n(p.c + z22n - z * sqrt(p.c * (1 - p.c)/n + z22n/(2 * n)))/(1 + 2 * z22n)\n[1] 0.4196787\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Can you explain to me why the underlying probability of success (p) is used in line 5? or maybe you could suggest where can I find more info about this YATES correction that affects the ESTIMATE.</p>\n\n<p>Thank you</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-12-07T10:10:47.810000", "posts_rownum": "posts_4902"}, "posts_5035": {"id": 5344, "owneruserid": 199, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 5345, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to choose nlme or lme4 R library for mixed effects models?", "tags": "<r><mixed-model><lme4-nlme>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I have fit a few mixed effects models (particularly longitudinal models) using <code>lme4</code> in <code>R</code> but would like to really master the models and the code that goes with them.</p>\n<p>However, before diving in with both feet (and buying some books) I want to be sure that I am learning the right library. I’m using the <a href=\"http://frank.mtsu.edu/~dkfuller/notes302/welcht.pdf\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Welch T-test</a> because the variance and/or sample size between benchmarks is most likely different. The critical value is pulled from a T-distribution table at 95% confidence <em>(two-sided)</em>.</p>\n\n<p>The Welch formula is pretty straight-forward, but I am fuzzy on interpreting a significant result. "posts_10510"}, "posts_10983": {"id": 11887, "owneruserid": 5003, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 15400, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What experimental design is this?", "tags": "<anova><repeated-measures><experiment-design>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I collect blood from <em>one</em> human (donor), separate leukocytes and put $2\\times10^6$ of them per each well of five:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>well 1: $2\\times10^6$ Lk (leukocytes)</li>\n<li>well 2: $2\\times10^6$ Lk    </li>\n<li>well 3: $2\\times10^6$ Lk    </li>\n<li>well 4: $2\\times10^6$ Lk  </li>\n<li>well 5: $2\\times10^6$ Lk</li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>(Lk consists of a mix of different sets of cells and one of them are lymphocytes (Lph)).</p>\n\n<p>Then I incubated the cells under different conditions (with the following substances in the same concentration (with the exception of well #1, of course)):</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>well 1: saline (serves as a zero control)</li>\n<li>well 2: substance A (is a native compound) </li>\n<li>well 3: substance B (is a chemically modified analogue of A)</li>\n<li>well 4: substance C (is a chemically modified analogue' of A)</li>\n<li>well 5: substance D (is a chemically modified analogue'' of A)</li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>Then I incubate the leucocytes for 24 hours.</p>\n\n<p>Then I run FACS and get percentages of lymphocytes expressing a receptor (CD69) of interest (Lph') (where the percentages is the ratio of Lph' to all Lph).</p>\n\n<p>Then I repeated the experiment 7 times: i.e. totally I collected blood from 8 different donors (so $n = 8$).</p>\n\n<p>With this experiment I want to know:<br>\nDoes a structure of a molecule affect the percentage/proportion of <em>activated</em> lymphocytes (Lph') (i.e. Lph bearing CD69 molecule)?</p>\n\n<p>My example data (<em>in percentages, %</em>) are:<br>\n<strong><pre>\nDonorID  cntrl  substanceA  substanceB  substanceC  substanceD</strong> \n20       5.1    12.42       10.10       9.58        8.54 \n21       4.07   9.96        14.12       10.79       12.24 \n22       3.94   4.92        13.04       15.96       9.37 \n25       0.60   3.24        8.94        0.61        3.62 \n26       1.72   13.96       2.48        3.44        3.12 \n27       0.53   3.36        1.40        4.00        0.81 \n28       0.97   3.88        2.33        3.77        3.31 \n31       0.15   4.05        1.45        2.44        1.47 \n32       0.58   1.92        2.47        2.33        4.92 \n33       1.02   6.03        4.40        4.80        3.88</pre></p>\n\n<hr>\n\n<p>SUMMARY:  </p>\n\n<p>So the experimental design can be characterized by the following terms:  </p>\n\n<ul>\n<li><em>ANOVA</em> as more than 2 groups are tested;  </li>\n<li><em>RM</em> as the statistical/experimental unit (\"Lph\") for every case is under different conditions;  </li>\n<li><em>one-way</em> there is one <em>fixed (within-subject) factor / independent variable</em> (\"conditioins\") with 5 levels; if I'm not mistaken in the light of linear mixed models the \"DonorID\" might be interpreted as an additional <em>random factor</em> (\"donor\").  </li>\n</ul>\n\n<hr>\n\n<p><em>Many thanks for the answers!</em></p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-06-14T01:07:19.033000", "posts_rownum": "posts_10983"}, "posts_11464": {"id": 12748, "owneruserid": 5311, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Looking for help identifing outliers in a pilot study to guide future hypothesis testing", "tags": "<outliers>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I am looking to study a particular type of error on a cognitive test to evaluate for potential clinical implications.  As there is no existing research on this variable, I would like to run a pilot evaluation on a relatively large pool of subject data from our clinic (feasibly this would be about 200 subjects) to see if there are any trends to guide hypothesis testing in future studies (e.g., are patients from a particular clinical population more likely to make this type of error than those from another population).  The data is such that a patient could potentially make 0-15 of these errors, although it's likely that there will be a strong tendency toward the 0-5 range.  </p>\n\n<p>Essentially, I am looking to identify subjects from within this pool who are making a relatively higher rate of these errors.  Is there a recognized format for doing this type of pilot work?  Barring that, what would your recommendations be?  </p>\n\n<p>This is obviously very exploratory, so I feel like I would have some latitude in defining what constitutes an 'outlier' for the purposes of this study, but any references or suggestions would be much appreciated.  </p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-07-07T02:14:59.487000", "posts_rownum": "posts_11464"}, "posts_12651": {"id": 13757, "owneruserid": 5647, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How do I weigh several variables at two levels to create an overall composite variable score?", "tags": "<correlation><latent-variable><composite>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<h3>Context</h3>\n\n<p>I am trying to find the <strong>correlation between two latent variables</strong>. Let's call them A and B. </p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>A has two dimensions. Let's call them Dimension 1 and 2. </li>\n<li>B also has two dimensions. Let's call them Dimension 3 and 4. </li>\n<li>The four dimensions (1, 2, 3 and 4) have several indicators each. Let's call them (a) and (b) for Dimension 1, (c), (d) and (e) for Dimension 2, (f) and (g) for Dimension 3 and (h), (i) and (j) for Dimension 4.</li>\n<li>I have measured the ten indicators (a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i and j) on a likert scale or else using cardinal numbers (e.g. one, two, three, four, etc.).</li>\n<li>I have then weighted the indicators using the likert scale codes that I created (e.g. 0 = not important, 1 = low importance, 2 = medium importance, 3 = high importance and 4 = absolute importance)</li>\n<li>I have then added the scores for all indicators to arrive at the dimension scores. This is my first weighting.</li>\n<li>I have then said that each dimension contributes 50% to the composite score of A or B and have standardised the dimension scores to 50% each. This is my second weighting. </li>\n<li>Finally I added the dimension scores to arrive at the composite score. </li>\n</ul>\n\n<p><strong>To give an example:</strong></p>\n\n<p>If I have a score of 2 for (a) and 3 for (b) then my total for Dimension 1 is 5. Similarly, if I have a score of 3 for (c), 4 for (d) and 2 for (e), then my total for Dimension 2 is 9. The score of 5 and 9 are the dimension scores, based on likert scale weights.</p>\n\n<p>As I said that each dimension contributes 50%, I have divided the obtained score by the total score for each dimension and multiplied it by 50%. So I have got the following:</p>\n\n<p>(2+3)/8 (remember this is based on two likert scale responses so the maximum score is 4 plus 4) x 50% = 0.31</p>\n\n<p>(3+4+2)/12 (remember this is based on three likert scale responses so the maximum score is 4 plus 4 plus 4) x 50% = 0.38</p>\n\n<p>I then added 0.31 and 0.38 and got 0.69. This is my composite score for Composite Variable A (which has 2 dimensions and 5 indicators; 2 for the first dimension and 3 for the second dimension). </p>\n\n<p>To make it comprehensible, I have multipled 0.69 by 100 to get 69 out of 100 scores. I want to run corrleation on the composite scores of A and B to see the relationship between them.</p>\n\n<p>As you would see, I have <strong>not done any complex statistical modeling</strong> using factor analysis etc but arrived at my final score using a system of subjective weighting based on relative importance (which is aligned to the likert scale coding in the first instance) and equal weighting in the second instance. I have used this approach to keep everything simple. I know it is subjecive weighting but I can justify it to some extent with theory and the rest with commonsense!</p>\n\n<h3>Questions</h3>\n\n<ul>\n<li><p>Am I doing this right? Is this approach robust enough? \n<strong>Remember, I don't want to complicate things!</strong> I am not statistically minded!</p></li>\n<li><p>Can I do correlation analysis on the composite scores of A and B? They are rank scores (based on weights) so is the Spearman Rank Correlation the way to go for the analysis? </p></li>\n</ul>\n", "creationdate": "2011-08-02T14:04:01.353000", "posts_rownum": "posts_12651"}, "posts_12779": {"id": 13902, "owneruserid": 5647, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How do I compare correlation coefficients of the same variables across different groups?", "tags": "<correlation><hypothesis-testing>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I am testing the correlation between Variable A and Variable B by gender and marital status.</p>\n\n<p>So I have the coefficients for males and females and single, married and other.</p>\n\n<p>I want to compare the correlation coefficient of male with female.</p>\n\n<p>Similarly, I want to compare the correlation coefficient of single with marrried and with other.</p>\n\n<p>Finally, I want to compare the correlation coefficient of single male with single female, married male with married female and other male and other female. I have these coefficients too.</p>\n\n<p><strong>What is the easiest way of making this comparison?</strong></p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-08-05T12:25:06.180000", "posts_rownum": "posts_12779"}, "posts_13065": {"id": 14219, "owneruserid": 3301, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How well does R scale to text classification tasks?", "tags": "<r><machine-learning><svm><text-mining><random-forest>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I am trying to get upto speed with R. Some additional pointers (to examples, sample code etc.) would be icing on the cake.</p>\n\n<p>EDIT 3: First off, thanks everyone for your comments. And secondly, I apologize, perhaps I should have given more context for the problem. I am new to R but not so much to text classification. I have already done pre-processing (stemming, stopword removal, tf-idf conversion etc.) on my some part of my data using <a href=\"http://tm.r-forge.r-project.org/\">tm</a> package, just to get a feel for things. tm was so slow even on about 200docs that I got concerned about scalability. Then I started playing with FSelector and even that was really slow. And that's the point at which I made my OP.</p>\n\n<p>EDIT 4: It just occurred to me that I have 10 classes and about ~300 training documents per class, and I am in fact building the termXdoc matrix out of the entire training set resulting in very high dimensionality. How does it compare in terms of accuracy to the usual multi-class implementation?    </p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-08-13T16:52:34.583000", "posts_rownum": "posts_13065"}, "posts_2322": {"id": 2410, "owneruserid": 253, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2411, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Can CART models be made robust?", "tags": "<regression><classification><robust><cart>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>A colleague in my office said to me today \"Tree models aren't good because they get caught by extreme observations\".</p>\n\n<p>A search here resulted in <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/1292/what-is-the-weak-side-of-decision-trees\">this thread</a> that basically supports the claim.</p>\n\n<p>Which leads me to the question - under what situation can a CART model be robust, and how is that shown?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-06T14:59:09.557000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2322"}, "posts_13080": {"id": 14237, "owneruserid": 5383, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 14283, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Normalisation for regression", "tags": "<regression><data-transformation>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>First off, I know little about statistics, so some of this question may seem naive.</p>\n\n<p>I'm trying to perform linear regression to model the relationship between x and y where:</p>\n\n<p>-x is a company's daily stock volume on a date</p>\n\n<p>-y is variable that is taken from the same date, however is something unrelated to stock volume.  It is the volume of activity on that wikipedia for that company.</p>\n\n<p>I assume that the variables need normalising.  Specifically, x needs to be normalised as overall index volume fluctuates.  My first thoughts were to divide the daily volume by the total index volume.  I'll do the same with the y variable.  </p>\n\n<p>I just wondered if this seems sensible?  Thanks</p>\n\n<p>EDIT:</p>\n\n<p>I've just noticed a typo in the question, the Y variable description has changed.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-08-14T11:22:31.383000", "posts_rownum": "posts_13080"}, "posts_13904": {"id": 15168, "owneruserid": 6096, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 15233, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Graphing effect size for coefficient of determination", "tags": "<data-visualization>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>If I have a significant correlation coefficient of r=.80 between Variable A and B, I can work out the effect size (coefficient of determination) by squaring it, which is 64%. </p>\n\n<p>I want to graph this in the simplest way possibe (given my non-statistical target audience). Can I use a 100% stacked bar graph for this purpose. This will show Variable B as 100% and on top of it would be Variable A which would be 64%. I can then graphically say that 64% of variance in Variable B can be attributed to Variable A. (Conversely, I can also graphically say that I am unsure of the remaining 36% of Variable B)  </p>\n\n<p>The appeal of this approach for me is that I can show the effect size between A and B on a number of variables (e.g. gender, age, education) in one graph. This will also make a colourful presentation (which is good for a non statistical target audience!).</p>\n\n<p>I have seen some textbooks showing two circles, each representing a variable (e.g. A and B). The part of the circles that overlaps illustrates the effect size. I thought doing a 100% stacked bar graph was a better way.</p>\n\n<p><strong>From the discussion below, it appears that the scatterplot is the way to go on this matter. However, how do I show 64% on a scatterplot?</strong></p>\n\n<p>I think the point is being missed in the discussion below. What ways exist to show the two methods are equivalent (or not).</p>\n\n<p>I'm thinking that plotting the results from a number of samples measured by both methods on a scatter graph is a good first step, but are there any good statistical methods ?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-22T21:15:52.347000", "posts_rownum": "posts_515"}, "posts_1615": {"id": 1687, "owneruserid": 937, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1762, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Applied statistics to find the minimum load for power factor floor", "tags": "<probability><standard-deviation>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>The problem I’m trying to solve is “How do I figure out how much gunpowder should I put into a cartridge so that I can give myself a good probability of making the minimum power factor?”</p>\n\n<p>I compete in USPSA/IPSC which requires that a competitors rounds make a minimum power factor. Power Factor is computed to be the FLOOR(average bullet velocity * bullet weight) / 1000) where velocity is in feet per second, and bullet weight is in grains. Note the use of FLOOR. No rounding is done. Only the integral part of the computation is used. The higher the power factor, the higher the felt recoil and harder it is to quickly do follow up shots. Since the sport is about firing shots as quickly and as accurately as possible, the lower the recoil the better.</p>\n\n<p>Different divisions within the sport have different power factor floors, but the particular division I compete in has a minimum of 165 Power Factor. The bullets I use are 180 gn bullets, and vary by about +/- 0.2 gn and is normally distributed. </p>\n\n<p>What makes this an interesting problem (and move it out of my meager stats and probability skills) is the testing procedure during a major match. Random sample of 8 rounds are collected. Of the 8 rounds, one is taken apart and the bullet is weighed for use in the formula above. Next, 3 rounds are fired and the average velocity is used. If the resulting power factor is below the minimum, then another 3 rounds are fired. The average of the 3 fastest velocities from the 6 rounds fired is now used to compute the power factor. If the resulting power factor is still below the floor, then the shooter has the option of having the last round taken apart and weighed or the last round fired. If the bullet is taken apart and it is heavier than the first bullet, the heavier weight is used to compute the power factor. If the last round is fired, the average of the 3 fastest velocities from the 7 rounds fired is used to compute the power factor.</p>\n\n<p>To add spice to this problem, not all chronographs used to measure bullet velocities are created equal. The chronograph industry acknowledges that there can be as much as +/- 4% variance between chronographs of different brands. Even more interesting is that the rules allow for the same chronograph used for a particular match to have +/- 4% variance over the duration of a match. I don’t know if either of these 4% variances are normally distributed or not.</p>\n\n<p>With my own chronograph, I test batches of a particular gunpowder load to get the average velocity and standard deviation. After statistical analyses of many different batches, I’ve confirmed that this data is normally distributed.</p>\n\n<p>The way I’m currently determining my minimum load is by finding the load the gives me 165 < FLOOR( target * 179.9 / 1000) where target =  (average velocity - standard deviation) * fudge factor. For fudge factor, I’ve unscientifically chosen 1.04. The 0.04 is the 4% variance between chronographs, but ignores the day-to-day allowable variance. I chose to just subtract just 1 standard deviation because it’ll only be 16% of the time that one bullet will be below the floor. In my mind, the probability of all the first 3 bullets all going below the floor is 0.16^3 which less than half a percent.</p>\n\n<p>My specific questions are: Am I going about computing the target the right way? Should my fudge factor include another 4% for the day-to-day variance allowed? Is the 1 standard deviation too much or too little? How should I write the formula for my target? </p>\n\n<p>Edit:\nAfter Srikant's initial response below let me add a couple of focusing questions and notes.</p>\n\n<p>I understand figuring out the error due to my measurements. Not much problem there unless I get really sloppy with quality control or maintenance. </p>\n\n<p>My grasp of probabilities is weak so please bear with me as I ask about computing probabilities:</p>\n\n<p>1) One of the key issues I need to deal with is figuring out how to correctly compute the probability for the testing process around the 7 rounds. It's pretty straight forward to me for the case of the first 3 rounds: (probability that the round is below the power flaw)^3. How do I account for the next 3 rounds and the last round?</p>\n\n<p>I can see computing the probabilities using combinations of bullets above or below the floor, but it's not quite a binary above or below. Let's assume that 6 rounds have been fired, and the average of the highest 3 rounds is 164.9. If the last round has at least 165.2, then the average of the highest 3 rounds out of 7 will be 165.</p>\n\n<p>2) The other issue I need to deal with is figuring out how to account for the 4% variance between my chrono and the match chrono, and how the match chrono is allowed to drift by 4% from day to day. Do I just assume the worst case and make sure that I'm at least 8% above 165 -- that is my rounds are shooting at least 179 power factor? Or do I try to assume some kind of normal distribution over the two 4% variances?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-14T14:00:16.297000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1615"}, "posts_1072": {"id": 1112, "owneruserid": 652, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1113, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to represent an unbounded variable as number between 0 and 1", "tags": "<normalization>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I want to represent a variable as a number between 0 and 1. Let x be a uniformly distributed random variable, i.e. p(x) = 0 if x < 0 and x ≥1; p(x) = 1 if 0 ≤ x <1.</p>\n\n<p>How would I compute the mean and variance of the variable x?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-09-20T17:34:55.513000", "posts_rownum": "posts_14484"}, "posts_1354": {"id": 1412, "owneruserid": 196, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1414, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Consequences of an improper link function in N alternative forced choice procedures (e.g. 2AFC)?", "tags": "<logistic><link-function>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>Background:  In some cognitive psychology research areas N-alternative forced choice tasks are common.  The most common of these is a two alternative forced choice (2AFC).  This usually takes the form of participants being given a stimulus and asked to make one of two judgement, e.g. the target stimuli is present/absent, the stimulus on the left is the same/different than the the one on the right, etc.  Designs in which the experimental data is from a 2AFC but there is only one data point per subject are rare, but do exist, e.g. some eye-witness identification research.  Since the dependent variable (correct/incorrect) is binary, these experiments are reasonable places to use logistic regression.  </p>\n\n<p>My question is this:  since chance performance is 50% in a 2AFC trial, is it still reasonable to use the standard logistic link function?  Specifically, the logistic function has a minimum value approaching 0% correct, but in practice participants in a 2AFC should be correct at least 50% of the time due to chance.  I imagine the following case in which it may present a problem:  an independent variable is assessing the difficulty of the discrimination (e.g. difficulty 1, easy - 5, hard; please note this is introduced in ordinal terms only for ease of comprehension - for the sake of this discussion consider this variable as being interval) - participants got 50% correct at 5 and 4, 75% correct at 3, 85% correct at 2, and 99% correct at 1.  Would using a standard logistic link function cause us to underestimate the slope? [I think so, but please correct me if I'm wrong, see below]</p>\n\n<p>Edit:  Those who have answered my question so far have expressed that the way in which I set up the problem was unclear.  I'm providing the sample below to help clear things up.</p>\n\n<pre><code>library(psyphy)\nmake.data <- function(zero,one)\n    {\n        return(c(rep(0,zero),rep(1,one)))\n    }\ncenter <- function(x) {return(scale(x,scale=FALSE))}\nlogit.data <- data.frame(Score=c(make.data(50,50),make.data(50,50),make.data(25,75),make.data(15,85),make.data(1,99)), Difficulty=rep(5:1,each=100))\nlogit.data$Difficulty2 <- center(logit.data$Difficulty)^2\nstandard <- glm(Score~center(Difficulty),data=logit.data,family=binomial) #standard link function\nstandard.2 <- glm(Score~center(Difficulty)+Difficulty2,data=logit.data,family=binomial) #standard link function, but better with a quadradic\nrevised.link <- glm(Score~center(Difficulty),data=logit.data,family=binomial(mafc.logit(2)))\nAIC(base)\nAIC(base.2)\nAIC(revised.link)\ncoef(base)\ncoef(base.2)\ncoef(revised.link)\n#plot\nplot(diffs,plogis(coef(standard)[1] +coef(standard)[2]*center(diffs)),xlab=\"Difficulty\",ylab=\"Pr(Correct)\",ylim=c(0,1),col=\"blue\",type=\"l\");abline(.5,0,col=\"Orange\");lines(diffs,plogis(coef(standard.2)[1]+coef(standard.2)[2]*center(diffs)+coef(standard.2)[3]*center(diffs)^2),col=\"Cyan\");lines(diffs,(p2afc(coef(revised.link)[1]+coef(revised.link)[2]*center(diffs))),col=\"Green\");lines(5:1,c(.55,.60,.75,.85,.99),col=\"Black\")\n</code></pre>\n\n<p><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/elxVG.jpg\" alt=\"alt text\"></p>\n\n<p>In the above image the orange horizontal line marks 50% correct responses.  The jagged black line represents the data supplied to the estimation equation (note the values for 4 and 5 disappear behind the orange 50% marker).  The blue line is the equation produced by a standard logistic link.  Note that it estimates below 50% accuracy when discrimination is most difficult (5).  The cyan line is the standard logistic link with a quadratic term.  The green line is a non-standard link that takes into account that the data comes from a 2AFC experiment where performance is very unlikely to fall below 50%.\nNote that the AIC for a model fit using a non-standard link function is superior to the standard logistic link function.  Also note that the slope for the standard equation is less than the slope for the standard equation with the quadratic term (which more accurately reflects the real data).  Thus, using a logistic function blindly on 2AFC data does (at least) appear to underestimate the slope.</p>\n\n<p>Is there a problem with my demonstration that means that I am not seeing what I think I am seeing?  If I'm correct, then what other consequences (if any) are there of using the generic logistic function with 2AFC data [presumably extensible to NAFC cases]?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-08T18:10:40.850000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1354"}, "posts_95": {"id": 97, "owneruserid": 114, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 104, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What are good basic statistics to use for ordinal data?", "tags": "<descriptive-statistics><ordinal-data><likert><faq>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I have some <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordinal_scale#Ordinal_scale\">ordinal data</a> gained from survey questions. My question is about the difference between the two type of data. </p>\n\n<p>When talking about applied statistic methodologies that apply in case 1 can be understood as a rephrasing of methodologies from case 2 through a projection into a finite dimensional subspace of a space of functions, it can be polynomes, splines, wavelet, Fourier, .... and will translate the functional problem into a finite dimensional vectorial problem (since in applied mathematic everything comes to be finite at some point). </p>\n\n<p><strong>My question is:</strong>  can we say that any statistical procedure that applies to functional data  can also be applied (almost directly) to high dimension data and that any procedure dedicated to high dimensional data can be (almost directly) applied to functional data ? </p>\n\n<p>If the answer is no, can you illustrate ?</p>\n\n<p>EDIT/UPDATE with the help of Simon Byrne's answer:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>sparsity (S-sparse assumption, $l^p$ ball and weak $l^p$ ball for $p<1$) is used as a structural assumption in high dimensional statistical analysis. </li>\n<li>\"smoothness\" is used as a structural assumption in functional data analysis. </li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>On the other hand, inverse Fourier transform and inverse wavelet transform are transforming sparcity into smoothness, and smoothness is transformed into sparcity by wavelet and fourier transform.
