To fix ideas, I propose to restrict to the classification framework in very high dimension (more features than observation).</p>\n\n<p><strong>Problem:</strong> Assume that for each variable $i=1,\\dots,p$ you have a measure of importance $T[i]$ than exactly measure the interest of feature $i$ for the classification problem. The problem of selecting a subset of feature to reduce optimally the classification error is then reduced to that of finding the number of features. </p>\n\n<p><strong>Question:</strong> What is the most efficient way to run cross validation in this case (cross validation scheme)? My question is not about how to write the code but on the version of cross validation to use when trying to find the number of selected feature (to minimize the classification error) but how to deal with the high dimension when doing cross validation (hence the problem above may be a bit like a 'toy problem' to discuss CV in high dimension). </p>\n\n<p><strong>Notations:</strong>  $n$ is the size of the learning set, p the number of features (i.e. the dimension of the feature space).  By very high dimension I mean p>>n (for example $p=10000$ and $n=100$). </p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-28T08:15:40.827000", "posts_rownum": "posts_868"}, "posts_999": {"id": 1028, "owneruserid": 608, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to interpret KL divergence quantitatively?", "tags": "<distributions><kullback-leibler><information-geometry>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I am comparing two distributions with KL divergence which returns me a non-standardized number that, according to what I read about this measure, is the amount of information that is required to transform one hypothesis into the other. I have two questions:</p>\n\n<p>a) Is there a way to quantify a KL divergence so that it has a more meaningful interpretation, e.g. like an effect size or a R^2? Any form of standardization?</p>\n\n<p>b) In R, when using KLdiv (flexmix package) one can set the 'esp' value (standard esp=1e-4) that sets all points smaller than esp to some standard in order to provide numerical stability. I have been playing with different esp values and, for my data set, I am getting an increasingly larger KL divergence the smaller a number I pick. What is going on? I would expect that the smaller the esp, the more reliable the results should be since they let more 'real values' become part of the statistic. No? I have to change the esp since it otherwise does not calculate the statistic but simply shows up as NA in the result table ... </p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-30T00:55:20.603000", "posts_rownum": "posts_999"}, "posts_1124": {"id": 1169, "owneruserid": 364, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1171, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "CI for a difference based on independent CIs", "tags": "<confidence-interval>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I'm looking to check my logic here. </p>\n\n<p>Say you measure a quantity in group A, and find the mean is 2 and your 95% confidence interval ranges from 1 to 3. Then you measure the same quantity in group B and find a mean of 4 with a 95% confidence interval that ranges from 3.5 to 4.5. Assuming that A & B are independent, what is the 95% confidence interval for the difference between the groups? Presumably you can compute this using standard t-statistics, but I'd like to know if it's also possible to compute an estimate based on the CI's alone.</p>\n\n<p>I reason that the lower bound of the CI of the difference should be the minimum credible difference between A & B; that is, the lower bound of the interval for B (3.5) minus upper bound of the interval for A (3), which yields a lower bound for the difference of 0.5. Similarly, the upper bound of the CI of the difference should be the maximum credible difference between A & B; that is, the upper bound of the interval for B (4.5) minus lower bound of the interval for A (1), which yields a lower bound for the difference of 3.5. This reasoning thus yields a confidence interval for the difference that ranges from 0.5 to 3.5.</p>\n\n<p>Does that make sense, or is this a case where logic and statistics diverge?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-03T12:20:09.890000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1124"}, "posts_4048": {"id": 4298, "owneruserid": 226, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 4314, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Use of kernel density estimate in Naive Bayes Classifier?", "tags": "<bayesian><kde>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>This question is a follow up to my earlier question <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/4220/probability-distribution-over-1-is-ok\">here</a> \nand is also related, in intent, to <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/3316/statistical-similarity-of-time-series\">this question</a>.</p>\n\n<p>On <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naive_Bayes_classifier\" rel=\"noreferrer\">this wiki page</a> <em>probability density values</em> from an assumed normal distribution for the training set are used to calculate a Bayesian posterior rather than actual probability values. However, if a training set is not normally distributed would it be equally as valid to use a <em>density value</em> taken from the <em>kernel density estimate</em> of the training set to calculate a Bayesian posterior? </p>\n\n<p>In its intended application this <em>kernel density estimate</em> would be taken from a theoretically ideal empirical data set generated by MC techniques. </p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-11-07T21:23:52.657000", "posts_rownum": "posts_4048"}, "posts_1237": {"id": 1289, "owneruserid": 760, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Visualizing multiple \"histograms\" (bar-charts)", "tags": "<pca><data-visualization><histogram><barplot>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I am having difficulties to select the right way to visualize data. Let's say we have <strong>bookstores</strong> that sells <strong>books</strong>, and every book has at least one <strong>category</strong>.</p>\n<p>For a bookstore, if we count all the categories of books, we acquire a histogram that shows the number of books that falls into a specific category for that bookstore.</p>\n<p>I want to visualize the bookstore behavior, I want to see if they favor a category over other categories. I don't want to see if they are favoring sci-fi all together, but I want to see if they are treating every category equally or not.</p>\n<p>I have ~1M bookstores.</p>\n<p>I have thought of 4 methods:</p>\n<ol>\n<li><p>Sample the data, show only 500 bookstore's histograms. Show them in 5 separate pages using 10x10 grid. Example of a 4x4 grid:</p>\n<p><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/LAOjc.png2.\" alt=\"multiple histograms 1\" /></p>\n</li>\n<li><p>Same as #1. But this time sort x axis values according to their count desc, so if there is a favoring it will be seen easily.</p>\n</li>\n<li><p>Imagine putting the histograms in #2 together like a deck and showing them in 3D. Something like this:<br />\n<img src=\"https://web.archive.org/web/20170712133139/https://www.statsoft.com/textbook/popups/popup110.gif\" alt=\"3D histogram\" /></p>\n</li>\n<li><p>Instead of using third axis suing color to represent colors, so using a heatmap (2D histogram):\n<img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/rHxg1.png\" alt=\"2D histogram\" /><br />\nIf generally bookstores prefer some categories to others it will be displayed as a nice gradient from left to right.</p>\n</li>\n</ol>\n<p>Do you have any other visualization ideas/tools to represent multiple histograms?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-05T10:03:34.997000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1237"}, "posts_1266": {"id": 1324, "owneruserid": 1356, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1326, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Parametric techniques for n-related samples", "tags": "<repeated-measures>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>The title is quite self-explanatory - I'd like to know if there's any other parametric technique apart from repeated-measures ANOVA, that can be utilized in order to compare several (more than 2) repeated measures?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-05T22:16:20.007000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1266"}, "posts_1328": {"id": 1385, "owneruserid": 438, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1404, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Techniques for Handling Incomplete/Missing Data", "tags": "<missing-data>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>My question is directed to techniques to deal with <em>incomplete</em> data during the classifier/model training/fitting.</p>\n\n<p>For instance, in a dataset w/ a few hundred rows, each row having let's say five dimensions and a class label as the last item, most data points will look like this:</p>\n\n<p>[0.74, 0.39, 0.14, 0.33, 0.34, 0]</p>\n\n<p>A few might look something like this:</p>\n\n<p><strong>[0.21, 0.68, ?, 0.82, 0.58, 1]</strong></p>\n\n<p>So it's those types of data points that are the focus of this Question.</p>\n\n<p>My initial reason for asking this question was a problem directly in front of me; however, before posting my Question, i thought it might be more useful if i re-phrased it so the answers would be useful to a larger portion of the Community.</p>\n\n<p>As a simple heuristic, let's divide these data-handling techniques based on when during the processing flow they are employed--before input to the classifier or during (i.e., the technique is inside the classifier).</p>\n\n<p>The best example i can think of for the latter is the clever 'three-way branching' technique used in Decision Trees.</p>\n\n<p>No doubt, the former category is far larger. The techniques i am aware of all fall into one of the groups below. </p>\n\n<p>While recently reviewing my personal notes on \"missing data handling\" i noticed that i had quite an impressive list of techniques. I just maintain these notes for general peace of mind and in case a junior colleague asks me how to deal with missing data. In actual practice, i don't actually use any of them, except for the last one.</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li><p><strong>Imputation</strong>: a broad rubric for a set of techniques which whose common\ndenominator (i believe) is that the\nmissing data is supplied directly by\nthe same data set--substitution\nrather than estimation/prediction.</p></li>\n<li><p><strong>Reconstruction</strong>: estimate the missing data points using an\nauto-associative network (just a\nneural network in which the sizes of\nthe input and output layers are\nequal--in other words, the output\nhas the same dimension as the\ninput); the idea here is to train\nthis network on complete data, then\nfeed it incomplete patterns, and\nread the missing values from the\noutput nodes.</p></li>\n<li><p><strong>Bootstrapping</strong>: (no summary necessary i shouldn't think, given\nit's use elsewhere in statistical\nanalysis).</p></li>\n<li><p><strong>Denial</strong>: quietly remove the data points with missing/corrupt elements\nfrom your training set and pretend\nthey never existed.</p></li>\n</ol>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-07T05:07:27.083000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1328"}, "posts_1388": {"id": 1444, "owneruserid": 159, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1446, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How should I transform non-negative data including zeros?", "tags": "<data-transformation><large-data>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>If I have highly skewed positive data I often take logs. But what should I do with highly skewed non-negative data that include zeros? I have seen two transformations used:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>$\\log(x+1)$ which has the neat feature that 0 maps to 0.</li>\n<li>$\\log(x+c)$ where c is either estimated or set to be some very small positive value.</li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>Are there any other approaches? Are there any good reasons to prefer one approach over the others?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-09T13:57:51.753000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1388"}, "posts_1523": {"id": 1595, "owneruserid": 890, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1632, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Python as a statistics workbench", "tags": "<r><spss><stata><python>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Lots of people use a main tool like Excel or another spreadsheet, SPSS, Stata, or R for their statistics needs. They might turn to some specific package for very special needs, but a lot of things can be done with a simple spreadsheet or a general stats package or stats programming environment.</p>\n\n<p>I've always liked Python as a programming language, and for simple needs, it's easy to write a short program that calculates what I need. Matplotlib allows me to plot it.</p>\n\n<p>Has anyone switched completely from, say R, to Python? R (or any other statistics package) has a lot of functionality specific to statistics, and it has data structures that allow you to think about the statistics you want to perform and less about the internal representation of your data. Python (or some other dynamic language) has the benefit of allowing me to program in a familiar, high-level language, and it lets me programmatically interact with real-world systems in which the data resides or from which I can take measurements. But I haven't found any Python package that would allow me to express things with \"statistical terminology\" – from simple descriptive statistics to more complicated multivariate methods.</p>\n\n<p>What can you recommend if I wanted to use Python as a \"statistics workbench\" to replace R, SPSS, etc.?</p>\n\n<p>What would I gain and lose, based on your experience?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-12T10:46:45.407000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1523"}, "posts_1605": {"id": 1676, "owneruserid": 110, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "I just installed the latest version of R. My specific questions are:</p>\n\n<p>1) is it appropriate to analyze data elicited from related (but not identical) questions/stimuli using repeated measures?</p>\n\n<p>2) Is it appropriate to analyze chunks of the data (e.g., cold pain magnitude estimates; cold stimuli threshold tests) separately?</p>\n\n<p>2) Would a different strategy (such as multilevel analysis / profile analysis / or some type of multivariate repeated measures ANOVA) be more appropriate?</p>\n\n<p>3) General recommendations and/or best practices for analyzing data such as this.</p>\n\n<p>Thank you for your feedback and input</p>\n\n<p>Patrick Welch</p>\n\n<p>note: I already searched the site for related questions (i.e., <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/859/anova-with-non-independent-observations\">ANOVA with non-independent observations</a> ; <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/1324/parametric-techniques-for-n-related-samples\">Parametric techniques for n-related samples</a>) but believe the current question to be different enough to warrant unique consideration.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-17T20:00:59.700000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1719"}, "posts_1733": {"id": 1815, "owneruserid": 174, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Recommended books on experiment design?", "tags": "<references><experiment-design>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>What are the panel's recommendations for books on design of experiments?</p>\n\n<p>Ideally, books should be still in print or available electronically, although that may not always be feasible. There are (at least) two methods to compute this value. </p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>Logrank method. As part of the Kaplan-Meier calculations, compute the number of observed events (deaths, usually) in each group ($Oa$, and $Ob$), and the number of expected events assuming a null hypothesis of no difference in survival ($Ea$ and $Eb$). The hazard ratio then is:\n$$\n    HR= \\frac{(Oa/Ea)}{(Ob/Eb)}\n$$</li>\n<li>Mantel-Haenszel method. First compute V, which is the sum of the hypergeometric variances at each time point. Then compute the hazard ratio as:\n$$\n HR= \\exp\\left(\\frac{(Oa-Ea)}{V}\\right)\n$$\nI got both these equations from chapter 3 of  Machin, Cheung and Parmar, <a href=\"http://rads.stackoverflow.com/amzn/click/0470870400\" rel=\"noreferrer\">Survival Analysis</a>. In this particular example, it is obvious that the logrank estimate is sensible, and the Mantel-Haenszel estimate is far off. "<binomial-distribution><likert><scales><psychometrics><psychology>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I've never liked how people typically analyze data from Likert scales as if error were continuous & Gaussian when there are reasonable expectations that these assumptions are violated at least at the extremes of the scales. What do you think of the following alternative:</p>\n\n<p>If the response takes value $k$ on an $n$-point scale, expand that data to $n$ trials, $k$ of which have the value 1 and $n-k$ of which have the value 0. Thus, we're treating response on a Likert scale as if it is the overt aggregate of a covert series of binomial trials (in fact, from a cognitive science perspective, this is actually an appealing model for the mechanisms involved in such decision making scenarios). With the expanded data, you can now use a mixed effects model specifying respondent as a random effect (also question as a random effect if you have multiple questions) and using the binomial link function to specify the error distribution.</p>\n\n<p>Can anyone see any assumption violations or other detrimental aspects of this approach?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-06T00:58:21.607000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2313"}, "posts_2391": {"id": 2492, "owneruserid": 795, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2498, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Is normality testing 'essentially useless'?", "tags": "<hypothesis-testing><normality-assumption><philosophical>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>A former colleague once argued to me as follows: </p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p>We usually apply normality tests to the results of processes that,\n  under the null, generate random variables that are only\n  <em>asymptotically</em> or <em>nearly</em> normal (with the 'asymptotically' part dependent on some quantity which we cannot make large); In the era of\n  cheap memory, big data, and fast processors, normality tests should\n  <em>always</em> reject the null of normal distribution for large (though not insanely large) samples. And so, perversely, normality tests should\n  only be used for small samples, when they presumably have lower power\n  and less control over type I rate.</p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p>Is this a valid argument? Is this a well-known argument? Are there well known tests for a 'fuzzier' null hypothesis than normality?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-08T17:47:21.820000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2391"}, "posts_2502": {"id": 2615, "owneruserid": 1250, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2664, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Analytical solutions to limits of correlation stress testing", "tags": "<correlation>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>Suppose I have some initial correlation matrix. I want to stress each correlation in the matrix by the same constant simultaneously (except the diagonal; lets call this global parallel stress since it affects the entire matrix by the same constant at the same time). I start with adding 0.01% to each correlation and check if the matrix is still PSD. I continue increasing the stress levels by small increments. Eventually I encounter a stress level above which the matrix would no longer be PSD. Let's call this the upper stress boundary. I repeat the same procedure for negative stresses and find the lower stress boundary.</p>\n\n<p>My general observation was that the minimum eigenvalue initial correlation matrix is roughly equal to the upper stress boundary. <strong>Is there an analytical solution for this problem?</strong></p>\n\n<p>Generally, I am more interested in the upper stress boundary. I stress the entire matrix at the same time because it is a simple way to reduce diversification benefit across all market variables. However, from a theoretical point of view it would be interesting to find out how to analytically calculate both lower and upper stress boundaries.</p>\n\n<p>EDIT: please see a previous thread, which might be relevant here (some brilliant idea's from kwak): <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/2572/correlation-stress-testing\">Correlation stress testing</a></p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-13T13:35:11.777000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2502"}, "posts_2621": {"id": 2746, "owneruserid": 1250, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2750, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to efficiently generate random positive-semidefinite correlation matrices?", "tags": "<random-generation><correlation-matrix>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I would like to be able to efficiently generate positive-semidefinite (PSD) correlation matrices. An average correlation, standard deviation of correlations, eigenvalues?</li>\n</ol>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-16T20:39:00.603000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2621"}, "posts_2771": {"id": 2917, "owneruserid": 1381, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Are these formulas for transforming P, LSD, MSD, HSD, CI, to SE as an exact or inflated/conservative estimate of $\\hat{\\sigma}$ correct?", "tags": "<multiple-comparisons><variance><data-transformation><meta-analysis>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<h2>Background</h2>\n\n<p>I am conducting a meta-analysis that includes previously published data. Often, differences between treatments are reported with P-values, least significant differences (LSD), and other statistics but provide no direct estimate of the variance.</p>\n\n<p>In the context of the model that I am using, an overestimate of variance is okay.</p>\n\n<h2>Problem</h2>\n\n<p>Here is a list of transformations to $SE$ where $SE=\\sqrt{MSE/n}$ <a href=\"http://eskes.psychiatry.dal.ca/Files/2003_-_Saville_-_Basic_statistics_and_the_inconsistency_of_m.pdf\" rel=\"noreferrer\">(Saville 2003)</a> that I am considering, feedback appreciated; below, I assume that $\\alpha=0.05$ so $1-^{\\alpha}/_2=0.975$  and variables are normally distributed unless otherwise stated:</p>\n\n<h2>Questions:</h2>\n\n<ol>\n<li><p>given $P$, $n$, and treatment means $\\bar X_1$ and $\\bar X_2$ \n$$SE=\\frac{\\bar X_1-\\bar X_2}{t_{(1-\\frac{P}{2},2n-2)}\\sqrt{2/n}}$$</p></li>\n<li><p>given LSD <a href=\"http://apsjournals.apsnet.org/doi/abs/10.1094/PHYTO.2004.94.9.1013\" rel=\"noreferrer\">(Rosenberg 2004)</a>, $\\alpha$, $n$, $b$ where $b$ is number of blocks, and $n=b$ by default for RCBD\n$$SE = \\frac{LSD}{t_{(0.975,n)}\\sqrt{2bn}}$$</p></li>\n<li><p>given MSD (minimum significant difference) <a href=\"http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/etc.5620190113/full\" rel=\"noreferrer\">(Wang 2000)</a>, $n$, $\\alpha$, df = $2n-2$\n$$SE = \\frac{MSD}{t_{(0.975, 2n-2)}\\sqrt{2}}$$</p></li>\n<li><p>given a 95% Confidence Interval <a href=\"http://eskes.psychiatry.dal.ca/Files/2003_-_Saville_-_Basic_statistics_and_the_inconsistency_of_m.pdf\" rel=\"noreferrer\">(Saville 2003)</a> (measured from mean to upper or lower confidence limit), $\\alpha$, and $n$ $$SE = \\frac{CI}{t_{(\\alpha/2,n)}}$$</p></li>\n<li><p>given Tukey's HSD, $n$, where $q$ is the 'studentized range statistic', $$SE = \\frac{HSD}{q_{(0.975,n)}}$$</p></li>\n</ol>\n\n<p>An R function to encapsulate these equations:</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li><p>Example Data: </p>\n\n<pre><code>data <- data.frame(Y=rep(1,5), \n                   stat=rep(1,5), \n                   n=rep(4,5), \n                   statname=c('SD', 'MSE', 'LSD', 'HSD', 'MSD') \n</code></pre></li>\n<li><p>Example Use:</p>\n\n<pre><code>transformstats(data)    \n</code></pre></li>\n<li><p>The <code>transformstats</code> function:</p>\n\n<pre><code>transformstats <- function(data) {\n  ## Transformation of stats to SE\n  ## transform SD to SE\n  if (\"SD\" %in% data$statname) {\n    sdi <- which(data$statname == \"SD\")\n    data$stat[sdi] <- data$stat[sdi] / sqrt(data$n[sdi])\n    data$statname[sdi] <- \"SE\"\n      }\n  ## transform MSE to SE\n  if (\"MSE\" %in% data$statname) {\n    msei <- which(data$statname == \"MSE\")\n    data$stat[msei] <- sqrt (data$stat[msei]/data$n[msei])\n    data$statname[msei] <- \"SE\"\n  }\n  ## 95%CI measured from mean to upper or lower CI\n  ## SE = CI/t\n  if (\"95%CI\" %in% data$statname) {\n    cii <- which(data$statname == '95%CI')\n    data$stat[cii] <- data$stat[cii]/qt(0.975,data$n[cii])\n    data$statname[cii] <- \"SE\"\n  }\n  ## Fisher's Least Significant Difference (LSD)\n  ## conservatively assume no within block replication\n  if (\"LSD\" %in% data$statname) {\n    lsdi <- which(data$statname == \"LSD\")\n    data$stat[lsdi] <- data$stat[lsdi] / (qt(0.975,data$n[lsdi]) * sqrt( (2 * data$n[lsdi])))\n    data$statname[lsdi] <- \"SE\"\n  }\n  ## Tukey's Honestly Significant Difference (HSD),\n  ## conservatively assuming 3 groups being tested so df =2\n  if (\"HSD\" %in% data$statname) {\n    hsdi <- which(data$statname == \"HSD\" & data$n > 1)\n    data$stat[hsdi] <- data$stat[hsdi] / (qtukey(0.975, data$n[lsdi], df = 2))\n    data$statname[hsdi] <- \"SE\"\n  }              \n  ## MSD Minimum Squared Difference\n  ## MSD = t_{\\alpha/2, 2n-2}*SD*sqrt(2/n)\n  ## SE  = MSD*n/(t*sqrt(2))\n  if (\"MSD\" %in% data$statname) {\n    msdi <- which(data$statname == \"MSD\")\n    data$stat[msdi] <- data$stat[msdi] * data$n[msdi] / (qt(0.975,2*data$n[lsdi]-2)*sqrt(2))\n    data$statname[msdi] <- \"SE\"\n  }\n  if (FALSE %in% c('SE','none') %in% data$statname) {\n    print(paste(trait, ': ERROR!!! data contains untransformed statistics'))\n  }\n  return(data)\n}\n</code></pre></li>\n</ol>\n\n<p><strong>References</strong></p>\n\n<p><a href=\"http://eskes.psychiatry.dal.ca/Files/2003_-_Saville_-_Basic_statistics_and_the_inconsistency_of_m.pdf\" rel=\"noreferrer\">Saville 2003Can J. (pdf)</a></p>\n\n<p><a href=\"http://apsjournals.apsnet.org/doi/abs/10.1094/PHYTO.2004.94.9.1013\" rel=\"noreferrer\">Rosenberg et al 2004 (link)</a></p>\n\n<p><a href=\"http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/etc.5620190113/full\" rel=\"noreferrer\">Wang et al. 2000 Env. From <a href=\"http://igraph.sourceforge.net/doc/R/fastgreedy.community.html\" rel=\"noreferrer\">the docs</a>:</p>\n<blockquote>\n<p>merges: A matrix with two column, this\nrepresents a dendogram and contains\nall the merges the algorithm\nperformed. Each line is one merge and\nit is given by the ids of the two\ncommunities merged. The community ids\nare integer numbers starting from zero\nand the communities between zero and\nthe number of vertices (N) minus one\nbelong to individual vertices. Obviously I would be comparing the distribution of values against a uniform distribution.  I vaguely remember using a Chi-square test in college. Each series covers the same period, although the actual dates in each time series may not all 'line up' exactly.</p>\n\n<p>That is to say, if the Time series were to be read into a 2D matrix, it would look something like this:</p>\n\n<pre><code>date     T1   T2   T3 .... TN\n1/1/01   100  59   42      N/A\n2/1/01   120  29   N/A     42.5\n3/1/01   110  N/A  12      36.82\n4/1/01   N/A  59   40      61.82\n5/1/01    05  99   42      23.68\n...\n31/12/01  100  59   42     N/A\n\netc \n</code></pre>\n\n<p>I want to write an R script that will segregate the time series {T1, T2, ... I am not quite sure how to go about this, since I am dealing with time series, and a pair of series that may move in sympathy over one interval, may not do so in a subsequent interval.</p>\n\n<p>I am sure there are far more experienced/clever people than me on here, so I would be grateful for any suggestions, ideas on what algorithm/heuristic to use for the distance measure and how to use that in clustering the time series. </p>\n\n<p>My guess is that there is NOT an established robust statistic method for doing this, so I would be very interested to see how people approach/solve this problem - thinking like a statistician.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-01T14:58:01.400000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3061"}, "posts_3211": {"id": 3400, "owneruserid": 1499, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 3411, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "From a statistical perspective, can one infer causality using propensity scores with an observational study?", "tags": "<causality><propensity-scores>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p><strong>Question:</strong> From the standpoint of statistician (or a practitioner), can one infer causality using <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Propensity_score\">propensity scores</a> with an observational study (<strong>not an experiment</strong>)?</p>\n\n<p>Please, do not want to start a flame war or a fanatical debate.</p>\n\n<p><strong>Background:</strong> Within our stat PhD program, we've only touched on causal inference through working groups and a few topic sessions.  However, there are some very prominent researchers in other departments (e.g. HDFS, Sociology) who are actively using them.</p>\n\n<p>I've already witnessed some pretty heated debate on this issue. It is not my intention to start one here.  That said, what references have you encountered?  What viewpoints do you have?  For example, one argument I've heard against propensity scores as a causal inference technique is that one can never infer causality due omitted variable bias -- if you leave out something important, you break the causal chain. Is this an unresolvable problem?</p>\n\n<p><strong>Disclaimer:</strong> This question may not have a correct answer -- completely cool with clicking cw, but I'm personally very interested in the responses and would be happy with a few good references which include real-world examples.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-07T23:27:47.727000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3211"}, "posts_7021": {"id": 7515, "owneruserid": 2260, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 7516, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What are some techniques for sampling two correlated random variables?", "tags": "<correlation><sampling><monte-carlo><stochastic-processes><copula>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>What are some techniques for sampling two correlated random variables:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li><p>if their probability\ndistributions are parameterized\n(e.g., log-normal)</p></li>\n<li><p>if they have non-parametric\ndistributions.</p></li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>The data are two time series for which we can compute non-zero correlation coefficients.  We wish to simulate these data in the future, assuming the historical correlation and time series CDF is constant.</p>\n\n<p>For case (2), the 1-D analogue would be to construct the CDF and sample from it.  So I guess, I could construct a 2-D CDF and do the same thing.  However, I wonder if there is a way to come close by using the individual 1-D CDFs and somehow linking the picks.</p>\n\n<p>Thanks!</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-02-22T20:43:25.633000", "posts_rownum": "posts_7021"}, "posts_3221": {"id": 3412, "owneruserid": 601, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 3415, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Comparing mixed effect models with the same number of degrees of freedom", "tags": "<r><mixed-model><model-selection>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I have an experiment that I'll try to abstract here.  Imagine I toss three white stones in front of you and ask you to make a judgment about their position.  I record a variety of properties of the stones and your response.   I do this over a number of subjects.  I generate two models.  One is that the nearest stone to you predicts your response, and the other is that the geometric center of the stones predicts your response.  So, using lmer in R I could write.</p>\n\n<pre><code>mNear   <- lmer(resp ~ nearest + (1|subject), REML = FALSE)\nmCenter <- lmer(resp ~ center  + (1|subject), REML = FALSE)\n</code></pre>\n\n<p><strong>UPDATE AND CHANGE - more direct version that incorporates several helpful comments</strong></p>\n\n<p>I could try</p>\n\n<pre><code>anova(mNear, mCenter)\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Which is incorrect, of course, because they're not nested and I can't really compare them that way.  I was expecting anova.mer to throw an error but it didn't.  But the possible nesting that I could try here isn't natural and still leaves me with somewhat less analytical statements.  When models are nested naturally (e.g. quadratic on linear) the test is only one way.  But in this case what would it mean to have asymmetric findings?</p>\n\n<p>For example, I could make a model three:</p>\n\n<pre><code>mBoth <- lmer(resp ~ center + nearest + (1|subject), REML = FALSE)\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Then I can anova.</p>\n\n<pre><code>anova(mCenter, mBoth)\nanova(mNearest, mBoth)\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>This is fair to do and now I find that the center adds to the nearest effect (the second command) but BIC actually goes up when nearest is added to center (correction for the lower parsimony).  This confirms what was suspected.</p>\n\n<p>But is finding this sufficient?  And is this fair when center and nearest are so highly correlated?</p>\n\n<p>Is there a better way to analytically compare the models when it's not about adding and subtracting explanatory variables (degrees of freedom)?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-08T12:34:11.673000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3221"}, "posts_3271": {"id": 3458, "owneruserid": 253, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 3459, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Alternatives to classification trees, with better predictive (e.g: CV) performance?", "tags": "<r><machine-learning><classification><cart>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I am looking for an alternative to Classification Trees which might yield better predictive power.</p>\n\n<p>The data I am dealing with has factors for both the explanatory and the explained variables.</p>\n\n<p>I remember coming across random forests and neural networks in this context, although never tried them before, are there another good candidate for such a modeling task (in R, obviously)?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-10T09:27:49.817000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3271"}, "posts_3341": {"id": 3532, "owneruserid": 8, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 3535, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Random numbers and the multicore package", "tags": "<r><random-generation><parallel-computing><multicore>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>When programming in R, I've used the <a href=\"http://www.rforge.net/doc/packages/multicore/multicore.html\" rel=\"noreferrer\">multicore</a> package a few times. However, I've never seen a statement about how it handles it's random numbers. Can anyone confirm that something sensible does happen?</p>\n\n<p><strong>Example</strong></p>\n\n<p>From the documentation, we have </p>\n\n<pre><code>x <- foreach(icount(1000), .combine = \"+\") %do% rnorm(4)\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>How are the <code>rnorm</code>`s generated?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-12T20:14:49.203000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3341"}, "posts_3348": {"id": 3539, "owneruserid": 1564, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 3546, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Inter-rater reliability for ordinal or interval data", "tags": "<reliability><psychometrics><agreement-statistics><cohens-kappa>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>Which inter-rater reliability methods are most appropriate for ordinal or interval data?</p>\n\n<p>I believe that \"Joint probability of agreement\" or \"Kappa\" are designed for nominal data. </li>\n</ol>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-16T01:44:55.913000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3467"}, "posts_3725": {"id": 3931, "owneruserid": 253, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 3934, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Intuitive explanation for dividing by $n-1$ when calculating standard deviation?", "tags": "<standard-error><intuition><teaching><bessels-correction><faq>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I was asked today in class why you divide the sum of square error by $n-1$ instead of with $n$, when calculating the standard deviation.</p>\n\n<p>I said I am not going to answer it in class (since I didn't wanna go into unbiased estimators), but later I wondered - <strong>is there</strong> an intuitive explanation for this?!</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-23T22:04:57.160000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3725"}, "posts_3807": {"id": 4030, "owneruserid": 1127, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Finding coefficients for VECM + exogenous variables", "tags": "<time-series><econometrics>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I want to extend the standard <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Error_correction_model\" rel=\"noreferrer\">VECM</a> form:</p>\n\n<pre>\nΔx[t] = δ0 + ... + Π x[t-1] + Φ1 Δx[t-1] + Φ1 Δx[t-2] + ... + ε\n</pre>\n\n<p>to include exogenous variables (i.e. variables that are participant in describing the relationships amongst <code>Δx[t]</code>, but are not in the dependent set <code>Δx[t]</code>). Both personal and second hand experience suggests that the paucity of statistical rigor in undergraduate and graduate training is rather ubiquitous within psychology. As such, I thought it would be useful for independent learners like myself to create a list of \"Statistical Sins\", tabulating statistical practices taught to grad students as standard practice that are in fact either superseded by superior (more powerful, or flexible, or robust, etc.) modern methods or shown to be frankly invalid. Anticipating that other fields might also experience a similar state of affairs, I propose a community wiki where we can collect a list of statistical sins across disciplines. Please, submit one \"sin\" per answer.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-11-15T18:46:37.113000", "posts_rownum": "posts_4281"}, "posts_4832": {"id": 5135, "owneruserid": 2091, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 5138, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Interpretation of R's lm() output", "tags": "<r><regression><interpretation>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>The help pages in R assume I know what those numbers mean, but I don't.\nI'm trying to really intuitively understand every number here. I will just post the output and comment on what I found out. There might (will) be mistakes, as I'll just write what I assume. Mainly I'd like to know what the t-value in the coefficients mean, and why they print the residual standard error. </p>\n\n<pre><code>Call:\nlm(formula = iris$Sepal.Width ~ iris$Petal.Width)\n\nResiduals:\n     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max \n-1.09907 -0.23626 -0.01064  0.23345  1.17532 \n</code></pre>\n\n<p>This is a 5-point-summary of the residuals (their mean is always 0, right?). The numbers can be used (I'm guessing here) to quickly see if there are any big outliers. Also you can already see it here if the residuals are far from normally distributed (they should be normally distributed).</p>\n\n<pre><code>Coefficients:\n                 Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    \n(Intercept)       3.30843    0.06210  53.278  < 2e-16 ***\niris$Petal.Width -0.20936    0.04374  -4.786 4.07e-06 ***\n---\nSignif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1 \n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Estimates $\\hat{\\beta_i}$, computed by least squares regression. Also, the standard error is $\\sigma_{\\beta_i}$. I'd like to know how this is calculated.  I have no idea where the t-value and the corresponding p-value come from. I know $\\hat{\\beta}$ should be normal distributed, but how is the t-value calculated?</p>\n\n<pre><code>Residual standard error: 0.407 on 148 degrees of freedom\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>$\\sqrt{ \\frac{1}{n-p} \\epsilon^T\\epsilon }$, I guess. But why do we calculate that, and what does it tell us?</p>\n\n<pre><code>Multiple R-squared: 0.134,  Adjusted R-squared: 0.1282 \n</code></pre>\n\n<p>$ R^2 = \\frac{s_\\hat{y}^2}{s_y^2} $, which is $ \\frac{\\sum_{i=1}^n (\\hat{y_i}-\\bar{y})^2}{\\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i-\\bar{y})^2} $. The ratio is close to 1 if the points lie on a straight line, and 0 if they are random.  What is the adjusted R-squared?</p>\n\n<pre><code>F-statistic: 22.91 on 1 and 148 DF,  p-value: 4.073e-06 \n</code></pre>\n\n<p>F and p for the <strong>whole</strong> model, not only for single $\\beta_i$s as previous. The F value is $ \\frac{s^2_{\\hat{y}}}{\\sum\\epsilon_i} $. The bigger it grows, the more unlikely it is that the $\\beta$'s do not have any effect at all.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-12-04T11:28:14.300000", "posts_rownum": "posts_4832"}, "posts_4944": {"id": 5249, "owneruserid": 183, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Simple, reliable, open, and interoperable plain text format for storing data", "tags": "<project-management>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>In a previous question I asked about tools for editing <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/5238/strategy-for-editing-comma-separated-value-csv-files\">CSV files</a>.</p>\n\n<p><a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/5238/strategy-for-editing-comma-separated-value-csv-files/5239#5239\">Gavin</a>\nlinked to a comment on R Help by <a href=\"http://thread.gmane.org/gmane.comp.lang.r.general/213174/focus=213179\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Duncan Murdoch</a>\nsuggesting that Data Interchange Format is a more reliable way to store data than CSV.</p>\n\n<p>For some applications a dedicated database management system is what is needed.\nHowever, for small scale data analysis projects something more light weight seems more suitable.</p>\n\n<p>Consider the following criteria for evaluating a file format:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li><strong>reliabile</strong>: the data entered should stay true to what has been entered; \ndata should open consistently in different software; </li>\n<li><strong>simple</strong>: it would be nice if the file format is easy to understand and ideally be\nreadable with a simple text editor; it should be easy to write a simple program to read and write the format.</li>\n<li><strong>open</strong>: the format should be open</li>\n<li><strong>interoperable</strong>: the file format should be supported by many systems</li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>I find tab and comma separated value formats fail on the reliability criterion.\nAlthough I suppose I could blame the importing and exporting programs rather than the file format.\nI often find myself having to make little adjustments to the options in \n<code>read.table</code> in order to prevent some strange character from breaking the loading of the data frame.</p>\n\n<p>Questions</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>Which file format best meets these needs?</li>\n<li>Is Data Interchange Format a better alternative? or does it have its own problems?</li>\n<li>Is there some other format that is preferable?</li>\n<li>Am I unfairly evaluating TSV and CSV? Let's assume that generally those two modes interfere, so there's no easy possibility to separate them by isolating certain sequence segments. I try the classic principal component analysis by finding the covariance matrix, then finding the set of eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors:<br>\n<img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/osv6x.png\" alt=\"experimental data pca\"></p>\n\n<p>White box dimensions represents the magnitude if the eigenvalues, box orientation represents the direction of eigenvectors.  </p>\n\n<p>It's clear that PCA first component deviates slightly from the high-magnitude mode direction, while the second component deviates greatly due to skewness of the lower-magnitude mode original direction.</p>\n\n<p>It is known that PCA, being based on eigenvectors, results in orthogonal basis of primary components. </p>\n\n<p>Is there other elegant methods (or PCA-derived methods) to obtain the non-orthogonal basis of primary skewed components?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-01-26T15:51:26.317000", "posts_rownum": "posts_6200"}, "posts_5038": {"id": 5347, "owneruserid": 634, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 5358, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How can I efficiently model the sum of Bernoulli random variables?", "tags": "<r><distributions><binomial-distribution><random-variable><poisson-binomial-distribution>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I am modeling a random variable (<span class=\"math-container\">$Y$</span>) which is the sum of some ~15-40k independent Bernoulli random variables (<span class=\"math-container\">$X_i$</span>), each with a different success probability (<span class=\"math-container\">$p_i$</span>). Formally, <span class=\"math-container\">$Y=\\sum X_i$</span> where <span class=\"math-container\">$\\Pr(X_i=1)=p_i$</span> and <span class=\"math-container\">$\\Pr(X_i=0)=1-p_i$</span>.</p>\n<p>I am interested in quickly answering queries such as <span class=\"math-container\">$\\Pr(Y\\leq k)$</span> (where <span class=\"math-container\">$k$</span> is given).</p>\n<p>Currently, I use random simulations to answer such queries. I randomly draw each <span class=\"math-container\">$X_i$</span> according to its <span class=\"math-container\">$p_i$</span>, then sum all <span class=\"math-container\">$X_i$</span> values to get <span class=\"math-container\">$Y'$</span>. I repeat this process a few thousand times and return the fraction of times <span class=\"math-container\">$\\Pr(Y'\\leq k)$</span>.</p>\n<p>Obviously, this is not totally accurate (although accuracy greatly increases as the number of simulations increases). Also, it seems I have enough data about the distribution to avoid the use simulations. Can you think of a reasonable way to get the exact probability <span class=\"math-container\">$\\Pr(Y\\leq k)$</span>?</p>\n<p>p.s.</p>\n<p>I use Perl & R.</p>\n<p><strong>EDIT</strong></p>\n<p>Following the responses I thought some clarifications might be needed. I will shortly describe the setting of my problem. Given is a circular genome with  circumference <code>c</code> and a set of <code>n</code> ranges mapped to it. For example, <code>c=3*10^9</code> and <code>ranges={[100,200],[50,1000],[3*10^9-1,1000],...}</code>. Note all ranges are closed (both ends are inclusive). Also note that we only deal with integers (whole units).</p>\n<p>I am looking for regions on the circle that are undercovered by the given <code>n</code> mapped ranges. So to test whether a given a range of length <code>x</code> on the circle is undercovered, I test the hypothesis that the <code>n</code> ranges are mapped randomly. The probability a mapped range of length <code>q>x</code> will fully cover the given range of length <code>x</code> is <code>(q-x)/c</code>. This probability becomes quite small when <code>c</code> is large and/or <code>q</code> is small. What I'm interested is the number of ranges (out of <code>n</code>) which cover <code>x</code>. This is how <code>Y</code> is formed.</p>\n<p>I test my null hypothesis vs. one sided alternative (undercoverage). Also note I am testing multiple hypothesis (different <code>x</code> lengths), and sure to correct for this.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-12-10T11:06:05.337000", "posts_rownum": "posts_5038"}, "posts_5051": {"id": 5360, "owneruserid": 569, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 5361, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Stepwise logistic regression and sampling", "tags": "<logistic><spss><stepwise-regression>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I am fitting a stepwise logistic regression on a set of data in SPSS. There is no predicting variable for \"c\", and x1 is a predictor for \"a\", assuming that x2 permits it.</p>\n\n<p>How can this situation be extracted from the fitted model? </p>\n\n<pre><code>N <- 200\nset.seed(5123)\nx1 <- runif(N)\nx2 <- runif(N)\nx3 <- runif(N)\ny <- sample(letters[1:3], N, T)\ny[x1 <.5] <- \"a\"\ny[x2 <.1] <- \"b\"\n\nfit <- rpart(y ~ x1+x2)\nfit2 <- prune(fit, cp= 0.07)\nplot(fit2)\ntext(fit2, use.n=TRUE)\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Thanks.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-12-13T19:24:57.693000", "posts_rownum": "posts_5130"}, "posts_5275": {"id": 10981, "owneruserid": 4670, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 17139, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Computing mathematical expectation of the correlation coefficient or $R^2$ in linear regression", "tags": "<regression><correlation>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'm re-posting a question from <a href=\"https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/32569/a-question-about-linear-regression\">math.stackexchange.com</a>, I think the current answer in math.se is not right.</p>\n\n<p>Select $n$ numbers from a set $\\{1,2,...,U\\}$, $y_i$ is the $i$th number selected, and $x_i$ is the rank of $y_i$ in the $n$ numbers. I need a PD matrix for the Cholesky update.</li>\n</ul>\n", "creationdate": "2011-01-19T01:00:36.910000", "posts_rownum": "posts_5997"}, "posts_6221": {"id": 6599, "owneruserid": 2798, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 6665, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Calibrating a multi-class boosted classifier", "tags": "<machine-learning><boosting>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I have read Alexandru Niculescu-Mizil and Rich Caruana's paper \"<a href=\"http://aaaipress.org/Papers/Workshops/2007/WS-07-05/WS07-05-006.pdf\" rel=\"noreferrer\">Obtaining Calibrated Probabilities from Boosting</a>\" and the discussion in <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/5196/why-use-platts-scaling\">this</a> thread. "acceptedanswerid": 13317, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Is $R^2$ useful or dangerous?", "tags": "<regression><r-squared>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I was skimming through <a href=\"http://www.stat.cmu.edu/~cshalizi/402/\">some lecture notes</a> by Cosma Shalizi (in particular, section 2.1.1 of the <a href=\"http://www.stat.cmu.edu/~cshalizi/402/lectures/02-truth-about-linear-regression/lecture-02.pdf\">second lecture</a>), and was reminded that you can get very low $R^2$ even when you have a completely linear model.</p>\n\n<p>To paraphrase Shalizi's example: suppose you have a model $Y = aX + \\epsilon$, where $a$ is known. Then $\\newcommand{\\Var}{\\mathrm{Var}}\\Var[Y] = a^2 \\Var[x] + \\Var[\\epsilon]$ and the amount of explained variance is $a^2 \\Var[X]$, so $R^2 = \\frac{a^2 \\Var[x]}{a^2 \\Var[X] + \\Var[\\epsilon]}$. This goes to 0 as $\\Var[X] \\rightarrow 0$ and to 1 as $\\Var[X] \\rightarrow \\infty$.</p>\n\n<p>Conversely, you can get high $R^2$ even when your model is noticeably non-linear. (Anyone have a good example offhand?)</p>\n\n<p>So when is $R^2$ a useful statistic, and when should it be ignored?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-07-20T20:32:55.510000", "posts_rownum": "posts_8274"}, "posts_8336": {"id": 8955, "owneruserid": 3136, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 8964, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Advice on explaining heterogeneity / heteroscedasticty", "tags": "<regression><mixed-model><references><residuals><heteroscedasticity>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I am looking for any help, advice or tips in how to explain heterogeneity / heteroscedasticity to biologists in my department. I am pretty sure it does, but I couldn't find a paper.  </li>\n<li>How serious a problem is heterogeneity? I have found conflicting views on this, while some say that model standard errors etc. will be unreliable, I have also read that it is only a problem if the heterogeneity is severe. How severe is severe?  </li>\n<li>Advice on modelling heterogeneity. Currently, I focus largely on the nlme package in R and the use of variance covariates, this is pretty simple and most people here use R so providing scripts is useful. I am also using the MCMCglmm package as well, but other suggestions are welcome, particularly for non-normal data.  </li>\n<li>Any other suggestions are welcome.  </li>\n</ol>\n", "creationdate": "2011-03-30T09:12:59.377000", "posts_rownum": "posts_8336"}, "posts_8439": {"id": 9071, "owneruserid": 2958, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 9073, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Intuitive explanation of contribution to sum of two normally distributed random variables", "tags": "<normal-distribution><conditional-probability>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>If I have two normally distributed independent random variables $X$ and $Y$ with means $\\mu_X$ and $\\mu_Y$ and standard deviations $\\sigma_X$ and $\\sigma_Y$ and I discover that $X+Y=c$, then (assuming I have not made any errors) the conditional distribution of $X$ and $Y$ given $c$ are also normally distributed with means \n$$\\mu_{X|c} = \\mu_X + (c - \\mu_X - \\mu_Y)\\frac{ \\sigma_X^2}{\\sigma_X^2+\\sigma_Y^2}$$ $$\\mu_{Y|c} = \\mu_Y + (c - \\mu_X - \\mu_Y)\\frac{ \\sigma_Y^2}{\\sigma_X^2+\\sigma_Y^2}$$\nand standard deviation \n$$\\sigma_{X|c} = \\sigma_{Y|c} = \\sqrt{ \\frac{\\sigma_X^2 \\sigma_Y^2}{\\sigma_X^2 + \\sigma_Y^2}}.$$</p>\n\n<p>It is no surprise that the conditional standard deviations are the same as, given $c$, if one goes up the other must come down by the same amount.  It is interesting that the conditional standard deviation does not depend on $c$.</p>\n\n<p>What I cannot get my head round are the conditional means, where they take a share of the excess $(c - \\mu_X - \\mu_Y)$ proportional to the original variances, not to the original  standard deviations.   </p>\n\n<p>For example, if they have zero means, $\\mu_X=\\mu_Y=0$, and standard deviations $\\sigma_X =3$ and $\\sigma_Y=1$ then conditioned on $c=4$ we would have $E[X|c=4]=3.6$ and $E[Y|c=4]=0.4$, i.e. in the ratio $9:1$ even though I would have intuitively thought that the ratio $3:1$ would be more natural.  <strong>Can anyone give an intuitive explanation for this?</strong></p>\n\n<p>This was provoked by <a href=\"https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/30365/posterior-distribution-after-having-partial-information-on-some-linear-combinatio\">a Math.SE question</a> </p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-04-02T01:28:12.757000", "posts_rownum": "posts_8439"}, "posts_8573": {"id": 9220, "owneruserid": 1913, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 10731, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What is the distribution of the Euclidean distance between two normally distributed random variables?", "tags": "<normal-distribution><distance-functions>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Assume you are given two objects whose exact locations are unknown, but are distributed according to normal distributions with known parameters (e.g. $a \\sim N(m, s)$ and $b \\sim N(v, t))$. We can assume these are both bivariate normals, such that the positions are described by a distribution over $(x,y)$ coordinates (i.e. $m$ and $v$ are vectors containing the expected $(x,y)$ coordinates for $a$ and $b$ respectively). We will also assume the objects are independent.</p>\n\n<p>Does anyone know if the distribution of the squared Euclidean distance between these two objects is a known parametric distribution? Or how to derive the PDF / CDF for this function analytically?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-04-05T19:10:30.120000", "posts_rownum": "posts_8573"}, "posts_8798": {"id": 9477, "owneruserid": 1084, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 9480, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to draw an interaction plot with confidence intervals?", "tags": "<r><data-visualization><confidence-interval><interaction>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>My attempts:</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li><p>I couldn't get confidence intervals in <code>interaction.plot()</code> </p></li>\n<li><p>and on the other hand <code>plotmeans()</code> from package 'gplot' wouldn't display two graphs. "title": "Can chi square be used to compare proportions?", "tags": "<chi-squared-test><hypothesis-testing><proportion>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I've read that the chi square test is useful to see if a sample is significantly different from a set of expected values.</p>\n<p>For example, here is a table of results of a survey regarding people's favourite colours (n=15+13+10+17=55 total respondents):</p>\n<pre><code>red, blue, green, yellow\n\n15, 13, 10, 17\n</code></pre>\n<p>A chi square test can tell me if this sample is significantly different from the null hypothesis of equal probability of people liking each colour.</p>\n<p>Question: Can the test be run on the proportions of total respondents who like a certain colour? Like below:</p>\n<pre><code>red, blue, green, yellow\n\n0.273, 0.236, 0.182, 0.309\n</code></pre>\n<p>Where, of course, <span class=\"math-container\">$0.273 + 0.236 + 0.182 + 0.309=1$</span>.</p>\n<p>If the chi square test is not suitable in this case, what test would be?</p>\n<p><strong>Edit</strong>: I tried @Roman Luštrik answer below, and got the following output, why am I not getting a p-value and why does R say "Chi-squared approximation may be incorrect"?</p>\n<pre class=\"lang-r prettyprint-override\"><code>chisq.test(c(0, 0, 0, 8, 6, 2, 0, 0), p = c(0.406197174, 0.088746395, \n             0.025193306, 0.42041479, 0.03192905, 0.018328576, \n             0.009190708, 0))\n    \n        Chi-squared test for given probabilities\n    \n    data:  c(0, 0, 0, 8, 6, 2, 0, 0) \n    X-squared = NaN, df = 7, p-value = NA\n    \n    Warning message:\n    In chisq.test(c(0, 0, 0, 8, 6, 2, 0, 0), p = c(0.406197174, \n           0.088746395,  :\n      Chi-squared approximation may be incorrect  \n</code></pre>\n", "creationdate": "2011-04-16T21:08:05.087000", "posts_rownum": "posts_8943"}, "posts_9099": {"id": 9807, "owneruserid": 4262, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Working with Likert scales in SPSS", "tags": "<spss><likert>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I performed a survey using a Likert 1 to 5 scale (totally agree/agree/neutral/ disagree/totally disagree) on 12 questions which are split into 3 statements which the respondent places a value of between 1 to 5 dependent on how much they agree or disagree - there are 36 statements in total.</p>\n\n<p>Respondents:</p>\n\n<pre><code>Group 1                          Group 2\narchitects UK   140 replied      Architects US   100 replied\nengineers UK    140 replied      Engineers US    100 replied\nContractors Uk  140 replied      Contractors US  100 replied\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>The data is in Excel.</p>\n\n<h3>Questions:</h3>\n\n<ol>\n<li>How do I input them in SPSS?</li>\n<li>How do I work out the frequency of replies for each recipient?</li>\n<li>How do I work out frequency of replies i.e agrees/disagrees etc for each group?</li>\n<li>How can I rank each individual question (12 of them)? Remember, there are 3 individual statements to each question.</li>\n<li>How do I compare UK architects to US architects to show congruence or not?</li>\n<li>How would show correlation between the two groups UK and US?</li>\n<li>Will SPSS develop graphs etc for me showing frequency or correlation?</li>\n</ol>\n", "creationdate": "2011-04-20T22:57:58.130000", "posts_rownum": "posts_9099"}, "posts_9147": {"id": 9859, "owneruserid": 3019, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 14654, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What are the disadvantages of the profile likelihood?", "tags": "<maximum-likelihood><likelihood><profile-likelihood>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Consider a vector of parameters $(\\theta_1, \\theta_2)$, with $\\theta_1$ the parameter of interest, and $\\theta_2$ a nuisance parameter.</p>\n\n<p>If $L(\\theta_1, \\theta_2 ; x)$ is the likelihood constructed from the data $x$, the profile likelihood for $\\theta_1$ is defined as $L_P(\\theta_1 ; x) = L(\\theta_1, \\hat{\\theta}_2(\\theta_1) ; x)$ where $ \\hat{\\theta}_2(\\theta_1)$ is the MLE of $\\theta_2$ for a fixed value of $\\theta_1$.</p>\n\n<p>$\\bullet$ Maximising the profile likelihood with respect to $\\theta_1$ leads to same estimate $\\hat{\\theta}_1$ as the one obtained by maximising the likelihood simultaneously with respect to $\\theta_1$ and $\\theta_2$.</p>\n\n<p>$\\bullet$ I think the standard deviation of $\\hat{\\theta}_1$ may also be estimated from the second derivative of the profile likelihood.</p>\n\n<p>$\\bullet$ The likelihood statistic for $H_0: \\theta_1 = \\theta_0$ can be written in terms of the profile likelihood: $LR = 2 \\log( \\tfrac{L_P(\\hat{\\theta}_1 ; x)}{L_P(\\theta_0 ; x)})$.</p>\n\n<p>So, it seems that the profile likelihood can be used exactly as if it was a genuine likelihood. Is it really the case ? What are the main drawbacks of that approach ? And what about the 'rumor' that the estimator obtained from the profile likelihood is biased (edit: even asymptotically) ? </p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-04-22T07:01:16.563000", "posts_rownum": "posts_9147"}, "posts_9173": {"id": 9885, "owneruserid": 2148, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 9915, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Application of machine learning methods in StackExchange websites", "tags": "<machine-learning>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I have a <strong>Machine Learning</strong> course this semester and the professor asked us to find a <strong>real-world problem</strong> and solve it by one of machine learning methods introduced in the class, as:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li><a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decision_tree_learning\">Decision Trees</a></li>\n<li><a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_neural_network\">Artificial Neural Networks</a></li>\n<li><a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Support_vector_machine\">Support Vector Machines</a></li>\n<li><a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instance-based_learning\">Instance-based Learning</a> (<a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-nearest_neighbor_algorithm\">kNN</a>, <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locally_weighted_regression\">LWL</a>)</li>\n<li><a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayesian_network\">Bayesian Networks</a></li>\n<li><a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning\">Reinforcement learning</a></li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>I am one of fans of <strong>stackoverflow</strong> and <strong>stackexchange</strong> and know <a href=\"http://blog.stackoverflow.com/category/cc-wiki-dump/\">database dumps</a> of these websites are provided to the public because they are awesome! I hope I could find a good machine learning challenge about these databases and solve it. </p>\n\n<p><strong>My idea</strong></p>\n\n<p>One idea came to my mind is predicting tags for questions based on the entered words in question body. I think the Bayesian network is the right tool for learning tags for a question but need more research.\nAnyway, after learning phase when user finishes entering the question some tags should be suggested to him. </p>\n\n<p><strong>Please tell me</strong>:</p>\n\n<p>I want to ask the stats community as experienced people about ML two questions:</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li><p>Do you think tag suggestion is at least a problem which has any chance to solve? Do you have any advice about it? I am a little worried because stackexchange does not implement such feature yet. </p></li>\n<li><p>Do you have any other/better idea for the ML project that is based on stackexchange database? I find it really hard to find something to <strong>learn</strong> from stackexchange databases. </p></li>\n</ol>\n\n<hr>\n\n<p><strong>Consideration about database errors:</strong>\nI would like to point that although the databases are huge and have many instances, they are not perfect and are prune to error. The obvious one is the age of users that is unreliable. Even selected tags for the question are not 100% correct. Anyway, we should consider the percent of correctness of data in selecting a problem. </p>\n\n<p><strong>Consideration about the problem itself:</strong> My project should not be about <code>data-mining</code> or something like this. It just should be an application of ML methods in real-world.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-04-22T22:27:24.467000", "posts_rownum": "posts_9173"}, "posts_9277": {"id": 10005, "owneruserid": 4340, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to convert a table into a graph in R", "tags": "<r><data-visualization>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I have a table I want to convert into a graph (bar-graph or line-graph)</p>\n<p>The first column has fixed values. I want to plot a graph of the fixed column against all the different twenty simulated columns.</p>\n<p>How do I go about it?</p>\n<h2>Edit</h2>\n<blockquote>\n<p>table name:bygrace</p>\n</blockquote>\n<pre><code>V1    V2   V3   V4   V5                 \n100    16   11   -6    1                               \n120   -17  -12    7   -2                               \n140    18   13   -8    3                              \n150   -19  -14    9   -4                              \n210    20   15  -10   -5\n</code></pre>\n<p>Actually, my table looks like the one above.\nThe first column V1 represents Premiums charged by an insurance company,say last year (for 5 policyholders/policies)\nAfter critical analysis of the portfolio, the company decides to increase or decrease the premium amount for some of the customers.\nHowever, the company does not know exactly by how much it should increase of decrease the premiums for fear that it would lose customers.\nFor this reason, four different scenarios/simulations are considered which are represented by the next four columns(V2 through V5) respectively.</p>\n<p>Now the task is to plot the premium amounts in V1 against these four different scenarios(bar-graph or line-graph; I think bar will be better).</p>\n<p>And my question is can this be done on one graph/at once? If yes, how shoul I go about it?\nOr do I have to plot the premium against each column separately?</p>\n<p>In fact, I have spent the whole of yesterday and today on this but I have not been able to get the desired result.</p>\n<p>Someone gave me an answer to try.And I am going to do that because it has given me an idea and I am very thankful to the one!</p>\n<p>Many thanks to everyone for their help</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-04-26T20:15:47.633000", "posts_rownum": "posts_9277"}, "posts_9508": {"id": 10251, "owneruserid": 74, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 10256, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What is the objective function of PCA?", "tags": "<pca>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Principal component analysis <em>can use</em> matrix decomposition, but that is just a tool to get there.</p>\n\n<p>How would you find the principal components without the use of matrix algebra?</p>\n\n<p>What is the objective function (goal), and what are the constraints?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-05-02T23:10:16.580000", "posts_rownum": "posts_9508"}, "posts_9612": {"id": 10363, "owneruserid": 914, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Data mining: How should I go about finding the functional form?", "tags": "<regression><machine-learning><algorithms><model-selection><data-mining>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'm curious about repeatable procedures that can be used to discover the functional form of the function <code>y = f(A, B, C) + error_term</code> where my only input is a set of observations (<code>y</code>, <code>A</code>, <code>B</code> and <code>C</code>). Please note that the functional form of <code>f</code>is unknown.</p>\n\n<p>Consider the following dataset:</p>\n\n<pre>\nAA  BB  CC  DD  EE  FF\n==  ==  ==  ==  ==  ==\n98  11  66  84  67  10500\n71  44  48  12  47  7250\n54  28  90  73  95  5463\n34  95  15  45  75  2581\n56  37  0   79  43  3221\n68  79  1   65  9   4721\n53  2   90  10  18  3095\n38  75  41  97  40  4558\n29  99  46  28  96  5336\n22  63  27  43  4   2196\n4   5   89  78  39  492\n10  28  39  59  64  1178\n11  59  56  25  5   3418\n10  4   79  98  24  431\n86  36  84  14  67  10526\n80  46  29  96  7   7793\n67  71  12  43  3   5411\n14  63  2   9   52  368\n99  62  56  81  26  13334\n56  4   72  65  33  3495\n51  40  62  11  52  5178\n29  77  80  2   54  7001\n42  32  4   17  72  1926\n44  45  30  25  5   3360\n6   3   65  16  87  288\n</pre>\n\n<p>In this example, assume that we know that <code>FF = f(AA, BB, CC, DD, EE) + error term</code>, but we're not sure about the functional form of <code>f(...)</code>.</p>\n\n<p>What procedure/what methods would you use to arrive at finding the functional form of <code>f(...)</code>?</p>\n\n<p>(Bonus point: What is your best guess at the definiton of <code>f</code> given the data above? :-) And yes, there is a \"correct\" answer that will yield an <code>R^2</code> in excess of 0.99.)</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-05-05T16:26:00.037000", "posts_rownum": "posts_9612"}, "posts_9620": {"id": 10382, "owneruserid": 4487, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "General advice on forming an index of attitude to the environment from a set of Likert items", "tags": "<factor-analysis><scales><reliability>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I am going to make an environmental index to be used as an explanatory variable in a regression model. For making this index, I asked  respondents a set of questions about their environmental attitudes. Each question has 5 response options from 1=“completely agree” to 5=“completely disagree”.\nI'm going to summarize each these categories as one index.</p>\n\n<p><strong>What general advice can be offered for creating such an index?</strong></p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-05-06T01:11:14.787000", "posts_rownum": "posts_9620"}, "posts_9741": {"id": 10510, "owneruserid": 364, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "References containing arguments against null hypothesis significance testing?", "tags": "<hypothesis-testing><statistical-significance><references><p-value>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>In the last few years I've read a number of papers arguing against the use of null hypothesis significance testing in science, but didn't think to keep a persistent list. A colleague recently asked me for such a list, so I thought I'd ask everyone here to help build it. To start things off, here's what I have so far:</p>\n<ul>\n<li><a href=\"https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21077903/\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Johansson (2011) "Hail the impossible: p-values, evidence, and likelihood."</a></li>\n<li><a href=\"https://web.archive.org/web/20201025053416/https://www.dgps.de/fachgruppen/methoden/mpr-online/issue16/art1/article.html\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Haller & Kraus (2002) "Misinterpretation of significance: A problem students share with their teachers."</a></li>\n<li><a href=\"https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18087943/\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Wagenmakers (2007) "A practical solution to the pervasive problem of p-values."</a></li>\n<li><a href=\"https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2009-24989-001\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Rodgers (2010) "The epistemology of mathematical and statistical modeling: A quiet methodological revolution."</a></li>\n<li><a href=\"https://doi.org/10.3758%2FBF03208815?from=SL\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Dixon (1998) "Why scientists value p-values."</a></li>\n<li><a href=\"https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15732688/\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Glover & Dixon (2004) "Likelihood ratios: a simple and flexible statistic for empirical psychologists."</a></li>\n</ul>\n", "creationdate": "2011-05-08T16:09:04.040000", "posts_rownum": "posts_9741"}, "posts_10000": {"id": 10789, "owneruserid": 4608, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 10791, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Why are random variables defined as functions?", "tags": "<probability><random-variable><measure-theory>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'm having problems understanding the concept of a random variable as a function.  I understand the mechanics (I think) but I do not understand the motivation...</p>\n\n<p>Say $(\\Omega, B, P) $ is a probability triple, where $\\Omega = [0,1]$, $B$ is the Borel-$\\sigma$-algebra on that interval and $P$ is the regular Lebesgue measure.  Let $X$ be a random variable from $B$ to $\\{1,2,3,4,5,6\\}$ such that $X([0,1/6)) = 1$, $X([1/6,2/6)) = 2$, ..., $X([5/6,1]) = 6$, so $X$ has a discrete uniform distribution on the values 1 through 6.  </p>\n\n<p>That's all good, but I do not understand the necessity of the original probability triple... we could have directly constructed something equivalent as $(\\{1,2,3,4,5,6\\}, S, P_x)$ where $S$ is all the appropriate $\\sigma$-algebra of the space, and $P_x$ is a measure that assigns to each subset the measure (# of elements)/6.  Also, the choice of $\\Omega=[0,1]$ was arbitrary-- it could've been $[0,2]$, or any other set.</p>\n\n<p>So my question is, why bother constructing an arbitrary $\\Omega$ with a $\\sigma$-algebra and a measure, and define a random variable as a map from the $\\sigma$-algebra to the real line?  </p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-05-13T22:24:15.883000", "posts_rownum": "posts_10000"}, "posts_10147": {"id": 10964, "owneruserid": 3248, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 10972, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "In convergence in probability or a.s. convergence w.r.t which measure is the probability?", "tags": "<random-variable><probability>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I was presenting proofs of WLLN and a version of SLLN (assuming bounded 4th central moment) when somebody asked which measure is the probability with respect too and I realised that, on reflection, I wasn't quite sure.</p>\n\n<p>It seems that it is straightforward, since in both laws we have a sequence of $X_{i}$'s, independent RVs with identical mean and finite variance. There is only one random variable in sight, namely the $X_{i}$, so the probability must be w.r.t the distribution of the $X_{i}$, right? But then that doesn't seem quite right for the strong law since the typical proof technique is then to define a new RV $S_{n} := \\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_{i}$ and work with that, and the limit is <em>inside</em> the probability:</p>\n\n<p>$\nPr \\left[\\lim_{n \\rightarrow \\infty}\\frac{1}{n}\\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_{i} = E[X_{i}]\\right]=1\n$</p>\n\n<p>So now it looks as if the RV is the sums over $n$ terms, so the probability is over the distribution of the sums $S_{n}$, where $n$ is no longer fixed. Is that correct? If it is, how would we go about constructing a suitable probability measure on the sequences of partial sums?</p>\n\n<p>Happy to receive intuitive responses as to what is going on as well as formal ones using e.g. real or complex analysis, undergrad probability/statistics, basic measure theory. I've read <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/2230\">Convergence in probability vs. almost sure convergence</a> and associated links, but find no help there.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-05-19T10:43:13.270000", "posts_rownum": "posts_10147"}, "posts_10255": {"id": 11102, "owneruserid": 1977, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 11103, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Factor analysis problem -- singular covariance matrix?", "tags": "<spss><factor-analysis><python>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'm having trouble performing factor analysis on my dataset.</p>\n\n<p>When I perform the factor analysis in SPSS (default settings), it works fine. Redundant dimensions need to be removed\"</p>\n\n<p>Upon looking into the MDP documentation, it says \"...returns the Maximum A Posteriori estimate of the latent variables.\"  Being a factor analysis newbie, I wasn't too clear on what this meant, but I tried changing the default extraction method in SPSS from \"principal components\" to \"maximum likelihood\".  Then, in SPSS, I get the error:</p>\n\n<p>\"This matrix is not positive definite.\"</p>\n\n<p>Are these two errors the same thing?  Regardless, what can I do to fix my dataset so that the covariance matrix is not singular?</p>\n\n<p>Thanks!</p>\n\n<p><strong>edit:</strong> OK, so I was trying to keep things simplified, but perhaps its better to just explain everything from the start.</p>\n\n<p>I have a series of documents. (Although I think technically, SPSS is doing PCA even though its under the 'Factor Analysis' heading).</p>\n\n<p>I tried using MDP's PCANode, but that doesn't seem to give me anything close to what I want.  Strangely, if I transpose my matrix, the factor analysis does work (it will group the terms, instead of the documents).</p>\n\n<p>Hopefully this all makes a little more sense now...</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-05-22T03:56:56.093000", "posts_rownum": "posts_10255"}, "posts_10519": {"id": 11381, "owneruserid": 4238, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 11382, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to report asymmetrical confidence intervals of a proportion?", "tags": "<r><confidence-interval><binomial-distribution>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I've calculated the proportion of chicks fledged out of the number of eggs hatched in each year using <code>prop.test()</code> in R.
