God forbid, if required to defend this accuracy before the client, how could this be justified?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-06-01T09:00:07.850000", "posts_rownum": "posts_10556"}, "posts_10571": {"id": 11436, "owneruserid": 557, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "$L_1$ or $L_.5$ metrics for clustering?", "tags": "<clustering><distance-functions><rule-of-thumb>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Does anyone use the $L_1$ or $L_.5$ metrics for clustering, rather than $L_2$ ?<br>\nAggarwal et al.,\n<a href=\"http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/download?doi=10.1.1.23.7409&rep=rep1&type=pdf\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">On the surprising behavior of distance metrics in high dimensional space</a>\nsaid (in 2001) that</p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p>$L_1$ is consistently more preferable\n  then the Euclidean distance metric\n  $L_2$ for high dimensional data mining\n  applications</p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p>and claimed that $L_.5$ or $L_.1$ can be better yet.</p>\n\n<p>Reasons for using $L_1$ or $L_.5$ could be theoretical or experimental,\ne.g. sensitivity to outliers / Kabán's papers,\nor programs run on real or synthetic data (reproducible please).\nAn example or a picture would help my layman's intuition.</p>\n\n<p>This question is a follow-up to Bob Durrant's answer to\n<a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/6314/when-is-nearest-neighbor-meaningful-today\">When-is-nearest-neighbor-meaningful-today</a>.\nAs he says, the choice of $p$ will be both data and application dependent;\nnonetheless, reports of real experience would be useful.</p>\n\n<p><hr>\nNotes added Tuesday 7 June:</p>\n\n<p>I stumbled across\n\"Statistical data analysis based on the L1-norm and related methods\",\nDodge ed., 2002, 454p, isbn 3764369205 — dozens of conference papers.</p>\n\n<p>Can anyone analyze distance concentration for i.i.d. exponential features ?\nOne reason for exponentials is that $|exp - exp| \\sim exp$;\nanother (non-expert) is that it's the max-entropy distribution $\\ge$ 0;\na third is that some real data sets, in particular SIFTs,\nlook roughly exponential.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-06-01T16:42:07.290000", "posts_rownum": "posts_10571"}, "posts_10717": {"id": 11595, "owneruserid": 4496, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 11777, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Whether to use an offset in a Poisson regression when predicting total career goals scored by hockey players", "tags": "<r><regression><poisson-distribution><generalized-linear-model><count-data>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I've got a question concerning wheter or not to use an offset. For example there could be a player picked up who has 50 goals in 100 games and another player who has 20 goals in 50 games and so on.</p>\n\n<p>What am I supposed to do when I'd like to estimate the number of goals? \nIs it really necessary to use an offset here? </p>\n\n<p>References:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>See <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/11182/when-to-use-an-offset-in-a-poisson-regression\">this previous question discussing when to use offsets in Poisson regression in general.</a></li>\n</ul>\n", "creationdate": "2011-06-05T14:26:51.900000", "posts_rownum": "posts_10717"}, "posts_10919": {"id": 11812, "owneruserid": 4054, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 11814, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Sanity check: how low can a p-value go?", "tags": "<hypothesis-testing><p-value><sample-size><statistical-power>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I am using a ranksum test to compare the median of two samples ($n=120000$) and have found that they are significantly different with: <code>p = 1.12E-207</code>. Like this, for example:</p>\n\n<pre><code>d   <- data.frame(a=factor(sample(c('a1','a2'), 100, rep=T)),\n                  b=factor(sample(c('b1','b2'), 100, rep=T)));\nd$y <- as.numeric(d$a)*rnorm(100, mean=.75, sd=1) +\n       as.numeric(d$b)*rnorm(100, mean=1.2, sd=1) +\n       as.numeric(d$a)*as.numeric(d$b)*rnorm(100, mean=.5, sd=1) +\n       rnorm(100);\n</code></pre>\n\n<ol>\n<li><p>In the absence of a significant interaction, by default (i.e. <code>contr.treatment</code>) the output of <code>Anova()</code> is the overall significance of <code>a</code> over all levels of <code>b</code> and of <code>b</code> over all levels of <code>a</code>, is that right?</p></li>\n<li><p>How should I specify a contrast that would allow me to test the significance of effect <code>a</code> with <code>b</code> being held constant at level b1, of effect <code>a</code> with <code>b</code> being held constant at level b2, and of the interaction <code>a:b</code>? </p></li>\n</ol>\n", "creationdate": "2011-07-13T15:52:10.600000", "posts_rownum": "posts_11967"}, "posts_12157": {"id": 13197, "owneruserid": 196, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 13201, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Differences between MANOVA and Repeated Measures ANOVA?", "tags": "<anova><repeated-measures><manova><sphericity>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<ul>\n<li>What is the difference between a repeated measures ANOVA over some factor (say experimental condition) and a MANOVA?</li>\n<li>In particular one website I stumbled across suggested that MANOVA does not make the same assumption of sphericity that repeated measures ANOVA does, is that true?  \n\n<ul>\n<li>If so, why would one not just always use MANOVA? </li>\n</ul></li>\n<li>I am trying to conduct a repeated measures ANOVA with multiple DVs, what is the appropriate approach?   </li>\n</ul>\n", "creationdate": "2011-07-18T15:20:42.077000", "posts_rownum": "posts_12157"}, "posts_12217": {"id": 13259, "owneruserid": 5471, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 13286, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What is the distribution of maximum of a pair of iid draws, where the minimum is an order statistic of other minima?", "tags": "<distributions><probability><extreme-value><order-statistics>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Consider $n\\cdot m$ independent draws from cdf $F(x)$, which is defined over 0-1, where $n$ and $m$ are integers.  Arbitrarily group the draws into $n$ groups with m values in each group.  Look at the minimum value in each group.  Take the group that has the greatest of these minima.  Now, what is the distribution that defines the maximum value in that group?\nMore generally, what is the distribution for the $j$-th order statistic of $m$ draws of $F(x)$, where the kth order of those m draws is also the pth order of the n draws of that kth order statistic?</p>\n\n<p>All of that is at the most abstract, so here is a more concrete example.\nConsider 8 draws of $F(x)$.  Group them into 4 pairs of 2.  Compare the minimum value in each pair.  Select the pair with the highest  of these 4 minima.  Label that draw \"a\".  Label the other value in that same pair as \"b\".  What is the distribution $F_b(b)$?  We know $b>a$.  We know a is the maximum of 4 minimums of $F(x)$, of $F_a(a) = (1-(1-F(x))^2)^4$.  What is $F_b(b)$? </p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-07-19T18:05:43.903000", "posts_rownum": "posts_12217"}, "posts_12439": {"id": 13518, "owneruserid": 5558, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 13525, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How do I develop a metric for comparisons that involves a combination of variables at different scales?", "tags": "<correlation>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I am trying to select the best answer from a set of samples, using two variables at different scales. </p>\n\n<p>In the data below, each row indicates the accuracy of a given measurement, the number of times it occurs in the sample set, and the answer that it indicates.  </p>\n\n<p>Accuracy:0.00886982324861, Frequency:5.0, Answer:1.0<br>\nAccuracy:0.0104663914334,  Frequency:1.0, Answer:2.0<br>\nAccuracy:0.0112727390014,  Frequency:1.0, Answer:2.0<br>\nAccuracy:0.0143046058573,  Frequency:3.0, Answer:1.0<br>\nAccuracy:0.0251741710747,  Frequency:1.0, Answer:1.0<br>\nAccuracy:0.0322055218681,  Frequency:1.0, Answer:2.0<br></p>\n\n<p>Until now, I have been ignoring the accuracy and simply selecting the answer that occurs more frequently i.e., Answer 1 occurs 9 times, Answer 2 occurs 3 times, so select answer 1.  </p>\n\n<p>A product of frequency and accuracy produces a metric that takes both into account, but the different scales weights frequency disproportionately more than accuracy.</p>\n\n<p>How can I calculate a metric that allows me to use both accuracy and frequency, but accounts for their different scales? </p>\n\n<p>Your help is greatly appreciated,\nJohn</p>\n\n<p>*EDIT\nThanks for your response. "tags": "<classification><random-forest>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Based on a <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/124/statistical-classification-of-text/143#143\">response</a> to the question \"<a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/124/statistical-classification-of-text\">Statistical classification of text</a>\", I've decided that I want to use a <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_forest\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">random forest</a> to perform various classifications of text.</p>\n\n<p>Specifically, I am getting YouTube video data from their XML feeds.  Here is <a href=\"http://gdata.youtube.com/feeds/api/videos/ltkMAcv2cas\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">an example</a>:</p>\n\n<pre><code><entry gd:etag=\"W/\"DUQBR347eCp7I2A9WhdXFEQ.\"\">\n    <id>tag:youtube.com,2008:video:ltkMAcv2cas</id>\n    <published>2010-12-23T18:11:28.000Z</published>\n    <updated>2011-08-28T02:09:16.000Z</updated>\n    <category scheme=\"http://schemas.google.com/g/2005#kind\"\n        term=\"http://gdata.youtube.com/schemas/2007#video\"/>\n    <category scheme=\"http://gdata.youtube.com/schemas/2007/keywords.cat\" \n        term=\"SSF4AE\"/>\n    <!-- More categories/keywords here -->\n    <title>SSF4AE Mago 2D God VS Kazunoko aka Inoue</title>\n    <!-- More video information here, description, etc -->\n</entry>\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>With that, I have very specific data that I believe I can use as the basis for variables in a random forest:</p>\n\n<pre><code>Variable    Value\n--------    -----\nTitle       SSF4AE Mago 2D God VS Kazunoko aka Inoue\nCategory    SSF4AE\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Looking at the video and based on the title/categories, I know that this is a video of the game <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Street_Fighter_IV#Arcade_Edition\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Super Street Fighter 4: Arcade Edition</a> (SSF4AE).</p>\n\n<p>Looking at the <a href=\"http://www.alglib.net/dataanalysis/decisionforest.php\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">alglib Decision Forest</a>, I also read the <a href=\"http://www.alglib.net/dataanalysis/generalprinciples.php\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">general principals of data analysis methods</a>, which speaks about encoding specifically for the algorithms on alglib; while I won't use it specifically, I believe it expanded my understanding of how data should be represented for a random forest.</p>\n\n<p>Basically, using the above data, I'd need to transform each data point into a number of some sort.</p>\n\n<p>For example, I could transform this into the following variables:</p>\n\n<pre><code>Variable                 Value\n--------                 -----\nHas \"SSF4AE\" in Title        1\nEquals \"SSF4AE\"              1\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Now, assuming I know that this video is for SSF4AE, and that I know that SSF4AE is a common acronym used to identify the game, would using the above as variables work for a random forest for training and classification?</p>\n\n<p>Of course, that's a small set, and it's a very rough set of variables; my understanding is that a random forest basically will create nodes where there is a threshold for the variable, values over this fall on one side of the tree, values under on the other side.</p>\n\n<p>In the above example, there are only two options, true or false.</p>\n\n<p>However, I imagine I can do something like get the <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tf%E2%80%93idf\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">term-frequency/inverse document frequency</a> and use that (using <a href=\"http://incubator.apache.org/lucene.net/\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Lucene.NET</a> or <a href=\"http://www.elasticsearch.org/\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">elasticsearch</a>), like so (numbers are not accurate)</p>\n\n<pre><code>Variable                               Value\n--------                               -----\nTerm Query for \"SSF4AE\" in Title        0.36\nTerm Query for \"SSF4AE\" in Category     1.00\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>And then train the random forest on that.</p>\n\n<p>I assume that if the variables were done as above, then I could also place things such as boosts on the variables (in the tf/idf calculation) where I see that they are more prominent or I feel I want them to have more weight.</p>\n\n<p>And finally, I can add more variables, but they have to be very specific.  For example, I <em>know</em> that if there is a character <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Street_Fighter_characters#Yun_and_Yang\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Yun</a> that only appears in SSF4AE, (not previous versions of Street Fighter 4), as well as in <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Street_Fighter_III\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Street Fighter III</a>.  To that end, I can add two more variables:</p>\n\n<pre><code>Variable                               Value\n--------                               -----\nTerm Query for \"SSF4AE\" in Title        0.36\nTerm Query for \"SSF4AE\" in Category     1.00\nOne character is Yun                       1\nTerm Query for \"3S\" in Title            0.00\nTerm Query for \"3SO\" in Title           0.00\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>(\"3SO\" and \"3S\" being common acronyms for Street Fighter III: Third Strike)</p>\n\n<p>However, for another video, which I know is for 3S, I the variables might look like this:</p>\n\n<pre><code>Variable                               Value\n--------                               -----\nTerm Query for \"SSF4AE\" in Title        0.00\nTerm Query for \"SSF4AE\" in Category     0.00\nOne character is Yun                       1\nTerm Query for \"3S\" in Title            0.54\nTerm Query for \"3SO\" in Title           0.00\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Where the training set would indicate that video is for 3S.</p>\n\n<p>That said, are these feasible ways of going about determining the variables of a random forest?</p>\n\n<p>Also, if I understand correctly, the random forest will also indicate which variables contributed the most to the classification, so I can discard them during classification later (if I want) or add different ones to get better classifications I have two distinct motivations for asking, which may well lead to different suggestions:</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li><p>I'd like to better understand the statistics motivation behind many problems considered by probabilists.</p></li>\n<li><p>I'd like to know how to better interpret the results of Monte Carlo simulations which I sometimes do to form mathematical conjectures.</p></li>\n</ol>\n\n<p>I'm open to the possibility that the best way to go is not to look for something like \"Statistics for Probabilists\" and just go to a more introductory source.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-21T13:50:08.847000", "posts_rownum": "posts_396"}, "posts_7": {"id": 7, "owneruserid": 38, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 18, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Locating freely available data samples", "tags": "<dataset><sample><population><teaching>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I've been working on a new method for analyzing and parsing datasets to identify and isolate subgroups of a population without foreknowledge of any subgroup's characteristics.  While the method works well enough with artificial data samples (i.e. datasets created specifically for the purpose of identifying and segregating subsets of the population), I'd like to try testing it with live data.</p>\n\n<p>What I'm looking for is a freely available (i.e. non-confidential, non-proprietary) data source. Anybody know why we take this square approach as a standard?</p>\n\n<p>The definition of standard deviation:</p>\n\n<p>$\\sigma = \\sqrt{E\\left[\\left(X - \\mu\\right)^2\\right]}.$\r</p>\n\n<p>Can't we just take the absolute value instead and still be a good measurement?</p>\n\n<p>$\\sigma = E\\left[|X - \\mu|\\right]$\r</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-19T21:04:39.057000", "posts_rownum": "posts_76"}, "posts_171": {"id": 183, "owneruserid": 166, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 518, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What tools could be used for applying clustering algorithms on MovieLens?", "tags": "<clustering>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I need to analyze the 100k MovieLens dataset for clustering with two algorithms of my choice, between the likes of k-means, agnes, diana, dbscan, and several others. Why not simply always use the Welch adjusted t?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-20T14:19:41.383000", "posts_rownum": "posts_293"}, "posts_567": {"id": 577, "owneruserid": 196, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 767, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Is there any reason to prefer the AIC or BIC over the other?", "tags": "<modeling><aic><cross-validation><bic><model-selection>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>The AIC and BIC are both methods of assessing model fit penalized for the number of estimated parameters.  As I understand it, BIC penalizes models more for free parameters than does AIC.  Beyond a preference based on the stringency of the criteria, are there any other reasons to prefer AIC over BIC or vice versa?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-23T20:49:12.340000", "posts_rownum": "posts_567"}, "posts_353": {"id": 372, "owneruserid": 252, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 381, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What are the key statistical concepts that relate to data mining?", "tags": "<probability><data-mining><cart>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>What topics in statistics are most useful/relevant to data mining?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-21T04:26:07.550000", "posts_rownum": "posts_353"}, "posts_393": {"id": 411, "owneruserid": 89, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Motivation for Kolmogorov distance between distributions", "tags": "<distributions><probability><hypothesis-testing><mathematical-statistics>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>There are many ways to measure how similar two probability distributions are.  Among methods which are popular (in different circles) are:</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li><p>the Kolmogorov distance: the sup-distance between the distribution functions;</p></li>\n<li><p>the Kantorovich-Rubinstein distance: the maximum difference between the expectations w.r.t. the two distributions of functions with Lipschitz constant $1$, which also turns out to be the $L^1$ distance between the distribution functions;</p></li>\n<li><p>the bounded-Lipschitz distance: like the K-R distance but the functions are also required to have absolute value at most $1$.</p></li>\n</ol>\n\n<p>These have different advantages and disadvantages.  Only convergence in the sense of 3. actually corresponds precisely to convergence in distribution; convergence in the sense of 1. or 2. is slightly stronger in general.  (In particular, if $X_n=\\frac{1}{n}$ with probability $1$, then $X_n$ converges to $0$ in distribution, but not in the Kolmogorov distance. However, if the limit distribution is continuous then this pathology doesn't occur.) </p>\n\n<p>From the perspective of elementary probability or measure theory, 1. is very natural because it compares the probabilities of being in some set. A more sophisticated probabilistic perspective, on the other hand, tends to focus more on expectations than probabilities. Also, from the perspective of functional analysis, distances like 2. or 3. based on duality with some function space are very appealing, because there is a large set of mathematical tools for working with such things.</p>\n\n<p>However, my impression (correct me if I'm wrong!) is that in statistics, the Kolmogorov distance is the usually preferred way of measuring similarity of distributions.  I can guess one reason: if one of the distributions is discrete with finite support -- in particular, if it is the distribution of some real-world data -- then the Kolmogorov distance to a model distribution is easy to compute.  (The K-R distance would be slightly harder to compute, and the B-L distance would probably be impossible in practical terms.)</p>\n\n<p>So my question (finally) is, are there other reasons, either practical or theoretical, to favor the Kolmogorov distance (or some other distance) for statistical purposes?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-21T13:39:06.783000", "posts_rownum": "posts_393"}, "posts_477": {"id": 490, "owneruserid": 223, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 606, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Variable selection procedure for binary classification", "tags": "<machine-learning><classification><multiple-comparisons><multivariate-analysis><feature-selection>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>What are the <strong>variable/feature  selection that you prefer</strong> for binary classification when there are many more variables/feature than observations in the learning set? The aim here is to discuss what is the feature selection procedure that reduces the best the classification error. </p>\n\n<p>We can <strong>fix notations</strong> for consistency: for $i \\in \\{0, 1\\}$, let $\\{x_1^i,\\dots, x_{n_i}^i\\}$ be the learning set of observations from group $i$.   So $n_0 + n_1 = n$ is the size of the learning set. We set $p$ to be the number of features (i.e. the dimension of the feature space). Let $x[i]$ denote the $i$-th coordinate of $x \\in \\mathbb{R}^p$. </p>\n\n<p>Please give full references if you cannot give the details. </p>\n\n<p>EDIT (updated continuously):  Procedures proposed in the answers below </p>\n\n<ul>\n<li><strong>Greedy forward selection</strong> <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/490/variable-selection-procedure-for-binary-classification/497#497\">Variable selection procedure for binary classification</a></li>\n<li><strong>Backward elimination</strong> <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/490/variable-selection-procedure-for-binary-classification/501#501\">Variable selection procedure for binary classification</a></li>\n<li><strong>Metropolis scanning / MCMC</strong> <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/490/variable-selection-procedure-for-binary-classification/505#505\">Variable selection procedure for binary classification</a></li>\n<li><strong>penalized logistic regression</strong> <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/490/variable-selection-procedure-for-binary-classification/606#606\">Variable selection procedure for binary classification</a></li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>As this is community wiki there can be more discussion and update</p>\n\n<p>I have one remark: in a certain sense, you all give a procedure that permit ordering of variables but not variable selection (you are quite evasive on how to select the number of features, I guess you all use cross validation?) Can you improve the answers in this direction? (as this is community wiki you don't need to be the answer writter to add an information about how to select the number of variables? I have openned a question in this direction here <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/880/cross-validation-to-select-the-number-of-used-variables-in-very-high-dimensional\">Cross validation in very high dimension (to select the number of used variables in very high dimensional classification)</a>)</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-22T11:10:29.417000", "posts_rownum": "posts_477"}, "posts_565": {"id": 575, "owneruserid": 196, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 762, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Post-hocs for within subjects tests?", "tags": "<r><repeated-measures><multiple-comparisons><post-hoc><sphericity>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>What is the preferred method for for conducting post-hocs for within subjects tests?  I've seen published work where Tukey's HSD is employed but a review of Keppel and Maxwell & Delaney suggests that the likely violation of sphericity in these designs makes the error term incorrect and this approach problematic.  Maxwell & Delaney provide an approach to the problem in their book, but I've never seen it done that way in any stats package.  Is the approach they offer appropriate?  Would a Bonferroni or Sidak correction on multiple paired sample t-tests be reasonable?  An acceptable answer will provide general R code which can conduct post-hocs on simple, multiple-way, and mixed designs as produced by the <code>ezANOVA</code> function in the <code>ez</code> package, and appropriate citations that are likely to pass muster with reviewers.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-23T20:14:05.327000", "posts_rownum": "posts_565"}, "posts_882": {"id": 899, "owneruserid": 219, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Separating two populations from the sample", "tags": "<dataset><outliers><expectation-maximization>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'm trying to separate two groups of values from a single data set. Which is not ideal, but seem to produce reasonable enough result.</p>\n\n<p>Is my assumption statistically sound? What would be a better way to go about this?</p>\n\n<p>p.s. please fix the tags someone.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-28T13:53:18.503000", "posts_rownum": "posts_882"}, "posts_901": {"id": 920, "owneruserid": 559, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 940, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Test if probabilities are statistically different?", "tags": "<hypothesis-testing>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I completed a Monte Carlo simulation that consisted of one million ($10^6$) individual simulations. The simulation returns a variable, $p$, that can be either 1 or 0. I then weight the simulations based on predefined criteria and calculate the probability of $p$. I also calculate a risk ratio using $p$:</p>\n\n<p>$$\\text{Risk ratio} = P(p|\\text{test case}) / P(p|\\text{control case})$$</p>\n\n<p>I had eight Monte Carlo runs, which consist of one control case and seven test cases. </p>\n\n<p>I need to know if the probabilities of $p$ are statistically different compared to the other cases. I know I can use a multiple comparison test or nonparametric ANOVA to test individual variables, but how do I do this for probabilities? </p>\n\n<hr>\n\n<p>For example are these two probabilities statistically different?:</p>\n\n<p><em>Probabilities</em>:</p>\n\n<p>$P(p|\\text{test #3}) = 4.08 \\times 10^{-5}$</p>\n\n<p>$P(p|\\text{test #4}) = 6.10 \\times 10^{-5}$</p>\n\n<p><em>Risk Ratios</em>:</p>\n\n<p>$\\text{Risk Ratio}(\\text{test #3}) = 0.089$</p>\n\n<p>$\\text{Risk Ratio}(\\text{test #4}) = 0.119$ </p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-28T17:15:09.090000", "posts_rownum": "posts_901"}, "posts_954": {"id": 973, "owneruserid": 223, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1020, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Free data set for very high dimensional classification", "tags": "<machine-learning><classification><dataset><large-data>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>What are the <strong>freely available data set for classification with more than 1000 features</strong> (or sample points if it contains curves)? </p>\n\n<p>There is already a community wiki about free data sets:\n<a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/7/locating-freely-available-data-samples/\">Locating freely available data samples</a></p>\n\n<p>But here, it would be nice to have a <strong>more focused list that can be used more conveniently</strong>, also I propose the following rules:</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li>One post <strong>per dataset</strong> </li>\n<li><strong>No</strong> link to set of dataset </li>\n<li><p>each data set <strong>must</strong> be associated with</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li><p>a <strong>name</strong> (to figure out what it is about)  and a link to the dataset (R datasets can be named with package name)</p></li>\n<li><p>the number of features (let say it is <strong>p</strong>) the size of the dataset (let say it is <strong>n</strong>) and the number of labels/class (let say it is <strong>k</strong>)    </p></li>\n<li><p>a typical <strong>error rate</strong> from your experience (state the used algorithm in to words) or from the litterature (in this last case link the paper) </p></li>\n</ul></li>\n</ol>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-29T12:02:28.347000", "posts_rownum": "posts_954"}, "posts_5423": {"id": 5750, "owneruserid": 888, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 5754, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Look and you shall find (a correlation)", "tags": "<correlation><multiple-comparisons><permutation-test>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I have several hundred measurements. Among these there should (statistically) be a high correlation, even if the data is completely random (each measure has only about 100 datapoints).</p>\n\n<p>When I find a correlation, how do I include the information about how hard I looked for a correlation, into it? </p>\n\n<p>I am not at a high level in statistics, so please bear with me.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-12-25T22:16:04.897000", "posts_rownum": "posts_5423"}, "posts_1293": {"id": 1352, "owneruserid": 144, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1384, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "References for how to plan a study", "tags": "<references><experiment-design>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>In an average (median?) conversation about statistics you will often find yourself discussing this or that method of analyzing this or that type of data. In my experience, careful study design with special thought with regards to the statistical analysis is often neglected (working in biology/ecology, this seems to be a prevailing occurrence). Statisticians often find themselves in a gridlock with insufficient (or outright wrong) collected data. To paraphrase Ronald Fisher, they are forced to do a post-mortem on the data, which often leads to weaker conclusions, if at all.</p>\n\n<p>I would like to know which references you use to construct a successful study design, preferably for a wide range of methods (e.g. <em>t</em>-test, GLM, GAM, ordination techniques...) that helps you avoid pitfalls mentioned above.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-06T08:06:13.193000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1293"}, "posts_1240": {"id": 1292, "owneruserid": 217, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1297, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What is the weak side of decision trees?", "tags": "<machine-learning><nonparametric><cart>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p><a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decision_tree\">Decision trees</a> seems to be a very understandable machine learning method.\nOnce created it can be easily inspected by a human which is a great advantage in some applications. </p>\n\n<p>What are the practical weak sides of Decision Trees?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-05T10:42:44.327000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1240"}, "posts_1329": {"id": 1386, "owneruserid": 795, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1390, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Robust t-test for mean ", "tags": "<hypothesis-testing><t-test><finance><robust>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I am trying to test the null $E[X] = 0$, against the local alternative $E[X] > 0$, for a random variable $X$, subject to mild to medium skew and kurtosis of the random variable. Following suggestions by Wilcox in 'Introduction to Robust Estimation and Hypothesis Testing', I have looked at tests based on the trimmed mean, the median, as well as the M-estimator of location (Wilcox' \"one-step\" procedure). These robust tests do outperform the standard t-test, in terms of power, when testing with a distribution that is non-skewed, but leptokurtotic.</p>\n\n<p>However, when testing with a distribution that is skewed, these one-sided tests are either far too liberal or far too conservative under the null hypothesis, depending on whether the distribution is left- or right-skewed, respectively. For example, with 1000 observations, the test based on the median will actually reject ~40% of the time, at the nominal 5% level. The reason for this is obvious: for skewed distributions, the median and the mean are rather different. However, in my application, I really need to test the mean, not the median, not the trimmed mean.</p>\n\n<p><strong>Is there a more robust version of the t-test that actually tests for the mean, but is impervious to skew and kurtosis?</strong></p>\n\n<p>Ideally the procedure would work well in the no-skew, high-kurtosis case as well. The 'one-step' test is almost good enough, with the 'bend' parameter set relatively high, but it is less powerful than the trimmed mean tests when there is no skew, and has some troubles maintaining the nominal level of rejects under skew.</p>\n\n<p><strong>background:</strong> the reason I really care about the mean, and not the median, is that the test would be used in a financial application. For example, if you wanted to test whether a portfolio had positive expected log returns, the mean is actually appropriate because if you invest in the portfolio, you will experience all the returns (which is the mean times the number of samples), instead of $n$ duplicates of the median.  That is, I really care about the sum of $n$ draws from the R.V. $X$. </p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-07T05:18:58.967000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1329"}, "posts_1423": {"id": 1475, "owneruserid": null, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1491, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": "anonymous", "title": "Visualization software for clustering", "tags": "<data-visualization><clustering><software>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I want to cluster ~22000 points. After a satisfactory rotation, the rotated factor loading matrix <strong>L'</strong> will have the same ability to represent the correlation matrix and it can be used as the factor loading matrix, instead of the unrotated matrix <strong>L</strong>.</p>\n\n<p>The purpose of rotation is to make the rotated factor loading matrix have some desirable properties. One of the methods used is to rotate the factor loading matrix such that the rotated matrix will have a <strong>simple structure</strong>.</p>\n\n<p>L. L. Thurstone introduced the Principle of Simple Structure, as a general guide for factor rotation:</p>\n\n<h2>Simple Structure Criteria:</h2>\n\n<ol>\n<li>Each row of the factor matrix should contain at least one zero</li>\n<li>If there are m common factors, each column of the factor matrix should have at least m zeros</li>\n<li>For every pair of columns in the factor matrix, there should be several variables for which entries approach zero in the one column but not in the other</li>\n<li>For every pair of columns in the factor matrix, a large proportion of the variables should have entries approaching zero in both columns when there are four or more factors</li>\n<li>For every pair of columns in the factor matrix, there should be only a small number of variables with nonzero entries in both columns</li>\n</ol>\n\n<p>The ideal simple structure is such that:</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li>each item has a high, or meaningful, loading on one factor only and</li>\n<li>each factor have high, or meaningful, loadings for only some of the items.</li>\n</ol>\n\n<p>The problem is that, trying several combinations of rotation methods along with the parameters that each one accepts (especially for oblique ones), the number of candidate matrices increases and it is very difficult to see which one better meets the above criteria.</p>\n\n<p>When I first faced that problem I realized that I was unable to select the best match by merely 'looking' at them, and that I needed an algorithm to help me decide. Under the stress of project's deadlines, the most I could do was to write the following code in MATLAB, which accepts one rotation matrix at a time and returns (under some assumptions) whether each criterion is met or not.\nA new version (If I would ever tried to upgrade it) would accept a 3d matrix (a set of 2d matrices) as an argument, and the algorithm should return the one that better fits the above criteria.</p>\n\n<p>How would you extract an algorithm out of those criteria? I am just asking for your opinions (I also think that there's been criticism over the usefulness of the method by itself) and perhaps better approaches to the rotation matrix selection problem. </p>\n\n<p>Also, I would like to know what software do you prefer to perform FA. If it's R, what package do you use? (I must admit that if I had to do FA, I would turn to SPSS again). If someone wants to provide some code, I would prefer R or MATLAB. </p>\n\n<p>P.S. The above <a href=\"http://books.google.gr/books?id=5Jyaa2LQWbQC&pg=PA132&lpg=PA132&dq=%22The+criteria+of+simple+structure+was+originally+proposed%22&source=bl&ots=OXsCeU0Nzi&sig=qfiLMUyXsgwPunWBgNdSEeBNm34&hl=el&ei=huZeS5nkApTE4gaC67HsCw&sa=X&oi=book_result&ct=result&resnum=1&ved=0CAcQ6AEwAA#v=onepage&q=%22The%20criteria%20of%20simple%20structure%20was%20originally%20proposed%22&f=false\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Simple Structure Criteria formulation</a> can be found in the book <em>\"Making Sense of Factor Analysis\"</em> by PETT, M., LACKEY, N., SULLIVAN, J.</p>\n\n<p>P.S.2 (from the same book): <em>\"A test of successful factor analysis is the extent to which it can reproduce the original corr matrix. If you also used oblique solutions, among all select the one that generated the greatest number of highest and lowest factor loadings.\"</em> \nThis sounds like another constraint that the algorithm could use.</p>\n\n<p>P.S.3 This question has also been asked <a href=\"https://stackoverflow.com/questions/2139703/fa-choosing-rotation-matrix-based-on-simple-structure-criteria\">here</a>. However, I think it fits better on this site.</p>\n\n<pre><code>function [] = simple_structure_criteria (my_pattern_table)\n%Simple Structure Criteria\n%Making Sense of Factor Analysis, page 132\n\ndisp(' ');\ndisp('Simple Structure Criteria (Thurstone):');\ndisp('1. Each row of the factor matrix should contain at least one zero');\ndisp( '2. If there are m common factors, each column of the factor matrix should have at least m zeros');\ndisp( '3. For every pair of columns in the factor matrix, there should be several variables for which entries approach zero in the one column but not in the other');\ndisp( '4. For every pair of columns in the factor matrix, a large proportion of the variables should have entries approaching zero in both columns when there are four or more factors');\ndisp( '5. For every pair of columns in the factor matrix, there should be only a small number of variables with nonzero entries in both columns');\ndisp(' ');\ndisp( '(additional by Pedhazur and Schmelkin) The ideal simple structure is such that:');\ndisp( '6. Each item has a high, or meaningful, loading on one factor only and');\ndisp( '7. Each factor have high, or meaningful, loadings for only some of the items.');\n\ndisp('')\ndisp('Start checking...')\n\n%test matrix\n%ct=[76,78,16,7;19,29,10,13;2,6,7,8];\n%test it by giving: simple_structure_criteria (ct)\n\nct=abs(my_pattern_table);\n\nitems=size(ct,1);\nfactors=size(ct,2);\nmy_zero = 0.1;\napproach_zero = 0.2;\nseveral = floor(items / 3);\nsmall_number = ceil(items / 4);\nlarge_proportion = 0.30;\nmeaningful = 0.4;\nsome_bottom = 2;\nsome_top = floor(items / 2);\n\n% CRITERION 1\ndisp(' ');\ndisp('CRITERION 1');\nfor i = 1 : 1 : items\n    count = 0;\n    for j = 1 : 1 : factors\n        if (ct(i,j) < my_zero)\n            count = count + 1;\n            break\n        end\n    end\n    if (count == 0)\n        disp(['Criterion 1 is NOT MET for item ' num2str(i)])\n    end\nend\n\n\n% CRITERION 2\ndisp(' ');\ndisp('CRITERION 2');\nfor j = 1 : 1 : factors \n    m=0;\n    for i = 1 : 1 : items\n        if (ct(i,j) < my_zero)\n            m = m + 1;\n        end\n    end\n    if (m < factors)\n        disp(['Criterion 2 is NOT MET for factor ' num2str(j) '. m = ' num2str(m)]);\n    end\nend\n\n% CRITERION 3\ndisp(' ');\ndisp('CRITERION 3');\nfor c1 = 1 : 1 : factors - 1\n    for c2 = c1 + 1 : 1 : factors\n        test_several = 0;\n        for i = 1 : 1 : items\n            if ( (ct(i,c1)>my_zero && ct(i,c2)<my_zero) || (ct(i,c1)<my_zero && ct(i,c2)>my_zero) ) % approach zero in one but not in the other\n                test_several = test_several + 1;\n            end\n        end\n        disp(['several = ' num2str(test_several) ' for factors ' num2str(c1) ' and ' num2str(c2)]);\n        if (test_several < several)\n            disp(['Criterion 3 is NOT MET for factors ' num2str(c1) ' and ' num2str(c2)]);\n        end\n    end\nend\n\n% CRITERION 4\ndisp(' ');\ndisp('CRITERION 4');\nif (factors > 3)\n    for c1 = 1 : 1 : factors - 1\n        for c2 = c1 + 1 : 1 : factors\n            test_several = 0;\n            for i = 1 : 1 : items\n                if (ct(i,c1)<approach_zero && ct(i,c2)<approach_zero) % approach zero in both\n                    test_several = test_several + 1;\n                end\n            end\n            disp(['large proportion = ' num2str((test_several / items)*100) '% for factors ' num2str(c1) ' and ' num2str(c2)]);\n            if ((test_several / items) < large_proportion)\n                pr = sprintf('%4.2g',  (test_several / items) * 100 );\n                disp(['Criterion 4 is NOT MET for factors ' num2str(c1) ' and ' num2str(c2) '. Proportion is ' pr '%']);\n            end\n        end\n    end\nend\n\n% CRITERION 5\ndisp(' ');\ndisp('CRITERION 5');\nfor c1 = 1 : 1 : factors - 1\n    for c2 = c1 + 1 : 1 : factors\n        test_number = 0;\n        for i = 1 : 1 : items\n            if (ct(i,c1)>approach_zero && ct(i,c2)>approach_zero) % approach zero in both\n                test_number = test_number + 1;\n            end\n        end\n        disp(['small number = ' num2str(test_number) ' for factors ' num2str(c1) ' and ' num2str(c2)]);\n        if (test_number > small_number)\n            disp(['Criterion 5 is NOT MET for factors ' num2str(c1) ' and ' num2str(c2)]);\n        end\n    end\nend\n\n% CRITERION 6\ndisp(' ');\ndisp('CRITERION 6');\nfor i = 1 : 1 : items\n    count = 0;\n    for j = 1 : 1 : factors\n        if (ct(i,j) > meaningful)\n            count = count + 1;\n        end\n    end\n    if (count == 0 || count > 1)\n        disp(['Criterion 6 is NOT MET for item ' num2str(i)])\n    end\nend\n\n% CRITERION 7\ndisp(' ');\ndisp('CRITERION 7');\nfor j = 1 : 1 : factors \n    m=0;\n    for i = 1 : 1 : items\n        if (ct(i,j) > meaningful)\n            m = m + 1;\n        end\n    end\n    disp(['some items = ' num2str(m) ' for factor ' num2str(j)]);\n    if (m < some_bottom || m > some_top)\n        disp(['Criterion 7 is NOT MET for factor ' num2str(j)]);\n    end\nend\ndisp('')\ndisp('Checking completed.')\nreturn\n</code></pre>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-18T07:36:59.733000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1730"}, "posts_1766": {"id": 1848, "owneruserid": 991, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1849, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Bayesian rating system with multiple categories for each rating", "tags": "<bayesian>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I'm implementing a rating system to be used on my website, and I think the Bayesian average is the best way to go about it. Every item will be rated in six different categories by the users. I don't want items with only one high rating to shoot to the top though, which is why I want to implement a Bayesian system.</p>\n\n<p>Here is the formula:</p>\n\n<pre><code>Bayesian Rating = ( (avg_num_votes * avg_rating) + (this_num_votes * this_rating) ) / (avg_num_votes + this_num_votes)\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Because the items will be rated in 6 different categories, should I use the average of the sums of those categories as \"this_rating\" for the Bayesian system? For instance, take one item with two ratings (scale of 0-5):</p>\n\n<pre><code>Rating 1:\n  Category A: 3\n  Category B: 1\n  Category C: 2\n  Category D: 4\n  Category E: 5\n  Category F: 3\n  Sum: 18\n\nRating 2:\n  Category A: 2\n  Category B: 3\n  Category C: 3\n  Category D: 5\n  Category E: 0\n  Category F: 1\n  Sum: 14\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Should \"this_rating\" be simply the average of the sums listed above? Is my thinking correct, or should a Bayesian system be implemented for each category as well (or is that overthinking it)?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-18T16:43:11.870000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1766"}, "posts_1882": {"id": 1961, "owneruserid": 253, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1981, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Can you use normal correlation for vectors with only 2 (or 3), ordered, levels?", "tags": "<r><correlation><association-measure><ordinal-data>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>When one wants to compute the correlation of two vectors of a continues variables, one uses pearson (or spearman) correlation.</p>\n\n<p><strong>But what should (can) one use for the case of two vectors with 2 (or 3) ordered levels only?  Is spearman enough, or does it require another method?</strong></p>\n\n<p>I remember coming across someone who once claimed to me that OR (odds ratio) is more fitting for such situations (for 2 by 2 tables, where order has no meaning), is this true?</p>\n\n<p>Here is an example R code, for allowing of answers relating to the same example:</p>\n\n<pre><code>set.seed(10)\n\nx2 <- sample(c(-1,1),50, T)\nx3 <- sample(c(-1:1),50, T)\ny3 <- sample(c(-1:1),50, T)\ny2 <- sample(c(-1,1),50, T)\n\ncor(x3,y3, method = c(\"spearman\"))\ncor(x2,y2, method = c(\"spearman\"))\ncor(x3,y2, method = c(\"spearman\"))\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>p.s: for the 2 by 2 case, I followed from the comments that categorical \"measures of association\" is the term to look for.  However, Part of the time I am comparing 2 on 3 tables, where on the factor with 3 levels there is order - so I would like to take use of that information.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-20T17:15:43.887000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1882"}, "posts_1884": {"id": 1963, "owneruserid": 919, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 1976, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Looking for good introductory treatment of meta-analysis", "tags": "<modeling><meta-analysis>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>A (non-statistician) colleague has been encountering meta-analyses in papers he reviews for medical journals and is looking for a good introductory level treatment so he can educate himself.  Any recommendations?  Favorites?  Books, monographs, nontechnical survey articles would all be fine.</p>\n\n<p>(Yes, he's familiar with the Wikipedia entry and other stuff readily accessible by a Google search, such as <a href=\"http://www.jerrydallal.com/LHSP/meta.htm\">Jerry Dallal's nice little article</a>.)</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-20T18:06:04.580000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1884"}, "posts_3093": {"id": 3270, "owneruserid": 776, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 3278, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Interpreting 2D correspondence analysis plots", "tags": "<interpretation><correspondence-analysis><biplot>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I've been searching the internet far and wide... I have yet to find a really good overview of how to interpret 2D correspondence analysis plots. Could someone offer some advice on interpreting the distances between points? </p>\n\n<p>Perhaps an example would help, here is a plot that's found on many of the websites I've seen that discuss correspondence analysis. The red triangles represent eye colour and the black dots represent hair colour.</p>\n\n<p><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/nVOUx.jpg\" alt=\"alt text\"></p>\n\n<p>Looking at the graph above, could you make a few statements about what you see in these data. Points of interest about the different dimensions and relationships between triangles and dots? </p>\n\n<p>An explanation of row-points verses column points, and the use of the word \"profile\" with particular focus on the example would be instrumental. </p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-02T22:12:51.957000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3093"}, "posts_1901": {"id": 1980, "owneruserid": 183, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Complete substantive examples of reproducible research using R", "tags": "<r><references><reproducible-research>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p><strong>The Question:</strong> Are there any good examples of <a href=\"https://reproducibleresearch.net/\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">reproducible research</a> using R that are freely available online?</p>\n<p><strong>Ideal Example:</strong>\nSpecifically, ideal examples would provide:</p>\n<ul>\n<li>The raw data (and ideally meta data explaining the data),</li>\n<li>All R code including data import, processing, analyses, and output generation,</li>\n<li>Sweave or some other approach for linking the final output to the final document,</li>\n<li>All in a format that is easily downloadable and compilable on a reader's computer.</li>\n</ul>\n<p>Ideally, the example would be a journal article or a thesis where the emphasis is on an actual applied topic as opposed to a statistical teaching example.</p>\n<p><strong>Reasons for interest:</strong>\nI'm particularly interested in applied topics in journal articles and theses, because in these situations, several additional issues arise:</p>\n<ul>\n<li>Issues arise related to data cleaning and processing,</li>\n<li>Issues arise related to managing metadata,</li>\n<li>Journals and theses often have style guide expectations regarding the appearance and formatting of tables and figures,</li>\n<li>Many journals and theses often have a wide range of analyses which raise issues regarding workflow (i.e., how to sequence analyses) and processing time (e.g., issues of caching analyses, etc.).</li>\n</ul>\n<p>Seeing complete working examples could provide good instructional material for researchers starting out with reproducible research.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-21T04:58:11.600000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1901"}, "posts_2149": {"id": 2230, "owneruserid": 1106, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2232, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Convergence in probability vs. almost sure convergence", "tags": (Or, in fact, any of the different types of convergence, but I mention these two in particular because of the Weak and Strong Laws of Large Numbers.)</p>\n\n<p>Sure, I can quote the definition of each and give an example where they differ, but I still don't quite get it.</p>\n\n<p>What's a good way to understand the difference? Why is the difference important? Is there a particularly memorable example where they differ?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-31T03:57:21.193000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2149"}, "posts_2153": {"id": 2234, "owneruserid": 253, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2235, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Alternatives to logistic regression in R", "tags": "<r><regression><logistic><classification><predictive-models>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I would like as many algorithms that perform the same task as logistic regression.  That is  algorithms/models that can give a prediction to a binary response (Y) with some explanatory variable (X).</p>\n\n<p>I would be glad if after you name the algorithm, if you would also show how to implement it in R.  Here is a code that can be updated with other models:</p>\n\n<pre><code>set.seed(55)\nn <- 100\nx <- c(rnorm(n), 1+rnorm(n))\ny <- c(rep(0,n), rep(1,n))\nr <- glm(y~x, family=binomial)\nplot(y~x)\nabline(lm(y~x), col='red', lty=2)\nxx <- seq(min(x), max(x), length=100)\nyy <- predict(r, data.frame(x=xx), type='response')\nlines(xx, yy, col='blue', lwd=5, lty=2)\ntitle(main='Logistic regression with the \"glm\" function')\n</code></pre>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-31T10:02:07.947000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2153"}, "posts_2221": {"id": 2306, "owneruserid": 1150, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2307, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Feature selection for \"final\" model when performing cross-validation in machine learning", "tags": "<machine-learning><classification><cross-validation><feature-selection><genetics>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I am getting a bit confused about feature selection and machine learning\nand I was wondering if you could help me out.  I have a microarray dataset that is\nclassified into two groups and has 1000s of features.  My aim is to get a small number of genes (my features) (10-20) in a signature that I will in theory be able to apply to\nother datasets to optimally classify those samples.  As I do not have that many samples (<100), I am not using a test and training set but using Leave-one-out cross-validation to help\ndetermine the robustness.  I have read that one should perform feature selection for each split of the samples i.e.</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li>Select one sample as the test set</li>\n<li>On the remaining samples perform feature selection</li>\n<li>Apply machine learning algorithm to remaining samples using the features selected</li>\n<li>Test whether the test set is correctly classified</li>\n<li>Go to 1.</li>\n</ol>\n\n<p>If you do this, you might get different genes each time, so how do you\nget your \"final\" optimal gene classifier? i.e. what is step 6.</p>\n\n<p>What I mean by optimal is the collection of genes that any further studies\nshould use.  For example, say I have a cancer/normal dataset and I want\nto find the top 10 genes that will classify the tumour type according to\nan SVM.  I would like to know the set of genes plus SVM parameters that\ncould be used in further experiments to see if it could be used as a\ndiagnostic test.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-02T10:25:42.330000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2221"}, "posts_2286": {"id": 2374, "owneruserid": 1154, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2375, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Factor analysis of questionnaires composed of Likert items", "tags": "<factor-analysis><scales><psychometrics><likert><psychology>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I used to analyse items from a psychometric point of view. But now I am trying to analyse other types of questions on motivation and other topics. These questions are all on Likert scales. My initial thought was to use factor analysis, because the questions are hypothesised to reflect some underlying dimensions.</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>But is factor analysis appropriate?</li>\n<li>Is it necessary to validate each question regarding its dimensionality ? </li>\n<li>Is there a problem with performing factor analysis on likert items?</li>\n<li>Are there any good papers and methods on how to conduct factor analysis on Likert and other categorical items?</li>\n</ul>\n", "creationdate": "2010-09-04T11:15:48.317000", "posts_rownum": "posts_2286"}, "posts_2392": {"id": 2493, "owneruserid": 1227, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2497, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Managing error with GPS routes (theoretical framework?)", "tags": "<error><sampling>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I'm looking for the appropriate theoretical framework or speciality to help me deal with understanding how to deal with the errors that the GPS system has - especially when dealing with routes.</p>\n<p>Fundamentally, I'm looking for the requirements on the data and any algorithms to use to be able to establish the length of a trail. The answer needs to be trustworthy.</p>\n<p>A friend of mine was the race director of a race which was billed as 160km but the Garmin watches everybody has makes it more like 190km+. It caused quite some grief at the finish line, let me tell you!</p>\n<p>So my friend went back to the course with various GPS devices in order to remap it and the results are interesting.</p>\n<p>Using a handheld Garmin Oregon 300 she got 33.7km for one leg. For the same leg on a wrist watch Garmin Forerunner 310xt it came out to 38.3km.</p>\n<p>When I got the data from the Oregon it was obvious that it was only recording data every 90 seconds or so. The Forerunner does it every couple of seconds.</p>\n<p>When I plotted the data from the Oregon I could see that it got confused by some switchbacks and put a line straight through them and a curve was made a little less.</p>\n<p>However, I muse that the difference in the recording frequency is much of the explanation. i.e. by recording every couple of seconds the Forerunner is closer to the real route. However, there will be an amount of error because of the way GPS works. If the points recorded are spread around the real route randomly (because of the error) then the total distance will be larger than the real route. (A wiggle line going either side of a straight line is longer than the straight line).</p>\n<p>So, my questions: 1. Are there any techniques I can use on a single dataset to reduce the error in a valid way? 2. Does my theory about the difference in recording frequency hold water? 3. If I have multiple recordings of the same routes are there any valid techniques to combine them to get closer to the real route?</p>\n<p>As I say, I don't really know what to search for to find any useful science about this. I'm looking for ways to establish just how long a given piece of trail is and it is very important to people. I'm sure somebody here knows better.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-04T08:33:05.990000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3119"}, "posts_2437": {"id": 2547, "owneruserid": 285, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 2550, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Why is median age a better statistic than mean age?", "tags": "<mean><median><types-of-averages>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<ul>\n<li>If you look at <a href=\"http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=world+population\" rel=\"noreferrer\">Wolfram Alpha</a></li>\n</ul>\n\n<p><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/x0ILQ.png\" alt=\"alt text\"></p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>Or this Wikipedia page <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_median_age\" rel=\"noreferrer\">List of countries by median age</a></li>\n</ul>\n\n<p><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/QBtjT.png\" alt=\"alt text\"></p>\n\n<p>Clearly <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Median\" rel=\"noreferrer\"><strong>median</strong></a> seems to be the statistic of choice when it comes to ages.</p>\n\n<p>I am not able to explain to myself why <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_mean\" rel=\"noreferrer\"><strong>arithmetic mean</strong></a> would be a worse statistic. X_N$, where $X_i$ are i.i.d. r.v. and $P(X_i = 1) = p$, and $p$ is an unknown parameter.</p>\n\n<p>Obviously, one can find an estimate for $p$: $\\hat{p}:=(X_1+\\dots+X_N)/N$.</p>\n\n<p>My question is how can I build a confidence interval for $p$?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-11-20T12:05:26.533000", "posts_rownum": "posts_4476"}, "posts_3704": {"id": 3911, "owneruserid": 1393, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "When are confidence intervals useful?", "tags": "<confidence-interval><interpretation>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>If I understand correctly a confidence interval of a parameter is an interval constructed by a <em>method</em> which yields intervals containing the true value for a specified proportion of samples. So the 'confidence' is about the method rather than the interval I compute from a particular sample. </p>\n\n<p>As a user of statistics I have always felt cheated by this since the space of all samples is hypothetical. All I have is one sample and I want to know what that sample tells me about a parameter.</p>\n\n<p>Is this judgement wrong? Are there ways of looking at confidence intervals, at least in some circumstances, which would be meaningful to users of statistics?</p>\n\n<p>[This question arises from second thoughts after dissing confidence intervals in a math.se answer <a href=\"https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/7564/calculating-a-sample-size-based-on-a-confidence-level/7572#7572\">https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/7564/calculating-a-sample-size-based-on-a-confidence-level/7572#7572</a> ]</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-23T07:48:41.417000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3704"}, "posts_3739": {"id": 3947, "owneruserid": 1224, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 3954, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Help me understand Support Vector Machines", "tags": "<machine-learning><classification><svm>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I understand the basics of what a Support Vector Machines' aim is in terms of classifying an input set into several different classes, but what I don't understand is some of the nitty-gritty details. What is their purpose?</p>\n\n<p>I'm doing a classification problem where I've captured pressure readings from sensors I've placed on the insole of a shoe. A subject will sit, stand, and walk for a couple of minutes while pressure data is recorded. I want to train a classifier to be able to determine whether a person is sitting, standing or walking and be able to do that for any future test data. What classifier type do I need to try? What is the best way for me to train a classifier from the data I've captured? I have 1000 entries for sitting, standing and walking (3x1000=3000 total), and they all have the following feature vector form. (pressurefromsensor1, pressurefromsensor2, pressurefromsensor3, pressurefromsensor4)</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-24T15:11:52.427000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3739"}, "posts_3802": {"id": 4023, "owneruserid": 1727, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Chi-square test for equality of distributions: how many zeroes does it tolerate?", "tags": "<distributions><chi-squared-test><contingency-tables>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I am comparing two groups of mutants each of which can have only one out of 21 different phenotypes. I would like to see whether distribution of these outcomes is similar between two groups. I found an <a href=\"http://www.fon.hum.uva.nl/Service/Statistics/EqualDistribX2.html\">online test</a> \n that calculates the \"Chi-square test for equality of distributions\" and gives me some plausible results. However, I have quite a few zeroes in this Table, so can I use chi-square in this case at all? </p>\n\n<p>Here is the table with two groups and counts of particular phenotypes:</p>\n\n<pre><code>2 1\n2 3\n1 6\n1 4\n13 77\n7 27\n0 1\n0 4\n0 2\n2 7\n2 3\n1 5\n1 9\n2 6\n0 3\n3 0\n1 3\n0 3\n1 0\n1 2\n0 1\n</code></pre>\n", "creationdate": "2010-10-27T14:39:11.707000", "posts_rownum": "posts_3802"}, "posts_3938": {"id": 4175, "owneruserid": 1614, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 4324, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Resampling, binomial, z- and t-test: help with real data", "tags": "<r><hypothesis-testing>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I am trying to understand how I can use resampling techniques to compliment my pre-planned analyses. This is not homework. I have a 5 sided die. 30 subjects call a number (1-5) and then roll the die. If it matches it's a hit, if not it's a miss. Each subject does this 25 times. </p>\n\n<p>N is the the number of trials (=25) and p is the probability of getting it correct (=.2) then the population value (mu) of the mean number correct is n*p=5. The population standard deviation, sigma, is square-root(n*p*[1-p]), which is 2.</p>\n\n<p>The experimental hypothesis (H1) is that subjects in this study will score above chance (above mu). The null hypothesis (H0) assumes a binomial distribution for each subject (they will score at mu).</p>\n\n<p>[<em>Please don't get too worried about why I am doing this. If it helps you to understand the problem then you can think of it as an ESP test (and therefore I am testing the ability of subjects to score above mu). Also if it helps, imagine that the task is a virtual reality die throwing task, where the virtual 5-sided die performs according to chance. There can be no bias from an imperfect die because the die is virtual.</em>]</p>\n\n<p>Okay. So before I conducted the \"experiment\" I had planned to compare the 30 subjects score with a one-sample t-test (comparing it to the null that mu=5). Then I discovered that the one-sample z-test was a more powerful test given what we know about the null hypothesis. Okay.</p>\n\n<p>Here is a simulation of my data in R:</p>\n\n<pre><code>binom.samp1 <- as.data.frame(matrix(rbinom(30*1, size=25, prob=0.2), ncol=1))\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Now R has a binom.test function, which gives the p-value regarding the number of successes over the number of trials. For my collected data (not the simulated data given):</p>\n\n<pre><code>>binom.test(174, 750, 1/5, alternative=\"g\")\nnumber of successes = 174, number of trials = 750, p-value = 0.01722\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Now the one-sample t-test that I had originally planned to use (mainly because I'd never heard of the alternatives - should've paid more attention in higher statistics):</p>\n\n<pre><code>>t.test(binom.samp1-5, alternative=\"g\")\nt = 1.7647, df = 29, p-value = 0.04407\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>and for completedness sake: the one-sample z-test (<a href=\"http://rgm2.lab.nig.ac.jp/RGM2/R_man-2.9.0/library/BSDA/man/z.test.html\" rel=\"nofollow\">BSDA package</a>):</p>\n\n<pre><code>>z.test(binom.samp1, mu=5, sigma.x=2, alternative=\"g\")\nz = 2.1909, p-value = 0.01423\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>So. My first question is, <strong>am I right in concluding that the <a href=\"http://sekhon.berkeley.edu/stats/html/binom.test.html\" rel=\"nofollow\">binom.test</a> is the correct test given the data and hypothesis?</strong> In other words, does <em>t</em> approximate to <em>z</em> which approximates to the exact binom.test (<a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernoulli_trial\" rel=\"nofollow\">Bernoulli trial</a>)?</p>\n\n<p>Now my second question relates to the resampling methods.
