To predict into the future, I did a simple linear or 2nd order trend analysis of the dummy coefficients, and converted that into a percentage of the most recent year of sales (i.e. next year is predicted sell 20% more than the previous year).</p>\n\n<p>If that was unclear, I have uploaded a few screen caps to  <a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/njQd1.jpg\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">https://i.stack.imgur.com/njQd1.jpg</a></p>\n", "creationdate": "2017-08-01T15:15:04.153000", "posts_rownum": "posts_199668"}, "posts_206448": {"id": 306149, "owneruserid": 87150, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 352187, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Interpreting 95% confidence intervals for relative risk (known true RR, 100 samples)", "tags": "<confidence-interval><simulation><relative-risk>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Let's assume that we are investigating how tobacco smoking is associated with incident lung cancer in a population. In the full population, the true relative risk of lung cancer associated with tobacco smoking is 2.</p>\n\n<p>Next, we collect 100 random samples from the population. For each sample, we calculate 95% confidence intervals for the relative risk of lung cancer associated with tobacco smoking.</p>\n\n<p>What can we expect from the distribution of confidence intervals here:</p>\n\n<pre><code>A. 95/100 confidence intervals will include the true value RR=2\n   5/100 confidence intervals will not include the true value RR=2\nA2. As \"A\". Additionally, confidence intervals can freely include RR=1\nB. 95/100 confidence intervals will not include RR=1\n   5/100 confidence intervals will include RR=1  \n</code></pre>\n\n<p>I also provided a simplified picture that presents 20 (100 would be too much) confidence intervals as vertical bars.</p>\n\n<p><a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/NWqDa.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/NWqDa.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></a></p>\n\n<p>Edit: <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/158570/interpretation-of-confidence-interval\">This</a> post seemed to reach the consensus that \"A\" was true, but calculated means was used as an example instead of relative risk measures. </p>\n", "creationdate": "2017-10-03T22:07:22", "posts_rownum": "posts_206448"}, "posts_207131": {"id": 307227, "owneruserid": 43775, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 307219, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Predicting the next state is not the usual starting point in reinforcement learning*. Instead there are two main approaches:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li><p>Predict future cumulative reward from a given state or state/action pair (called \"return\" or \"utility\"), and choose actions that maximise this quantity. Sometimes \"advantage\" is used as the quantity, which is the difference between average expected return and that for the given action.</p></li>\n<li><p>Predict the action that will produce the best future accumulated reward directly, and adjust the predictions depending on results of experience.</p></li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>The two approaches are often combined in \"Actor-Critic\" methods, and this would be a reasonable approach when you have continuous action space.</p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p>I would give a positive reward depending on the final distance to the goal, and small negative reward for each action, to encourage the agent to reach the goal quickly. </p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p>Generally with reinforcement learning you should avoid using <em>heuristics</em> and only provide rewards that measure the goal. So a positive reward for <em>reaching</em> the goal (or if the task is episodic, then reward based on final distance from the goal), and a negative reward per time step would be my suggestion. One way of framing state values in RL is that they are learnable heuristics - you set up the problem with rewards matching goals, and the agent learns local heuristics from experience of its attempts to reach the goal.</p>\n\n<p><a href=\"https://medium.com/emergent-future/simple-reinforcement-learning-with-tensorflow-part-8-asynchronous-actor-critic-agents-a3c-c88f72a5e9f2\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">This article on the cutting edge AC3 algorithm</a> might help you get started - it may jump in a bit deep if you want to learn the underlying theory. But it shows an implementation that you could make use of, and if you have time you could work from <a href=\"https://medium.com/emergent-future/simple-reinforcement-learning-with-tensorflow-part-0-q-learning-with-tables-and-neural-networks-d195264329d0\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">the start of the tutorial series</a>, which walks through the basics first (using TensorFlow).</p>\n\n<hr>\n\n<p>* It can be a useful addition to have a next-state predictor, as demonstrated <a href=\"https://medium.com/@awjuliani/simple-reinforcement-learning-with-tensorflow-part-3-model-based-rl-9a6fe0cce99\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">in part 3 of the same tutorial series on Medium</a>. It can also be used for planning moves several steps in advance. However, it is  not the primary driver of RL agents.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2017-10-10T15:41:54.100000", "posts_rownum": "posts_207131"}, "posts_216133": {"id": 321259, "owneruserid": 58675, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 320084, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Why involving random matrices? This seems much simpler:</p>\n\n<p>$$\\mathbb{E}\\left[\\left(\\hat{\\boldsymbol\\theta} -\n \\boldsymbol\\theta\\right)^{T}\\left(\\hat{\\boldsymbol\\theta} -\n \\boldsymbol\\theta\\right)\\right] =\n \\frac{1}{m^2}\\mathbb{E}\\left[\\sum_{i=1}^{m}\\left(\\hat{\\boldsymbol\\theta}_i-\\boldsymbol\\theta\\right)^T\\sum_{j=1}^{m}\\left(\\hat{\\boldsymbol\\theta}_j-\\boldsymbol\\theta\\right)\\right]=\n\\frac{1}{m^2}\\mathbb{E}\\left[\\sum_{i=1}^{m}\\left(\\hat{\\boldsymbol\\theta}_i-\\boldsymbol\\theta\\right)^T\\left(\\hat{\\boldsymbol\\theta}_i-\\boldsymbol\\theta\\right)\\right] + \\frac{1}{m^2}\n  \\mathbb{E}\\left[\\sum_{i=1}^{m}\\sum_{j\\neq i}^{m} \\left(\\hat{\\boldsymbol\\theta}_i-\\boldsymbol\\theta\\right)^T\\left(\\hat{\\boldsymbol\\theta}_j-\\boldsymbol\\theta\\right)\\right]$$</p>\n\n<p>Now,</p>\n\n<p>$$\\frac{1}{m^2}\\mathbb{E}\\left[\\sum_{i=1}^{m}\\left(\\hat{\\boldsymbol\\theta}_i-\\boldsymbol\\theta\\right)^T\\left(\\hat{\\boldsymbol\\theta}_i-\\boldsymbol\\theta\\right)\\right] = \\frac{1}{m^2}\\sum_{i=1}^{m}\\mathbb{E}\\left[\\left(\\hat{\\boldsymbol\\theta}_i-\\boldsymbol\\theta\\right)^T\\left(\\hat{\\boldsymbol\\theta}_i-\\boldsymbol\\theta\\right)\\right]=\\frac{m\\sigma^2}{m^2}=\\frac{\\sigma^2}{m}$$</p>\n\n<p>While, for $j\\neq i$, </p>\n\n<p>$$\\mathbb{E}\\left[\\left(\\hat{\\boldsymbol\\theta}_i-\\boldsymbol\\theta\\right)^T\\left(\\hat{\\boldsymbol\\theta}_j-\\boldsymbol\\theta\\right)\\right]=\\mathbb{E}\\left[\\hat{\\boldsymbol\\theta}_i^{'T}\\hat{\\boldsymbol\\theta}'_j\\right]=\\mathbb{E}\\left[\\hat{\\boldsymbol\\theta}'_i\\right]\\mathbb{E}\\left[\\hat{\\boldsymbol\\theta}'_j\\right]=0$$</p>\n\n<p>where the penultimate equivalence follows from the independence of   $\\hat{\\boldsymbol\\theta}'_i$ and $\\hat{\\boldsymbol\\theta}'_j$, and the last equivalence follows from the fact that they are both zero mean. </p>\n\n<p>Thus</p>\n\n<p>$$\\mathbb{E}\\left[\\left(\\hat{\\boldsymbol\\theta} -\n \\boldsymbol\\theta\\right)^{T}\\left(\\hat{\\boldsymbol\\theta} -\n \\boldsymbol\\theta\\right)\\right] So this is basically the null-case where you haven't really learned anything (and underfitted would seem to be apt).</p>\n\n<p>Adding such a constraint is odd - one already has $\\lambda$ in place to handle the tradeoff between model complexity and error. This constraint may be effective in finding a sparser solution (i.e., fewer support vectors) - of course, there is also the problem that the problem may not be solvable (i.e., for $t$ which is too large you have no solution). But there exist a large body of work already on finding sparse solutions to SVM which are well motivated - this constraint is not. Also adding in this constraint may alter the expression for $w$ itself, so it's not entirely clear what the end result would be.</p>\n\n<p>Adding an additional constraint in the dual will result in a new variable in the primal, and the primal objective will look different. It's largely a mechanical process to transform from dual -> primal, but someone else (or perhaps OP) can do that.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2018-09-02T09:54:04.367000", "posts_rownum": "posts_243208"}, "posts_245230": {"id": 368081, "owneruserid": 204068, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 368079, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>Instead of scaling your coefficients, transform your test data using your StandardScaler.</p>\n\n<pre><code>x1 = np.linspace(0., 10., 100)\ndata = pd.DataFrame({\"X1\":x1})\nfor i in range(2, 11): data[\"X{:d}\".format(i)] = data[\"X1\"]**i\nx1scl = scaler.transform(data)\nyp = model.predict(x1scl)\nplt.plot(X['X1'], Y, 'o')\nplt.plot(x1, yp, '--')\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>I tried it, this works. By the way, you are dividing your model coefficients by the std. of corresponding feature. But, you ignore the effect of the mean.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2018-09-21T19:49:22.683000", "posts_rownum": "posts_245230"}, "posts_245990": {"id": 369233, "owneruserid": 54725, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 369219, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>Welcome to StackExchange!</p>\n\n<p>To understand what he is saying, think about what neural networks are designed for: They are function <em>approximators</em>.  That is, you are trying to model a true function <span class=\"math-container\">$f : X \\rightarrow Y$</span> using some representation of the function.  Linear functions take this form <span class=\"math-container\">$f(X) = a \\; X + b$</span> (<span class=\"math-container\">$a$</span> and <span class=\"math-container\">$b$</span> are parameters to be learnt from data), and neural networks take on a more complex form: Each layer <span class=\"math-container\">$i$</span> computes a transformation <span class=\"math-container\">$f_i$</span>, and the final output is a composition of outputs from each layer <span class=\"math-container\">$i$</span>: <span class=\"math-container\">$f = f_n \\circ f_{n-1} \\ldots \\circ f_1$</span>.  For more information, check this nice chapter: <a href=\"http://neuralnetworksanddeeplearning.com/chap4.html\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Visual 'proof' that neural networks are good function approximators</a>.</p>\n\n<p>What Ian is saying in the video is that a composition of ReLU functions at each layer (that have worked so well in deep learning empirically) is a nice representation of piecewise linear functions.  This is because the composition of piecewise linear functions is also a piecewise linear function.  Which means that you could say that the output of a deep neural network is a specific linear function as long as the input lies within a small region.  You can see this visually here:</p>\n\n<p><a href=\"https://cs.stanford.edu/people/karpathy/convnetjs/demo/regression.html\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">https://cs.stanford.edu/people/karpathy/convnetjs/demo/regression.html</a></p>\n\n<p>Use this simple network definition:</p>\n\n<pre><code>layer_defs = [];\nlayer_defs.push({type:'input', out_sx:1, out_sy:1, out_depth:1});\nlayer_defs.push({type:'fc', num_neurons:20, activation:'relu'});\nlayer_defs.push({type:'regression', num_neurons:1});\n\nnet = new convnetjs.Net();\nnet.makeLayers(layer_defs);\n\ntrainer = new convnetjs.SGDTrainer(net, {learning_rate:0.01, momentum:0.0, batch_size:1, l2_decay:0.001});\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>You can also see that Ian's observation will not hold true for other functions (pick sigmoid and see for yourself).</p>\n\n<p><a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/AuTvM.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/AuTvM.png\" alt=\"Piecewise Linear Example in 1D\"></a></p>\n\n<p>Now you can see what he meant when he said the non-linearity is because of the parameters of the network.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2018-09-28T19:25:48.850000", "posts_rownum": "posts_245990"}, "posts_250656": {"id": 376522, "owneruserid": 95569, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 376534, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Probability of the sum of cards?", "tags": "<probability><self-study>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>The problem is basically as follows</p>\n\n<p>There are four cards with points <code>[1,2,3,4]</code>, every time I draw one card randomly and then put it back to the deck. As I keep drawing I record the sum of the points on the cards, I stop drawing if the sum is greater than or equal to five.</p>\n\n<p>If the final points is equal to five, I win, otherwise I lose. What's the probability of me winning?</p>\n\n<hr>\n\n<p>My attempt to solve this problem is, let <span class=\"math-container\">$p_n$</span> be the probability of the sum EVER equal to <span class=\"math-container\">$n$</span> after drawing enough number of times, specifically\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$p_1=\\frac{1}{4} \\text{ (draw 1 once)}$$</span>\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$p_2=\\frac{1}{4} + \\frac{1}{4}p_1 \\text{ (draw 2 once + draw 1 twice)} $$</span>\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$p_3=\\frac{1}{4} + \\frac{1}{4}p_1 + \\frac{1}{4}p_2 $$</span>\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$p_4=\\frac{1}{4} + \\frac{1}{4}p_1 + \\frac{1}{4}p_2 + \\frac{1}{4}p_3 $$</span>\nthen <span class=\"math-container\">$p_5=\\frac{1}{4}p_1 + \\frac{1}{4}p_2 + \\frac{1}{4}p_3 + \\frac{1}{4}p_4 = 369/1024$</span> should be the probability of winning at five.</p>\n\n<p>However I was told that the answer should be around 0.33 so I'm confused, is my answer correct?</p>\n\n<hr>\n\n<p><strong>Update</strong>\nIt turns out 0.33 (1/3) is the answer for sampling without replacement.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2018-11-12T04:12:15.080000", "posts_rownum": "posts_250656"}, "posts_253683": {"id": 381257, "owneruserid": 108813, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 381293, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Computing KL divergence in function for Bayesian Neural Networks (BNN) is computed. <a href=\"https://www.tensorflow.org/probability/api_docs/python/tfp/layers/Convolution2DFlipout\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">In the TensorFlow documentation they illustrate a BNN in practice where they train the network to minimise the negative of the <em>ELBO</em> (as seen below)</a>.</p>\n\n<pre><code>import tensorflow as tf\nimport tensorflow_probability as tfp\n\nmodel = tf.keras.Sequential([\n    tf.keras.layers.Reshape([32, 32, 3]),\n    tfp.layers.Convolution2DFlipout(\n        64, kernel_size=5, padding='SAME', activation=tf.nn.relu),\n    tf.keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(pool_size=[2, 2],\n                                 strides=[2, 2],\n                                 padding='SAME'),\n    tf.keras.layers.Flatten(),\n    tfp.layers.DenseFlipout(10),\n])\n\nlogits = model(features)\nneg_log_likelihood = tf.nn.softmax_cross_entropy_with_logits(\n    labels=labels, logits=logits)\nkl = sum(model.losses)\nloss = neg_log_likelihood + kl\ntrain_op = tf.train.AdamOptimizer().minimize(loss)\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>However, they seem to be computing the KL divergence as the sum of the losses of the network weights i.e. <code>kl = sum(model.losses)</code>. This is not how the KL divergence should be computed.</p>\n\n<p>They repeat it <a href=\"https://github.com/tensorflow/probability/blob/e00ab7df4b3865054a39f8af64e85e31123aba5c/tensorflow_probability/examples/bayesian_neural_network.py#L261\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">here too</a> : </p>\n\n<pre><code>  # Compute the -ELBO as the loss, averaged over the batch size.\n  neg_log_likelihood = -tf.reduce_mean(labels_distribution.log_prob(labels))\n  kl = sum(neural_net.losses) / mnist_data.train.num_examples\n  elbo_loss = neg_log_likelihood + kl\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>Am I missing something very basic? The exact KL divergence is something which is quite difficult to compute unless you make assumptions about the underlying probability distribution of the weights such as it following a Normal distribution in which case the KL divergence would be computed as:</p>\n\n<p><a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/zMEuA.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/zMEuA.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></a></p>\n\n<p>where <span class=\"math-container\">$\\theta$</span> is the weights, <span class=\"math-container\">$\\mu$</span> is the mean weight, and <span class=\"math-container\">$\\sigma$</span> is the standard deviation of the weight and <span class=\"math-container\">$\\mu'$</span> and <span class=\"math-container\">$\\sigma'$</span> are the means and standard deviations after the updates.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2018-12-10T12:13:17.607000", "posts_rownum": "posts_253683"}, "posts_707": {"id": 726, "owneruserid": 223, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Famous statistical quotations", "tags": "<references><history>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>What is your favorite statistical quote? So, in this case, if you have a column recording how many events there are, then <code>strata(numberofevents)</code> will fit a new baseline hazard between each event. </p>\n\n<p>There is actually a model called PWP-Gap Time which does calculate only time since previous event and thus assumes a separate baseline hazard for each 'chunk' of time.</p>\n\n<p>Prentice RL, Williams BJ, Peterson AV: On the regression analysis of multivariate failure time data. "posts_265096": {"id": 398918, "owneruserid": 97872, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 398832, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>The <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_the_unconscious_statistician\" rel=\"noreferrer\">law of the unconscious staistician</a> is a useful technique for computing the expected value of a random variable <span class=\"math-container\">$Z$</span> that can be written as a function of a random variable <span class=\"math-container\">$X$</span> that only relies on knowing the distribution of <span class=\"math-container\">$X$</span>, not necessarily of <span class=\"math-container\">$Z$</span>.</p>\n\n<h1>The Discrete Case</h1>\n\n<p>The law of the unconscious statistician can be proved in the discrete case with no reference to measure theory, and this special case can motivate the general formula.</p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p><strong>Theorem.</strong>\n  Let <span class=\"math-container\">$X$</span> be a random variable taking values in a countable set <span class=\"math-container\">$\\mathcal{X}$</span>.\n  Let <span class=\"math-container\">$\\mathcal{Z}$</span> be a countable subset of <span class=\"math-container\">$\\mathbb{R}$</span>, let <span class=\"math-container\">$f : \\mathcal{X} \\to \\mathcal{Z}$</span> be a function, and let <span class=\"math-container\">$Z = f(X)$</span>.\n  Assume that <span class=\"math-container\">$E[Z]$</span> exists.\n  Then\n  <span class=\"math-container\">$$\nE[Z] = \\sum_{x \\in \\mathcal{X}} f(x) P(X = x).\n$$</span></p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p><em>Proof.</em>\nSince <span class=\"math-container\">$Z$</span> is a discrete random variable, we have\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nE[Z]\n&= \\sum_{z \\in \\mathcal{Z}} z \\, P(Z = z) \\\\\n&= \\sum_{z \\in \\mathcal{Z}} z \\, P(f(X) = z)\n\\end{aligned}\n$$</span>\nNow notice that the event <span class=\"math-container\">$\\{f(X) = z\\}$</span> can be decomposed into a countable union of pairwise disjoint events based on what value <span class=\"math-container\">$X$</span> takes:\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$\n\\{f(X) = z\\}\n= \\bigcup_{\\substack{x \\in \\mathcal{X} \\\\ f(x) = z}} \\{X = x\\}.\n$$</span>\nUsing this observation, we may continue our calculation above:\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$\n\\begin{aligned}\nE[Z]\n&= \\sum_{z \\in \\mathcal{Z}} z \\, P(f(X) = z) \\\\\n&= \\sum_{z \\in \\mathcal{Z}} z \\, P\\left(\\bigcup_{\\substack{x \\in \\mathcal{X} \\\\ f(x) = z}} \\{X = x\\}\\right) \\\\\n&= \\sum_{z \\in \\mathcal{Z}} z \\sum_{\\substack{x \\in \\mathcal{X} \\\\ f(x) = z}} P(X = x) \\\\\n&= \\sum_{z \\in \\mathcal{Z}} \\sum_{\\substack{x \\in \\mathcal{X} \\\\ f(x) = z}} f(x) P(X = x) \\\\\n&= \\sum_{x \\in \\mathcal{X}} f(x) P(X = x)\n\\end{aligned}\n$$</span></p>\n\n<h1>The Absolutely Continuous Case</h1>\n\n<p>The law of the unconscious statistician for (absolutely) continuous random variables can intuitively be derived from the discrete case by making the usual substitutions that one makes when going from the discrete case to the continuous case: sums become integrals and probability mass functions become probability densities.</p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p><strong>Theorem.</strong>\n  Let <span class=\"math-container\">$X$</span> be an absolutely continuous random variable with probability density <span class=\"math-container\">$p_X$</span>.\n  Let <span class=\"math-container\">$f : \\mathbb{R} \\to \\mathbb{R}$</span> be a Borel-measurable function (e.g., any continuous or piecewise continuous or monotonic function satisfies this assumption), and let <span class=\"math-container\">$Z = f(X)$</span>.\n  Assume that <span class=\"math-container\">$E[Z]$</span> exists.\n  Then\n  <span class=\"math-container\">$$\nE[Z] = \\int_{\\mathbb{R}} f(x) p_X(x) \\, dx\n$$</span></p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p>This formula should make sense intuitively:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>The sum <span class=\"math-container\">$\\sum_{x \\in \\mathcal{X}}$</span> from the discrete case became the integral <span class=\"math-container\">$\\int_{\\mathbb{R}} \\cdots \\, dx$</span> in the continuous case.</li>\n<li>The probability mass function <span class=\"math-container\">$P(X = x)$</span> in the discrete case became the probability density <span class=\"math-container\">$p_X(x)$</span> in the continuous case.</li>\n</ul>\n\n<h1>Example</h1>\n\n<p>In the original question, you ask about computing <span class=\"math-container\">$E[Z]$</span>, where <span class=\"math-container\">$f(x) = e^{s x}$</span> for some <span class=\"math-container\">$s > 0$</span> and <span class=\"math-container\">$Z = f(X)$</span>.\nIf <span class=\"math-container\">$X$</span> is a discrete random variable taking values in a countable set <span class=\"math-container\">$\\mathcal{X}$</span>, then we get\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$\nE[Z]\n= \\sum_{x \\in \\mathcal{X}} e^{s x} P(X = x),\n$$</span>\nand if <span class=\"math-container\">$X$</span> is an absolutely continuous random variable with density <span class=\"math-container\">$p_X$</span>, then we get\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$\nE[Z]\n= \\int_{\\mathbb{R}} e^{s x} p_X(x) \\, dx.\n$$</span>\nYou can see that in both of these formulas, you only need to know the distribution of <span class=\"math-container\">$X$</span>.</p>\n\n<h1>The General Case</h1>\n\n<p>I can't help but mention the measure-theoretic result underlying this whole discussion.\nIn general, a random variable need not be discrete or absolutely continuous (e.g., what's the distribution of the sum of a binomial random variable and a Gaussian random variable? Is it discrete? Is it continuous?).\nFor this case, measure theory gives a concise formula for computing the expected value of a function of a random variable.</p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p><strong>Theorem.</strong>\n  Let <span class=\"math-container\">$(\\Omega, \\mathcal{F}, P)$</span> be a probability space, let <span class=\"math-container\">$(\\mathcal{X}, \\mathcal{B})$</span> be a measurable space, and let <span class=\"math-container\">$X : \\Omega \\to \\mathcal{X}$</span> be a random variable.\n  Let <span class=\"math-container\">$P_X = X_* P$</span> be the distribution of <span class=\"math-container\">$X$</span>, meaning that <span class=\"math-container\">$P_X$</span> is the probability measure on <span class=\"math-container\">$(\\mathcal{X}, \\mathcal{B})$</span> defined by the formula\n  <span class=\"math-container\">$$\nP_X(B) = P(X \\in B)\n$$</span>\n  for every set <span class=\"math-container\">$B \\in \\mathcal{B}$</span>.\n  Also, let <span class=\"math-container\">$f : \\mathcal{X} \\to \\mathbb{R}$</span> be a Borel-measurable function, and let <span class=\"math-container\">$Z = f(X)$</span> (more precisely, <span class=\"math-container\">$Z : \\Omega \\to \\mathbb{R}$</span> is the function composition <span class=\"math-container\">$Z = f \\circ X$</span>).\n  Assume <span class=\"math-container\">$E[Z] = \\int_\\Omega Z \\, dP$</span> exists.\n  Then\n  <span class=\"math-container\">$$\nE[Z]\n= \\int_{\\mathcal{X}} f(x) \\, dP_X(x).\n$$</span></p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p>This result is a special case of an even more general <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pushforward_measure#Main_property:_change-of-variables_formula\" rel=\"noreferrer\">change-of-variables formula</a> from measure theory that has nothing to do with probability.\nThe formulas for the discrete case and the absolutely continuous case that were given above fall out as special cases of this theorem after making the following observations:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>If <span class=\"math-container\">$X$</span> is a discrete random variable, then\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$\n\\int_{\\mathcal{X}} \\cdots \\, dP_X(x)\n= \\sum_{x \\in \\mathcal{X}} \\cdots P(X = x)\n$$</span>\n(formally, because <span class=\"math-container\">$P_X$</span> is absolutely continuous with respect to counting measure on <span class=\"math-container\">$\\mathcal{X}$</span>, and the Radon-Nikodym derivative is <span class=\"math-container\">$x \\mapsto P(X = x)$</span>).</li>\n<li>If <span class=\"math-container\">$X$</span> is an absolutely continuous random variable (with respect to Lebesgue measure) with probability density <span class=\"math-container\">$p_X$</span>, then <span class=\"math-container\">$\\mathcal{X} = \\mathbb{R}$</span> and\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$\n\\int_{\\mathcal{X}} \\cdots \\, dP_X(x)\n= \\int_{\\mathbb{R}} \\cdots p_X(x) \\, dx\n$$</span>\n(formally, this is because, by definition, <span class=\"math-container\">$P_X$</span> is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, and the Radon-Nikodym derivative is <span class=\"math-container\">$p_X$</span>).</li>\n</ul>\n", null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p><strong>The conclusion does not follow.</strong>  The family of distributions described at <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/a/84213/919\">How is the kurtosis of a distribution related to the geometry of the density function?</a> gives a counterexample.  These are densities <span class=\"math-container\">$f_{k,s}$</span> all of which have identical moments.  If we were, then, to shift one of them by some positive amount, all its moments would (strictly) increase.  Here is a plot of their distribution functions <span class=\"math-container\">$F_{k,s}$</span> (evaluated numerically):</p>\n<p><a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/T7m8b.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/T7m8b.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\" /></a></p>\n<p>Clearly neither dominates the other, even though all the moments of the red distribution exceed those of the black distribution.</p>\n<hr />\n<p>For those who would like to experiment with this family, here is the <code>R</code> code used to create these plots.</p>\n<pre class=\"lang-R prettyprint-override\"><code>f <- function(x, k=0, s=0) {\n  ifelse(x <= 0, 0, dnorm(log(x)) * (1 + s * sin(2 * k * pi * log(x))) / x)\n}\nff <- Vectorize(function(x, k=0, s=0, ...) {\n  integrate(\\(y) f(y, k, s), 0, x, ...)$value\n})\ncurve(ff(x), 0, 4, lwd = 2, ylim = 0:1, \n      ylab = "Probability", xlab = expression(italic(x)), cex.lab = 1.25)\ncurve(ff(x - 0.01, 1, 3/4), add = TRUE, lwd = 2, col = "Red")\n</code></pre>\n", "creationdate": "2022-11-25T16:57:28.977000", "posts_rownum": "posts_393683"}, "posts_400413": {"id": 605411, "owneruserid": 17414, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to motivate undergrads to take an Intro to Math Stats course", "tags": "<mathematical-statistics><teaching>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>How would you motivate an undergraduate student to take an Introduction to Mathematical Statistics course, if they know that much of their time will be spent proving results they've already seen in Introduction to Applied Statistics? That is, much (though certainly not all!) of the course is "just" about proving mathematically that standard methods for p-values and confidence intervals (z and t tests and intervals; F and chi-square tests) work as advertised.</p>\n<p>Context: I teach at a US small liberal arts college. Here is the course description for our version of this class:</p>\n<blockquote>\n<p><strong>Topics in Statistical Inference</strong> Building on their background in probability theory, students explore inferential methods in statistics and learn how to evaluate different estimation techniques and hypothesis-testing methods. Students learn techniques for modeling the response of a continuous random variable using information from several variables using regression modeling. Topics include maximum likelihood and other methods estimation, sample properties of estimators, including sufficiency, consistency, and relative efficiency, Rao-Blackwell theorem, tests of hypotheses, confidence, and resampling techniques.</p>\n</blockquote>\n<p>We have used textbooks such as Hogg, McKean, & Craig (<a href=\"https://www.pearson.com/en-us/subject-catalog/p/introduction-to-mathematical-statistics/P200000006211/9780137530687?tab=table-of-contents\" rel=\"noreferrer\">table of contents</a>) or Wackerly, Mendenhall, & Scheaffer (<a href=\"https://faculty.cengage.com/titles/9780495110811\" rel=\"noreferrer\">table of contents</a>).</p>\n<p>Our statistics majors are required to take Math Stats, but I try to give better motivation than just "it's required." And occasionally other students ask me why they should consider taking this course too. What are some ways I could convince them to see the value of taking Math Stats?</p>\n<p>I'll post my own answer with what I currently tell them, but I expect that the community here has other great suggestions.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2023-02-14T16:27:41.580000", "posts_rownum": "posts_400413"}, "posts_321": {"id": 338, "owneruserid": 89, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 322, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>Cover and Thomas's book <a href=\"http://rads.stackoverflow.com/amzn/click/0471062596\" rel=\"noreferrer\">Elements of Information Theory</a> is a good source on entropy and its applications, although I don't know that it addresses exactly the issues you have in mind.</p>\n", href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/7/locating-freely-available-data-samples\">Locating freely available data samples</a>  </p>\n</blockquote>\n\n\n\n<p>Where can I find freely accessible data sources?</p>\n\n<p>I'm thinking of sites like</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li><a href=\"http://www2.census.gov/census_2000/datasets/\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">http://www2.census.gov/census_2000/datasets/</a>?</li>\n</ul>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-19T21:50:16.260000", "posts_rownum": "posts_134"}, "posts_654": {"id": 668, "owneruserid": 319, "2010-07-26T20:19:12.447000", "posts_rownum": "posts_654"}, "posts_665": {"id": 681, "owneruserid": 279, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 288, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>You don't necessarily have to go Bayesian on your model, plain maximum likelihood estimation works just fine (though has no explicit solution). Multiple R packages (eg. aod or VGAM) will fit the distribution for you.</p>\n\n<p>Alternatively, you can use the quasi-likelihood based overdispersed binomial model that does not assume a beta-binomial distribution, just adjusts for the overdispersion. The <code>glm</code> function with the <code>quasibinomial</code> family will fit this model in R.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-26T21:13:43.743000", "posts_rownum": "posts_665"}, "posts_822": {"id": 836, "owneruserid": 334, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 834, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>It is a heuristic, and as such, has been subjected to <em>extensive</em> testing.  So when to trust it or not is not simple clear-cut and always-true decision.</p>\n\n<p>At a rough approximation, it trades off goodness of fit and number of variables (\"degrees of freedom\"). Much more, as usual, <a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akaike_information_criterion\" rel=\"nofollow\">at the Wikipedia article about AIC</a>.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-27T18:14:44.467000", "posts_rownum": "posts_822"}, "posts_843": {"id": 855, "owneruserid": 8, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 806, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I thought this was too obvious, until I saw this <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/795/normalization-of-series\">question</a>!</p>\n\n<p>When you normalise data, make sure you always have access to the raw data after normalisation. Of course, you could break this rule if you have a good reason, e.g. storage.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-27T20:05:20.027000", "posts_rownum": "posts_843"}, "posts_935": {"id": 955, "owneruserid": 175, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Data Analysis Work-- Is there Any Freelance Opportunity?", "tags": "<careers>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>Just wonder, is there any data analysis/ statistic/ data mining work that are available on freelance basis?</p>\n\n<p>This could be subjective and argumentative, which is why I put it as CW. </p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-29T03:25:03.290000", "posts_rownum": "posts_935"}, "posts_1036": {"id": 1068, "owneruserid": 493, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 1066, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<p>I'm not sure I understand your question exactly, but I assume you are looking for the probability mass at each point, where an event is defined as a subsegment covering a particular position.  If this is true, I believe you should be able to work out the exact probability mass function.</p>\n\n<p>For each subsegment of length K the distribution at a particular location between K and N-K+1 is uniform and proportional to K.  The distribution at the tails is stepwise increasing from 1 to K.  This can be seen by just working out one example.</p>\n\n<p>Given multiple subsegments of different sizes, simply add these functions up.  You can then normalize everything so the weights sum to one if you want a proper distribution function.  Given a length and a list of subsegment lengths, this probability mass function should be easy to code up in the language of your choice.</p>\n\n<p>If you are interested in the <em>number of segments</em> covering any point, this is simply the sum of Bernoulli random variables with different p, defined at each point using the same pmf.  The simplest approach would be to enumerate the possibilities from 1 to K.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-31T18:50:56.847000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1036"}, "posts_1041": {"id": 1073, "owneruserid": 638, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 373, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p><strong>To answer the original question</strong>: <em>Our intuition fails because of the narrative.  By relating the story in the same order as the tv script, we get confused.  It gets much easier if we think about what is going to happen in advance.  The quiz-master will reveal a goat, so our best chance is to select a door with a goat and then switch.  The storyline puts a lot of emphasis on the loss</em> <strong>caused by our action</strong> <em>in that one out of three chance that we happen to select the car.</em></p>\n\n<hr>\n\n<p>The original answer:</p>\n\n<p>Our aim is to eliminate <strong>both</strong> goats.  We do this by marking one goat ourselves.  The quizmaster is then forced to choose between revealing the car or the other goat. Revealing the car is out of the question, so the quizmaster will reveal and eliminate the one goat we did not know about.  We then switch to the remaining door, thereby eliminating the goat we marked with our first choice, and get the car.</p>\n\n<p>This strategy only fails if we do not mark a goat, but the car instead.  But that is unlikely: there are two goats and only one car.</p>\n\n<p>So we have a chance of 2 in 3 to win the car.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-07-31T21:33:59.133000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1041"}, "posts_1091": {"id": 1131, "owneruserid": 8, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 1126, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<blockquote>\n  <p>Save money</p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p>I build mathematical/statistical of cellular mechanisms. For example, how a particular protein affects cellular ageing. The role of the model is mainly prediction, but also to save money. It's far cheaper to employ a single modeller than (say) a few wet-lab biologists with the associated equipment costs. Of course modelling doesn't fully replace the experiment, it just aids the process.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-02T18:52:56.510000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1091"}, "posts_1094": {"id": 1134, "owneruserid": 5, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 1126, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 2.5", "body": "<blockquote>\n  <p>dimension reduction</p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p>Sometimes there can be too much data, so forming an initial model allows for further analysis. </p>\n", "creationdate": "2010-08-02T19:28:31.653000", "posts_rownum": "posts_1094"}, "posts_72488": {"id": 94250, "owneruserid": 686, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 94249, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>There are tons of these.  </p>\n\n<p>Suppose you have data on spouses and want to predict whether the husband or wife does more of the child care.</p>\n\n<p>Suppose you have data on students in classes and want to look at test scores.</p>\n\n<p>Or on left eyes and right eyes and want to predict acuity of vision.</p>\n\n<p>And lots more. </p>\n", "creationdate": "2014-04-18T12:55:08.277000", "posts_rownum": "posts_72488"}, "posts_15954": {"id": 17469, "owneruserid": 223, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 17405, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>You should include the sample size the following way. You need to understand the use of product measure in mathematical statistics. </p>\n\n<p>You observe $X_1,\\dots,X_n$ iid from $P_i$ ($i=0$ or $i=1$). This can be rephrased by: you observe ${\\bf P_i}=P_i\\otimes  P_i \\otimes \\dots \\otimes P_i=P_i^{\\otimes n}$, where $\\nu \\otimes \\mu$ is the <strong><a href=\"http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_measure\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">product measure</a></strong> obtained from $\\nu$ and $\\mu$. </p>\n\n<p>Now $KL({\\bf P_0},{\\bf P_1})=n  KL( P_0, P_1)$. I am sure you can easily get a result from that. Now if you are trying to work directlky with the TV distance (which is an idea, but certainly unpractical from my answer <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/17300/hypothesis-testing-and-total-variation-distance-vs-kullback-leibler-divergence/17315#17315\">here</a>), the thing you should try to evaluate (or upper bound) is: </p>\n\n<p>$2*TV({\\bf P_0},{\\bf P_1})=\\int_{\\mathbb{R}^n}|\\Pi_{j=1}^n\\phi_1(x_j)-\\Pi_{j=1}^n\\phi_0(x_j)|dx_1\\dots, dx_n$ (for $i=0,1$ $\\phi_i$ density of $P_i$). </p>\n", "creationdate": "2011-10-24T06:21:36.213000", "posts_rownum": "posts_15954"}, "posts_27631": {"id": 31174, "owneruserid": 12225, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 14246, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Multiple linear regression appears to me more appropriate than ANCOVA in this situation, as the journal reviewer recommends.</p>\n\n<p>Try running both a multiple regression and an ANCOVA, and comparing the results.  They probably will not be identical.</p>\n\n<p>ANCOVA and multiple linear regression are similar, but regression is more appropriate when the emphasis is on the dependent outcome variable, while ANCOVA is more appropriate when the emphasis is on comparing the groups from one of the independent variables.  In the experiment described above, the emphasis seems clearly to be on the outcome variable.</p>\n\n<p>Finally, unless you are really certain that you way of doing things is better than the Reviewer's, and can explain why, then you should probably just concede to the Reviewer's expertise, so you can get your paper published.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2012-06-26T21:15:10.337000", "posts_rownum": "posts_27631"}, "posts_32892": {"id": 38533, "owneruserid": 14590, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 38420, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>There is an irony that the standard way to do Bayesian computation is to use frequentist analysis of MCMC samples.  In this example we might consider $c$ to be closely related to the marginal likelihood, which we would like to calculate, but we are going to be Bayesian purists in the sense of to try to also do the computation in a Bayesian way.</p>\n\n<p>It is not common, but it is possible to do this integral in a Bayesian framework.  This involves putting a prior on the function $g()$ (in practice a Gaussian process) evaluating the function at some points, conditioning upon these points and computing an integral over the posterior over $g()$.  In this situation the likelihood involves evaluating $g()$ at a number of points, but $g()$ is otherwise unknown, therefore the likelihood is quite different to the likelihood given above.  The method is demonstrated in this paper <a href=\"http://mlg.eng.cam.ac.uk/zoubin/papers/RasGha03.pdf\">http://mlg.eng.cam.ac.uk/zoubin/papers/RasGha03.pdf</a></p>\n\n<p>I don't think anything went wrong with Bayesian methodology.  The likelihood as written treats $g()$ as known everywhere.  If this were the case then there would be no statistical aspect to the problem.  If $g()$ is assumed to be unknown except at a finite number of points Bayesian methodology works fine.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2012-10-03T04:28:34.177000", "posts_rownum": "posts_32892"}, "posts_37832": {"id": 46450, "owneruserid": 5339, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 46446, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Assume WLOG that everything is mean $0$. If you know the formula for the inverse of a matrix in block form, then it should be as simple as checking that</p>\n\n<p>$$(X, Y)^T V^{-1} (X, Y) = X^T A^{-1} X + (Y - \\mu_{Y | X})^T S^{-1} (Y - \\mu_{Y|X}) + c$$</p>\n\n<p>where $S$ is the Schur complement and $c$ is a constant and $\\mu_{Y|X} = B^TA^{-1}X$. Why is this all you need to do? Because this is precisely what is required to factor the Gaussian density\n$$\nf(x, y) = |2\\pi V|^{-1/2}\\exp\\left(-\\frac 1 2 (x, y)^T V^{-1} (x, y)\\right)\n$$\ninto a product of two Gaussians (one Gaussian representing the marginal of $X$ and the other the conditional distribution of $Y | X = x$). This, I think, just involves sticky algebra; one lesson here is that Schur complements play a nice algebraic role in the breaking up of quadratic forms that look like $z^T A^{-1}z$, but maybe someone can point out something deeper going on.</p>\n\n<p>The second part of the question, as stated currently, doesn't make any sense; $V^{-1} = 0$ is an impossible equation to satisfy. Maybe what you mean is that you want to show $\\mbox{Var}(X|Y) = 0$ provided that $V$ is singular? (This is false, by the way).</p>\n", "creationdate": "2012-12-22T20:43:43.527000", "posts_rownum": "posts_37832"}, "posts_39527": {"id": 48587, "owneruserid": 20119, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Can exploratory, and not confirmatory, factor analysis be used on dependent variables?", "tags": "<factor-analysis><confirmatory-factor>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'm working on my dissertation which is a multiple case study examining the use of performance information. My dissertation chair states that I need to use confirmatory factor analysis (CFA); however, after months of learning SPSS and completing other analyses through the system, I have just found out that CFA cannot be completed in SPSS without AMOS, and my school does not support AMOS.</p>\n\n<p>I've been working with a committee member and have been examining 2 and 3 factors related to my dependent variables which would help examine the underlying dimensions and associations with each factor but I'm concerned that I'll still be required to use CFA and have to learn a new statistical system.</p>\n\n<p>So my questions are:</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li>Can exploratory factor analysis (EFA) be conducted on dependent variables? and </li>\n<li>Is there a strong argument to use EFA over CFA?</li>\n</ol>\n", "creationdate": "2013-01-26T16:21:49.707000", "posts_rownum": "posts_39527"}, "posts_43431": {"id": 54696, "owneruserid": 22293, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 54698, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Repeated Measures ANOVA missing values - run separate models?", "tags": "<anova><repeated-measures><missing-data>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I am evaluating pre and post test data for 2 groups using repeated measures ANOVA. Given that I am missing a few data cells, the final n is reduced in the analysis. I'd like to know if I can run separate repeated measures ANOVA for each subtest (or combinations that have the same number of full data sets) rather than include them all in the same model to maximize the data analyzed. If I ran separate ANOVAs, are there implications for my interpretation of the output? Thank you for any advice.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2013-03-29T22:59:02.463000", "posts_rownum": "posts_43431"}, "posts_47700": {"id": 60212, "owneruserid": 9343, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 60172, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p><a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/44972/what-is-the-difference-between-laplace-approximation-and-modified-harmonic-me/44991#44991\">This</a> might help on sheding some light on marginal distribution calculation. Also, I would recommend to use a method through power posteriors introduced by <a href=\"http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1467-9868.2007.00650.x/abstract?deniedAccessCustomisedMessage=&userIsAuthenticated=false\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Friel and Pettitt</a>. This approach seems quite promissing, although it has some limitations. Or you could you Laplace approximation of posterior distribution by normal distribution: if histogram from MCMC looks symmetric and normal-like, than this could be quite good approximation.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2013-05-28T10:12:57.080000", "posts_rownum": "posts_47700"}, "posts_48237": {"id": 60919, "owneruserid": 26629, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 60920, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": "Wuschelbeutel Kartoffelhuhn", "title": "Are degrees of freedom $n-1$ for both the sample standard deviation of the individual observations and for the standard error of the sample mean?", "tags": "<variance><sample-size><standard-error>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I collect $n$ ($<20$) i.i.d. observations from any distribution. In order to compute the sample variance, I take \n$$s^2=\\sum_i \\frac{(\\bar{X}-X_i)^2}{n-1}$$</p>\n\n<p>If I want to build a confidence interval for the mean, I need the standard error of the sample mean. Do I divide by $n$, or by $n-1$ again?</p>\n\n<p>$$S.E. \\stackrel{?}{=}\\sqrt{\\frac{s^2}{n-1}}$$</p>\n", "creationdate": "2013-06-05T01:37:25.510000", "posts_rownum": "posts_48237"}, "posts_50369": {"id": 63529, "owneruserid": 27564, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 63515, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Sure, this absolutely makes sense. The only reason for defining a metric is to measure the distance between two entities in a way you want it. So you have to know what you want and then build your metric according to this.</p>\n\n<p>I have one comment about your metric: Think about whether two users rating the same movies might have an influence. Now in your metric giving a 1 and a 5 is the same as having not rated at all. In your example I would say the two user are (even if they contradict in their ratings) more similar two each other than to another user who doesn't even share ratings. Think about Amazon's “users who bought this, also bought” which doesn't take ratings into account at all. I would suggest adding a term in your metric, e.g number of commonly rated items.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2013-07-06T22:33:25.343000", "posts_rownum": "posts_50369"}, "posts_53636": {"id": 67552, "owneruserid": 29187, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 67547, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>In my opinion, it assumes that the errors lie on a family of gamma distributions, with the same shapes, and with the scales changing according the related formula.</p>\n\n<p>But it is difficult to do model diagnosis. Note that the simple QQ plot is not suitable here, because it is about the same distribution, while ours is a family of distributions with different variances.</p>\n\n<p>Naively, the residuals plot can be used to see that they have different scales but the same shape, usually with long tails.</p>\n\n<p>In my experience, the gamma GLM may be tried for some long tail distributed problems, and it is widely used in insurance and environment sectors, etc.\nBut the assumptions are difficult to test, and the model does not perform well usually, so different papers argue to use other family distributions with the same problem, like inverse Gaussian, etc.\nIn practice, it seems that such choices depends on expert judgement with the industrial experience. This limits the use of the gamma GLM.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2013-08-16T08:57:23.390000", "posts_rownum": "posts_53636"}, "posts_53861": {"id": 67842, "owneruserid": 23853, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 67839, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>It could be correct to combine lags and interaction terms, there is certainly no <em>a priori</em> reason why this would always be wrong. </p>\n\n<p>My guess is that StataCorp did not implement the combination of factor variables and time series operators <em>in the graphical user interface</em> in order to make the interface easier to use. The logic being that combining the two would make the menu a lot more complicated and the combination of the two would be just too rare to be worth the possible confusion. </p>\n\n<p>As you noticed, you can easily type the commands and that way combine the factor variable and time series operators. </p>\n", "creationdate": "2013-08-20T10:19:35.347000", "posts_rownum": "posts_53861"}, "posts_127905": {"id": 181695, "owneruserid": 48352, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to fix some coefficients when fitting a logistic regression", "tags": "<r><regression><logistic>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>In linear regression, if I have a model,</p>\n\n<pre><code>b0 + b1x1 + b2x2 + b3x3 + b4x4 = y\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>and I want to fix some of the coefficients ,say b1 = 1 and b3 = 2, I could just do the following</p>\n\n<pre><code>b0 + b2x2 + b4x4 = y - x1 - 2x3\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>and just fit a linear regression on the other three parameters on the new y. Is there a way to do this for logistic regression? The sigmoid function seems to complicate things. "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Overlap in Margin of Errors between sample and boosted sample?", "tags": "<confidence-interval>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>In an initial study on market share, I got a result of 33% for brand X, with a margin of error (MOE) of 3.4% (therefore a market share somewhere between 30%-36%).</p>\n\n<p>I then boosted that sample to n+600 a few months later, and got a result of 36%, but a MOE of 2.6% (therefore a market share somewhere between 33%-39%). </p>\n\n<p>Can I say that the \"true\" market share for Brand X lies in the area of overlap, i.e. between 33%-36%?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2017-02-06T19:29:10.510000", "posts_rownum": "posts_178008"}, "posts_104027": {"id": 143731, "owneruserid": 69510, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 64010, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p><em>In short</em>, I wouldn't use both the partial $R^2$ and the standardized coefficients in the same analysis, as they are not independent. I would argue that it is usually probably more intuitive to compare relationships using the standardized coefficients because they relate readily to the model definition (i.e. $Y = \\beta X$). The partial $R^2$, in turn, is essentially the proportion of unique shared variance between the predictor and dependent variable (dv) (so for the first predictor it is the square of the partial correlation $r_{x_1y.x_2...x_n}$). Furthermore, for a fit with a very small error all the coefficients' partial $R^2$ tend to 1, so they are not useful in identifying the relative importance of the predictors.</p>\n\n<hr>\n\n<p><strong>The effect size definitions</strong></p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>standardized coefficient, $\\beta_{std}$ - the coefficients $\\beta$ obtained from estimating a model on the standardized variables (mean = 0, standard deviation = 1). </li>\n<li><p>partial $R^2$- The proportion of residual variation explained by adding the predictor to the constrained model (the full model without the predictor). Same as:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>the square of the partial correlation between the predictor and the dependent variable, controlling for all the other predictors in the model. $R_{partial}^2 = r_{x_iy.X\\setminus x_i}^2$. </li>\n<li>partial $\\eta^2$ - the proportion of type III sums of squares from the predictor to the sum of squares attributed to the predictor and the error  $\\text{SS}_\\text{effect}/(\\text{SS}_\\text{effect}+\\text{SS}_\\text{error})$ </li>\n</ul></li>\n<li><p>$\\Delta R^2$ - The difference in $R^2$ between the constrained and full model. Equal to:</p>\n\n<ul>\n<li>squared semipartial correlation $r_{x_i(y.X\\setminus x_i)}^2$ </li>\n<li>$\\eta^2$ for type III sum of squares $\\text{SS}_\\text{effect}/\\text{SS}_\\text{total}$ - what you were calculating as partial $R^2$ in the question.</li>\n</ul></li>\n</ul>\n\n<p>All of these are closely related, but they differ as to how they handle the correlation structure between the variables. To understand this difference a bit better let us assume we have 3 standardized (mean = 0, sd = 1) variables $x,y,z$ whose correlations are $r_{xy}, r_{xz}, r_{yz}$. We will take $x$ as the dependent variable and $y$ and $z$ as the predictors. We will express all of the effect size coefficients in terms of the correlations so we can explicitly see how the correlation structure is handled by each. First we will list the coefficients in the regression model $x=\\beta_{y}Y+\\beta_{z}Z$ estimated using OLS. The formula for the coefficients:\n\\begin{align}\\beta_{y} = \\frac{r_{xy}-r_{yz}r_{zx}}{1-r_{yz}^2}\\\\\n\\beta_{z}= \\frac{r_{xz}-r_{yz}r_{yx}}{1-r_{yz}^2},\n\\end{align}\nThe square root of the $R_\\text{partial}^2$ for the predictors will be equal to:</p>\n\n<p>$$\\sqrt{R^2_{xy.z}} = \\frac{r_{xy}-r_{yz}r_{zx}}{\\sqrt{(1-r_{xz}^2)(1-r_{yz}^2)}}\\\\\n  \\sqrt{R^2_{xz.y}} = \\frac{r_{xz}-r_{yz}r_{yx}}{\\sqrt{(1-r_{xy}^2)(1-r_{yz}^2)}}\n$$</p>\n\n<p>the $\\sqrt{\\Delta R^2}$ is given by:</p>\n\n<p>$$\\sqrt{R^2_{xyz}-R^2_{xz}}= r_{y(x.z)} = \\frac{r_{xy}-r_{yz}r_{zx}}{\\sqrt{(1-r_{yz}^2)}}\\\\\n  \\sqrt{R^2_{xzy}-R^2_{xy}}= r_{z(x.y)}= \\frac{r_{xz}-r_{yz}r_{yx}}{\\sqrt{(1-r_{yz}^2)}}\n$$</p>\n\n<p>The difference between these is the denominator, which for the $\\beta$ and $\\sqrt{\\Delta R^2}$ contains only the correlation between the predictors. Please note that in most contexts (for weakly correlated predictors) the size of these two  will be very similar, so the decision will not impact your interpretation too much. Also, if the predictors that have a similar strength of correlation with the dependent variable and are not too strongly correlated the ratios of the $\\sqrt{ R_\\text{partial}^2}$ will be similar to the ratios of $\\beta_{std}$.</p>\n\n<p>Getting back to your code. The <code>anova</code> function in R uses type I sum of squares by default, whereas the partial $R^2$ as described above should be calculated based on a type III sum of squares (which I believe is equivalent to a type II sum of squares if no interaction is present in your model). The difference is how the explained SS is partitioned among the predictors. In type I SS the first predictor is assigned all the explained SS, the second only the \"left over SS\" and the third only the left over SS from that, therefore the order in which you enter your variables in your <code>lm</code> call changes their respective SS. This is most probably not what you want when interpreting model coefficients. </p>\n\n<p>If you use a type II sum of squares in your <code>Anova</code> call from the  <code>car</code> package in R, then the $F$ values for your anova will be equal to the $t$ values squared for your coefficients (since $F(1,n) = t^2(n)$). This indicates that indeed these quantities are closely tied, and should not be assessed independently. To invoke a type II sum of squares in your example replace <code>anova(mod)</code> with <code>Anova(mod, type = 2)</code>. If you include an interaction term you will need to replace it with type III sum of squares for the coefficient and partial R tests to be the same (just remember to change contrasts to sum using <code>options(contrasts = c(\"contr.sum\",\"contr.poly\"))</code> before calling <code>Anova(mod,type=3)</code>). Partial $R^2$ is the variable SS divided  by the variable SS plus the residual  SS. This will yield the same values as you listed from the <code>etasq()</code> output. Now the tests and $p$-values for your anova results (partial $R^2$) and your regression coefficients are the same.</p>\n\n<hr>\n\n<p><strong>Credit</strong></p>\n\n<ul>\n<li><p>The formula for the partial correlation is given in ttnphns answer here: <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/76815/multiple-regression-or-partial-correlation\">Multiple regression or partial correlation coefficient? And relations between the two</a></p></li>\n<li>The formula for semi partial correlation I found here: <a href=\"https://www3.nd.edu/~rwilliam/stats1/x92.pdf\" rel=\"noreferrer\">https://www3.nd.edu/~rwilliam/stats1/x92.pdf</a></li>\n<li>The observation that partial $R^2$ of all predictors will be 1 for a perfect fit, and thus not useful for comparing their relative importance was provided by amoeba in the comments to this question.</li>\n</ul>\n", "creationdate": "2015-03-27T18:09:20.393000", "posts_rownum": "posts_104027"}, "posts_110588": {"id": 154340, "owneruserid": 53690, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 154324, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Consider a number of I(1) processes that are cointegrated so that their linear combination is stationary. (Higher orders of integration and cointegration are straightforward to generalize to). </p>\n\n<p>When testing for cointegration using the Johansen or the Engle-Granger tests, original series (rather than their first differences) are used. </p>\n\n<p>The dependent variables of a VECM are the first differences. However, the software will normally require to input the original variables for estimating a VECM -- check the documentation carefully. </p>\n\n<p>All of this can be found in any modern time series textbook (e.g. Lutkepohl <a href=\"http://www.springer.com/us/book/9783540401728\" rel=\"nofollow\">\"New Introduction to Multiple Time Series Analysis\"</a> (2005)) or e.g. <a href=\"http://statmath.wu.ac.at/~hauser/LVs/FinEtricsQF/FEtrics_Chp4.pdf\" rel=\"nofollow\">here</a> (there are more good online resources, just search for \"vector error correction model\").</p>\n\n<p>Also note that in economic and financial applications it is normally enough to difference the data once to achieve stationarity. If the first differences of your data are nonstationary, perhaps your data is not only integrated of order one but also contain structural breaks or other \"unpleasant\" features. Differencing more than once need not be the best solution then.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2015-05-27T18:57:54.537000", "posts_rownum": "posts_110588"}, "posts_134804": {"id": 191901, "owneruserid": 3382, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 191885, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>i took your data (73 values) and used AUTOBOX ( a piece of software that I have helped develop ) and found a result that is akin to non-linearity. The acf of the residuals somewhat suggests randomness <a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/F0mGH.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/F0mGH.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></a> with the residual plot here <a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/mQiBY.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/mQiBY.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></a> . The actual/fit/forecast is here<a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/rP5sl.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/rP5sl.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></a> with forecasts here <a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/kjSVM.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/kjSVM.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></a> . The whole idea is that sometimes parameters and or error variance change over time. One shouldn't simply model all the data as if it were homogeneous as the composite/global parameters may not be uniformly representative due to an exogenous (i.e.unknown) factor. You could say that two sets of parameters .. one for the first 29 and one for the last 47 is a kind of nonlinearity as was (partly) suggested here. This is one of the possible \"elephants in the room\" that nobody talks about but I do.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2016-01-22T01:22:15.463000", "posts_rownum": "posts_134804"}, "posts_150362": {"id": 218418, "owneruserid": 119633, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 218493, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Comparing RMSE to model", "tags": "<logistic><poisson-distribution><rms>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'm assessing the accuracy of the prediction of my model using the RMSE on a new data set. Now the RMSE in itself doesn't give any indication of whether it is a good model since there is no threshold that says it is 'good'.
