"posts_46724"}, "posts_46727": {"id": 59021, "owneruserid": 686, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 59019, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I would not make an automatic choice. Sometimes you want a more parsimonious model, sometimes you want a less parsimonious model. Sometimes you want a model that is less parsimonious than either AIC or BIC recommends.</p>\n\n<p>In almost all cases you will want to look at several models and see which is the most useful to you, for your particular purposes, with your knowledge of the substantive area, with the amount of data you have. </p>\n\n<p>Attempts to automate these decisions are ways of saying to your boss \"Don't pay me so much, the computer does my thinking\".</p>\n\n<p>:-)</p>\n", "creationdate": "2013-05-14T18:54:26.863000", "posts_rownum": "posts_46727"}, "posts_59091": {"id": 74639, "owneruserid": 32337, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Transfer functions in R (TSA package)", "tags": "<r><time-series><arima>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>In Time Series models’ transfer functions there is a decay parameter in the\nformula (let’s call it b). In TSA package that decay parameter is not mentioned. When I used other software before (such as SAS) I used to determine b after analyzing ‘prewhitened series’. But\nin TSA package in R there is no need to specify the decay parameter once you analyze CCF?</p>\n\n<p>If not how am I going to know when the decay starts?</p>\n\n<p>I understand CCF is used after prewhitening to determine how to\nfilter the outputs but where b comes into the picture?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2013-11-05T14:10:31.143000", "posts_rownum": "posts_59091"}, "posts_69640": {"id": 90394, "owneruserid": 3277, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 90380, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<ul>\n<li><strong>Why are there negative values in the range of the plot?</strong> Because the input contingency table of positive values (e.g. frequencies) was\nstandardized by the analysis in a special way relative the central\npoint.</li>\n<li><strong>How is the center of the plot (i.e., the 0.0  point) found?</strong> It is the weighted mean row profile and the weighted mean column profile.\nIt is thus the locus of \"perfectly typical\" or predominant hair and eye colour.\nAccording to your data, brown hair and hazel eyes are the closest\ncandidates to be called \"typical\" of the population.</li>\n<li><strong>How did the black-brown points end up in the third quadrant of the plot?</strong> What quadrant - it doesn't matter. Row and column points\nwhich are close together tend to co-occure in the population. Blach\nhair and brown eyes normally go together, as blond hair and blue\neyes. Brown hair is also not uncommon with brown eyes; however, brown\nhair occurs very often in the population so it also is often seen with\ncombination with some other eyes, mostly hazel.</li>\n<li><strong>Why are red, hazel, & brown positive on the y-axis and negative on the x-axis?</strong> As said already, positive/negative sign doesn't matter\nitself. The general moral following from your map is that Dimension X\ncorresponds to blond vs brown/black opposition, and weaker (less\ndiscriminative of the population) Dimension Y corresponds to \"colourful\"\nvs \"plain\" opposition. Note that in simple correspondence analysis you are allowed to rotate the axes as you wish if it facilitates interpretation.</li>\n</ul>\n", "creationdate": "2014-03-18T08:24:51.273000", "posts_rownum": "posts_69640"}, "posts_97875": {"id": 134924, "owneruserid": 67430, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Tests for lognormal distribution", "tags": "<lognormal-distribution>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I have some data in the following manner.\n10\n3\n4\n5\n6\n9\n...</p>\n\n<p>I have to check that the difference between returns is log normal by doing ln(return/previous return).</p>\n\n<p>I know some tests for normality if i do (return - previous return) such as chi square test, kolmogorov-smirnov test, qq test.</p>\n\n<p>I was wondering if there are any similar tests for the lognormal, or perhaps if I could apply the normality tests in the same way</p>\n", "creationdate": "2015-01-26T01:46:06.837000", "posts_rownum": "posts_97875"}, "posts_107310": {"id": 148507, "owneruserid": 61826, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 136087, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>The std deviations given in the summary for a linear mixed model are not the std deviation for the variance estimates, they are just the estimates for the std deviation of the effects themselves, that is the square-roots of the variance estimates.\nThus, even if you calculate the std deviation of the fixed-effects variance estimate, you will not be able to compare the fixed and random variances on a graph using the random std deviations given by the summary. </p>\n", "creationdate": "2015-04-27T13:39:23.447000", "posts_rownum": "posts_107310"}, "posts_112342": {"id": 156886, "owneruserid": 21072, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 71946, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Is there any model, leave aside logistic regression, that it is not possible to overfit? </p>\n\n<p>Overfitting arises fundamentally because you fit to a sample & not the whole population. Artifacts of your sample can seem like features of the population and they are not and hence overfitting hurts. </p>\n\n<p>It is akin to a question of external validity. Using only the sample you are trying to get a model that gives you the best performance on the real population which you cannot see. </p>\n\n<p>Sure, some model forms or procedures are more likely to overfit than others but no model is ever truly immune from overfitting, is it? </p>\n\n<p>Even out-of-sample validation, regularization procedures etc. can only guard against over-fitting but there's no silver bullet. In fact, if one were to estimate one's confidence in making a real world prediction based on a fitted model one must always assume that some degree of overfitting has indeed happened. </p>\n\n<p>To what extent might vary, but even a model validated on a hold out dataset will rarely yield in-wild performance that matches what was obtained on the hold-out dataset. And overfitting is a big causative factor. </p>\n", "creationdate": "2015-06-14T07:34:51.983000", "posts_rownum": "posts_112342"}, "posts_119368": {"id": 168040, "owneruserid": 83751, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Requirement on data distribution when using certain data mining classifiers", "tags": "<distributions><data-mining><weka>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I am a little bit confused on whether data mining classifiers make any assumptions about the distribution of the data.\nI myself have a computer science background, but when I have discussions with an economist, he asks whether these classifiers do not make any assumptions of the distribution of the data (e.g. normal distribution).</p>\n\n<p>As far as I know, you can make a distinction between parametric and non-parametric classifiers in which the first is based on the statistical probability distribution of each class and the non-parametric classifier is used in case of an unknown density function.\nWhen I look at <a href=\"http://www.mecs-press.org/ijitcs/ijitcs-v4-n7/IJITCS-V4-N7-6.pdf\" rel=\"nofollow\">this paper</a> I find some classifiers being parametric (Bayes, Decision Trees, SVM) and some being non-parametric (Multilayer Perceptron).\n(Oddly enough, <a href=\"http://www.ise.bgu.ac.il/faculty/liorr/hbchap9.pdf\" rel=\"nofollow\">this paper</a> claims that decision trees are non-parametric.)</p>\n\n<p>However, <a href=\"http://weka.8497.n7.nabble.com/Normal-distribution-td810.html\" rel=\"nofollow\">here</a> I find that it is not necessary to test whether the data is normally distributed when using data mining tools.</p>\n\n<p>Do the data mining classifiers (esspecially in WEKA) require the input features and the feature that will be predicted to follow a certain distribution?\nIf so, do you know some references on which classifiers (J48,Naive Bayes, SVM,Random Forest, Multilayer Perceptron etc.) require which distribution?\nIf not, why isn't this necessary? </p>\n", "creationdate": "2015-08-20T12:36:26.750000", "posts_rownum": "posts_119368"}, "posts_290199": {"id": 437015, "owneruserid": 892, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 437001, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I think an improvement over what you have done is to compute for each user the vector of differences of word usage in the 70 categories, before and after the intervention. Thus, each user would be characterised by a vector of dimension 70. Next, I would perform a cluster analysis to show if some users separate from others in a consistent way; the results of that analysis will suggest, I expect, ways to proceed.</p>\n\n<p>You have to decide what distance to use between the 70-dimensional vectors, as I suspect some word catgegories may be much more populated than others. But surely you can come out with something reasonable.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2019-11-20T10:08:12.093000", "posts_rownum": "posts_290199"}, "posts_141812": {"id": 203933, "owneruserid": 4253, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 203929, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>To externally validate a regression model, don't refit the model.  All model parameters should be \"frozen\".  Start with a rigorous full-resolution smooth nonparametric calibration plot to check absolute predictive accuracy.  There are various tests for calibration accuracy, the most powerful of which is probably Spiegelhalter's.  Both these methods and many more, including indexes of predictive discrimination, are automatically done by the R <code>rms</code> package's <code>val.prob</code> function.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2016-03-27T12:05:03.300000", "posts_rownum": "posts_141812"}, "posts_133056": {"id": 189248, "owneruserid": 93788, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 189245, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>If you are assuming the treatment effect size and the sd of the outcome are the same in all three sites, then you don't need to account for center in your power calculation.</p>\n\n<p>This doesn't mean that the stratified randomization isn't likely to be improving your power in actual practice. Stratified randomization, matched randomization, minimization, and other forms of restricted randomization all increase your power through balancing (among the treatment arms) the distribution of covariates that are predictive of the outcome. However in your case, you are already accounting for this benefit if you are assuming a common sd for the outcome within each site. The sensibility of that assumed sd is what will largely drive the sensibility of your power calculation.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2016-01-04T21:24:19.380000", "posts_rownum": "posts_133056"}, "posts_148647": {"id": 214739, "owneruserid": 86652, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 214724, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>The difference is that with ABC you do not need an analytic expression for $P(x|\\theta)$ and instead approximate it by simulating data and seeing for which values of $\\theta$ simulated data most often (approximately) matches the observed data (with proposed values e.g. drawn randomly from the prior). For simple cases, such as a single binomial random variable with a not too large sample size you can even require an exact match and in those cases, there really is absolutely nothing you could not do with these posterior samples that you could not also do with standard MCMC samples. For more complex situations with continuous (even for multivariate discrete outcomes) and potentially multivariate outcomes requiring an exact match is no longer feasible. </p>\n\n<p>There are in fact MCMC versions of ABC, which addresses the issue that if you have a prior that does not closely resemble the posterior (e.g. because the prior is very uninformative) sampling by drawing from the prior is extremly inefficient, because you very rarely will get a close match between the observed and the simulated data.</p>\n\n<p>When $P(x|\\theta)$ is analytically available, I assume it will nearly always be preferrable to use a standard MCMC. I suppose it is conceivable that somehow the evaluation of $P(x|\\theta)$ is so incredibly computationally expensive that ABC performs better. Perhaps someone knows an example of this. In contrast I would consider ABC or MCMC-ABC (or one of the many other ABC variants) primarily when a standard MCMC approach is not an option, because $P(x|\\theta)$ is not analytically available. Of course there may be some other possible options in such cases (e.g. INLA, quadratic approximations to likelihoods etc.) that may be more efficient/successful for particular problems. In a way, any limitations in what you can do with posterior samples from ABC come from only requiring an aproximate match between the actual and the simulated data (if you could require an exact match, there would be no issues, at all). There are several good introductory papers e.g. this paper by <a href=\"http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/s11222-011-9288-2\">Marin et al. (2012)</a>. At least one of the co-authors (@Xi'an) is an active contributor here and I'd love to here his thoughts, too - I believe he may be able to say a lot more on the testing topic.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2016-05-26T07:39:08.687000", "posts_rownum": "posts_148647"}, "posts_156692": {"id": 229245, "owneruserid": 5739, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 229240, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>This is a partial answer since the question is wa-a-a-ay too broad.</p>\n\n<p>Maximum likelihood is an estimation method, not an imputation method, although some variations can be applied to missing data problems. It does not naturally produce imputations of any kind.</p>\n\n<p>Survey statisticians are usually very cautious working with heavily-model-dependent methods, such as any GLM-type models or even MI, as far as establishment surveys are concerned, because the data are usually very highly skewed. So on one hand, transformations towards normality seem like a knee-jerk reaction, but on the other hand, the imputed data have to satisfy a lot of accounting constraints. E.g., total revenue must equal the sum of total compensation, total cost of inputs, net interest payments, and profit... and I am sure I am forgetting something since I am not an accountant. If one or more of these is imputed from say a lognormal model, there is no guarantee that the accounting inequalities would hold.</p>\n\n<p>A <a href=\"http://rads.stackoverflow.com/amzn/click/047090304X\" rel=\"nofollow\">recent handbook on business surveys</a> has a chapter on editing and imputation that may help.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2016-08-10T18:51:04.377000", "posts_rownum": "posts_156692"}, "posts_158155": {"id": 231322, "owneruserid": 28500, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 231260, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>Regression coefficients in a Cox model are calculated from events, based on the covariate values of the individual having an event and the covariate values of all those still at risk at that time. With no events in the lowest-risk group of the 3 groups you thus have no ability to calculate the Cox coefficient for the lowest-risk group or its associated hazard ratio. That's different from a situation where some <em>combination</em> of covariates leads to quasi-separation, or where there are some events in a low-risk group but they all occur after those in another group.</p>\n\n<p>So your wall is insurmountable and impenetrable if you need a hazard ratio representing the lowest-risk category, based on a binned continuous marker, from your data. This is yet another reason to avoid binning a continuous marker, as frequently recommended on this site. Using the marker as a continuous predictor would give you a way to simply walk around the wall.</p>\n\n<p>If binning is necessary, you might be able to use the highest-risk group as the reference factor level and calculate the hazard ratio of the middle-risk group against that reference. But I see no way to get a corresponding hazard ratio for the lowest-risk group if it has no events.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2016-08-23T17:06:09.537000", "posts_rownum": "posts_158155"}, "posts_190603": {"id": 279749, "owneruserid": 131391, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 279752, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Which neural network package should i use?", "tags": "<neural-networks><nnet>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'm looking at running a neural network to predict the probability of a turtle becoming entangled in a fishing net. My input variables are fishing net characteristics that include continuos and categorical values (that i have scaled between 0 and 1) and my output is either 1(present) or 0 (absent).</p>\n\n<p>My question is:\nAm i correct in saying this is a classification problem and i should be using the 'nnet' package, since 'neuralnet' only deals with regression? </p>\n\n<p>Thanks for your time</p>\n\n<p>UPDATE: Here is some code i used for cross validating</p>\n\n<p>`ControlParameters<-trainControl(method=\"cv\",number=10, classProb=FALSE)</p>\n\n<p>parameterGrid<- expand.grid(layer1=1:5,layer2=1:5,layer3=1:5) </p>\n\n<p>Model1<-train(Turtles~Twine+Mesh+Black+Blue+Green+Red+Orange‌​+Yellow+Synthetic+Br‌​aided+Mono+Multi+X1+‌​X2+X3+X4+X5+X16,data‌​=train_Hypep,method=‌​'neuralnet', preProc = c(\"center\", \"scale\"),trControl=ControlParameters) `</p>\n", "creationdate": "2017-05-15T18:59:32.707000", "posts_rownum": "posts_190603"}, "posts_194083": {"id": 284963, "owneruserid": 11060, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Correlation in Distances of Points Within a Circle from Centre and One Other Point", "tags": "<correlation><spatial>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p><strong>Background</strong></p>\n\n<p>The travel cost method, a method used in economics to estimate the value of parks and other recreational sites, requires (as one step) estimating the relation between $VR_i$, the visit rate to the site for the $i$'th individual (or sometimes zone of origin), and $TC_i$, the corresponding travel cost to the site.  Travel cost is often roughly proportional to distance. Sometimes the visit rate is influenced by a second site, so that the true regression equation is of the form:</p>\n\n<p>$$VR_i = B_0 + B_1TC_i + B_2TCS_i$$</p>\n\n<p>where $TCS_i$ is the travel cost to the second site.  Regression theory implies that if the variable $TCS_i$ is omitted when estimating the relation between $VR_i$ and $TC_i$, then the estimates of $B_0$ and $B_1$ are likely to be biased, and that the amount and direction of bias will depend partly on the sign and magnitude of correlation between $TC_i$ and $TCS_i$. </p>\n\n<p><strong>Question</strong></p>\n\n<p>Abstracting from the above, suppose $A$ is the centre of a circle of radius $r$, and $B$ is a point at distance $d$ from $A$ ($d < r$).  Suppose a large number of points, indexed by $i$, are uniformly distributed by area within the circle.  Define random variables $X$ and $Y$ as the distances from $A$ and $B$ respectively to $i$.  What is the correlation coefficient $\\rho$ between $X$ and $Y$?  Either an exact formula or a good approximation would be useful.</p>\n\n<p><strong>What I Have Done</strong></p>\n\n<p>Starting from the formula:</p>\n\n<p>$$\\rho = \\frac{cov(X,Y)}{\\sigma_X\\sigma_Y}$$</p>\n\n<p>I calculated $\\mu_X$ and hence $\\sigma_X$ as follows:</p>\n\n<p>$$\\mu_X = \\int_0^r z.(2\\pi z/\\pi r^2) dz = \\int_0^r 2z^2/r^2 dz = \\bigg[ 2z^3/3r^2 \\bigg]_0^r = 2r/3$$</p>\n\n<p>$$\\sigma^2_X = \\int_0^r [z - (2r/3)]^2(2\\pi z/\\pi r^2) dz = \\int_0^r [z^2 - 4rz/3 + 4r^2/9](2z/r^2) dz$$\n$$\\sigma^2_X = \\frac{1}{r^2} \\int_0^r [2z^3 - 8rz^2/3 + 8r^2z/9] dz = \\frac{1}{r^2} \\bigg[\\frac{z^4}{2} - \\frac{8rz^3}{9} + \\frac{4r^2z^2}{9} \\bigg]_0^r$$\n$$\\sigma^2_X = \\frac{1}{r^2}\\bigg[\\frac{r^4}{2} - \\frac{8r^4}{9} + \\frac{4r^4}{9}\\bigg] = \\frac{r^2}{18}$$\n$$\\sigma_X = \\frac{r}{3\\sqrt{2}} \\approx 0.236r$$</p>\n\n<p>However, I'm not sure how to proceed to find $cov(X,Y)$ and $\\sigma_Y$, which appear to need more sophisticated applications of calculus.</p>\n\n<p>Intuitively, I can see that there will be a positive correlation when $d$ is much smaller than $r$, so that A and B are relatively close together, but I'm not sure whether the correlation will become negative for larger $d$.</p>\n\n<p><strong>Update 14/6/2017</strong></p>\n\n<p>Prompted by whuber's comment I estimated $\\rho$ for the case with $B$ on the edge of the circle by an approximate method. A distribution of 120 points within the circle was defined as follows. The circle was imagined divided into 10 concentric rings of equal width. Numbering the rings from the centre, their areas are in the ratio $1:3:5:...:2n-1:...:19$. Along the middle of each ring, 12 points were positioned at intervals of 30 degrees relative to the line $AB$. The distance of each point from $B$ was found using the cosine rule. In calculating $\\rho$, values associated with points were weighted by the areas of their respective rings (this is equivalent to having the number of points in each ring proportional to its area). This gave the following results (rounded to 3 significant figures):</p>\n\n<p>$$\\sigma_X = 0.235r$$</p>\n\n<p>$$\\sigma_Y = 0.470r$$</p>\n\n<p>$$cov(X,Y) = 0.0175r^2$$</p>\n\n<p>$$\\rho = 0.158$$</p>\n\n<p>This estimate of $\\rho$ is reasonably close to whuber's 0.164. </p>\n", "creationdate": "2017-06-12T15:58:54.837000", "posts_rownum": "posts_194083"}, "posts_175105": {"id": 255868, "owneruserid": 60621, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 257305, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to include in a regression two factors where one level of one factor is necessarily nested with one level of another factor?", "tags": "<regression><categorical-data><fixed-effects-model>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I've got a situation where I have a series of individuals who have two factors describing their health.  Factor A has 3 levels while factor B has 4 levels.  Biologically, level 1 of factor A appears if and only if factor B is level 1.  Therefore, I have data structured like this:</p>\n\n<pre><code>ID   Factor A  Factor B   Score\n1      a        alpha       0.1\n2      a        alpha       0.2\n3      b        beta        0.3\n4      b        gamma       0.4\n5      b        delta       0.5\n6      c        beta        0.6\n7      c        gamma       0.7\n8      c        delta       0.8\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>I'm interested in studying the effects of both factors, but I'm struggling with how to properly code this.  Giving each factor their own full set of dummy codes is rank deficient and leaving out a level of either factor creates a model with impossible combinations (ie level <em>a</em> ONLY occurs with level <em>alpha</em>, and vice versa).  <strong>How could I code these fixed effects so that I can investigate the impact of both factors on our score?  Additionally, how would I interpret this coding scheme?</strong></p>\n\n<p>EDIT:  To give some further context on how this happens, Factor A is series of related diseases (each phenotypically similar, but genetically different) while Factor B is severity of that diseased state.  So <em>a</em> is the control group while <em>alpha</em> is healthy severity.  These two occur contemporaneously by necessity (ie a healthy severity must be a control while a control can be nothing but healthy).</p>\n", "creationdate": "2017-01-12T15:31:55.227000", "posts_rownum": "posts_175105"}, "posts_183324": {"id": 268357, "owneruserid": 153643, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 268419, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "What hypothesis test should I use to test if a binary variable is dependent on an ordinal value?", "tags": "<hypothesis-testing><mathematical-statistics><categorical-data><ordinal-data><binary-data>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I have a number of finishes in football which are labeled either goal or miss. For each shot I know the standings in the game at the time of the shot, which I use to calculate <code>gamestate</code> for the shooting team (1 = leading, 0 = tied, -1 = trailing). I have calculated the conversion rate for each value of <code>gamestate</code>.  </p>\n\n<p>I want to test if the outcome is dependent on <code>gamestate</code> and would like to reject the hypothesis that the outcome of a shot is not dependent on <code>gamestate</code>. </p>\n\n<p><strong>Question:</strong> Does this makes sense? For each patient, he can have one or two measures. Theses measures are classified by the group. However, there exist correlation across the multiple measures for each patient, so the group means are correlated. I want to use the mixed effect model:</p>\n\n<p>$Y_{ij}=Group_{ij}*\\beta$ + $Group_{ij}*U_i$ + $\\epsilon_{ij}$</p>\n\n<p>Where Group is a 1 by 2 design matrix and $U_i$ is a vector with two random variables, $var(U_i)$=[$\\sigma_{ij}$], $U_i$ and $\\epsilon_{ij}$ are i.i.d.. Therefore</p>\n\n<p>$cov(Y_{i1},Y_{i2'})=\\sigma_{Group_1,Group_2}$</p>\n\n<p>and</p>\n\n<p>$cov(Y_{ij},Y_{i'j'})=0$</p>\n\n<p>I've tried to use SAS and R to fit the above model. However SAS will give me \"Did not converge\" and R will say \"the random-effects parameters and the residual variance (or scale parameter) are probably unidentifiable\"</p>\n\n<p>Here is my R code for simulation:</p>\n\n<pre><code>getdata<-function(n){\n  set.seed(1)\n  groupMean=c(1,2)\n  data=c()\n  sig=matrix(data=c(1,0.5,0.5,1),nrow = 2)\n  for(i in 1:n){\n    rndEffect=mvrnorm(1,c(0,0),sig)\n    repeatNum=sample(1:2,1)\n    for(j in 1:repeatNum){\n      group=sample(1:2,1)\n      y=groupMean[group]+rndEffect[group]+rnorm(1)\n      data=rbind(data,c(y,group,i))\n    }\n\n  }\n  data=as.data.frame(data)\n  names(data)=c(\"y\",\"group\",\"id\")\n  data$group=as.factor(data$group)\n  return(data)\n}\n\nmydata=getdata(10)\nmodel <- lmer(y ~ group-1 + (0+group|id),mydata)\n</code></pre>\n\n<p>I know there are several existing answers related to this question, but none of them can solve my problem, the most related one is here:</p>\n\n<p><a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/95676/how-to-compare-two-sides-of-patients-with-multiple-measures-per-patient\">How to compare two sides of patients with multiple measures per patient?</a></p>\n\n<p>Unfortunately, their suggestion is the same as mine and the answer doesn't have the model or the code.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2017-04-19T15:07:19.723000", "posts_rownum": "posts_187348"}, "posts_200554": {"id": 297015, "owneruserid": 100048, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 296955, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "body": "<p>I'd say the distinction between engineering and learning is subjective. This is how I differentiate them,</p>\n\n<p><strong>Feature Engineering:</strong></p>\n\n<p>Handcrafting new variables from the existing ones.</p>\n\n<p>eg: BMI, when the weight and the height are available</p>\n\n<p><strong>Feature Learning:</strong></p>\n\n<p>Letting your system figure out what are the best features for the problem at hand.</p>\n\n<p>The <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feature_learning\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">wikipedia page</a> is a good resource to read more. They probably made a typo in their publication. </p>\n\n<p>The <a href=\"https://www.socscistatistics.com/pvalues/chidistribution.aspx\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">site</a> I used to compute the p-value.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2018-09-18T21:53:57.243000", "posts_rownum": "posts_244865"}, "posts_245281": {"id": 368157, "owneruserid": 219255, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 368159, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Determine AR term from PACF plot", "tags": "<time-series><mathematical-statistics><arima><acf-pacf>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I have the a time series data, the acf and pacf for which have been displayed below:\n<a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/WyEol.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/WyEol.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></a></p>\n\n<p><a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/cBUo5.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/cBUo5.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></a></p>\n\n<p>I get that MA term is 1. But I'm confused about AR term since it is geometrically decaying from 7th lag. Do I need to transform the data again to eliminate this?</p>\n\n<p>PS: This data has already been differenced once.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2018-09-22T11:19:55.817000", "posts_rownum": "posts_245281"}, "posts_249376": {"id": 374517, "owneruserid": 225264, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 357162, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>You didn't mention you train strategy, assuming that you use pretrained ImageNet weights:</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li>You should first freeze everything but your last added dense layer\nand train it for some epochs (say 10).  </li>\n<li>Then you might want to train only 1/2 or 1/4 of all layers counting\nfrom the last one. Especially if your data is natural images. The\ngoal is to fine-tune abstract layers without overfitting the\nnetwork.</li>\n</ol>\n\n<p>Even if you train it from the scratch, from provided log it's quite clear that your model just overfits the training data without learning generalizable features.</p>\n\n<p>To prevent that:</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li>Use heavy data augmentation</li>\n<li>Add weight decay to all layers and set it to ~ 1e-4 or 1e-5</li>\n<li>As mentioned above, decrease the number of trainable layers,\nfreezing them from left to right if you use pre-trained weights.</li>\n</ol>\n", "creationdate": "2018-10-30T21:25:46.520000", "posts_rownum": "posts_249376"}, "posts_252717": {"id": 379829, "owneruserid": 11887, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 87336, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>Partially answered in comments:</p>\n\n<p>Clearly <span class=\"math-container\">$(x−a)/(b−a)$</span> maps <span class=\"math-container\">$x \\in [a,b]$</span> to <span class=\"math-container\">$[0,1]$</span>. logit(x) maps (0,1) to (−∞,∞). – Nick Cox</p>\n\n<p>indeed the inverse of any continuous-strictly-monotonic-cdf-on-(−∞,∞) maps (0,1) to (−∞,∞). There's uncountable infinities of choices. – Glen_b   </p>\n", "creationdate": "2018-12-01T21:59:44.927000", "posts_rownum": "posts_252717"}, "posts_253954": {"id": 381633, "owneruserid": 226981, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "PROC GENMOD Negative Binomial doesn't predict zeros", "tags": "<regression><sas><negative-binomial-distribution><poisson-regression>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I am using PROC GENMOD with time series data, I have tried to work with Negative Binomial, Poisson, GEE and Zero Inflated Poisson, but in each case when I score my validation dataset, I am getting predicted values which are never zero.</p>\n\n<p>E.g. A customer might buy fuel every 4 weeks, the model does not predict the weeks in between fuel fills as zeros.</p>\n\n<p>Is there a better way of predicting the weeks with zero fuel fills? I assumed Negative Binomial would be able to do this, but the lack of predicted zero outcomes, which represent 78% of the fuel filling weeks (by customer) has made this model ineffective.</p>\n\n<p>Thanks in advance!!</p>\n", "creationdate": "2018-12-12T11:08:20.800000", "posts_rownum": "posts_253954"}, "posts_256788": {"id": 386716, "owneruserid": 232372, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "When does my autoencoder start to overfit?", "tags": "<neural-networks><overfitting><unsupervised-learning><autoencoders><stochastic-gradient-descent>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I am working on anomaly detection using an <strong>autoencoder</strong> neural network with <span class=\"math-container\">$1$</span> hidden layer. This is an <strong>unsupervised</strong> setting, as I do not have previous examples of anomalies. The input data has patterns but also varies a lot, hence, is partly stochastic in nature.</p>\n\n<p>For understanding purposes, I trained a (complete) autoencoder with dimensions input = <span class=\"math-container\">$500$</span>, hidden = <span class=\"math-container\">$500$</span>, output = <span class=\"math-container\">$500$</span> and sigmoid functions in the hidden and output layer. My training data has dimension <span class=\"math-container\">$X\\in[0,1]^{5000\\times500}$</span> (500 variables, 5000 samples). I used <span class=\"math-container\">$3$</span> algorithms, with learning rate <span class=\"math-container\">$0.01$</span>, mini batch size <span class=\"math-container\">$64$</span>, and pretty much the standard algo-parameters in Keras/TensorFlow:</p>\n\n<ol>\n<li>standard stochastic gradient descent (SGD)</li>\n<li>advanced/extended SGD with Nesterov momentum <span class=\"math-container\">$0.9$</span> and learning rate decay <span class=\"math-container\">$10^{-8}$</span></li>\n<li>Adam optimizer (<span class=\"math-container\">$\\beta_1=0.9$</span>, <span class=\"math-container\">$\\beta_2=0.999$</span>, learning rate decay <span class=\"math-container\">$0$</span>)</li>\n</ol>\n\n<p>The image below shows the corresponding error curves. In my case both keep decreasing (except for Adam) so I would say \"keep training\". On the other hand I know intuitively that I should not train so long because there must be some overfitting going on. So how do I know when to stop training, how would you interpret the result below? Would I be right, to just take Adam and use 250 epochs (even though it has a wide bias between training/validation sets)?</p>\n\n<p><a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/qL2fH.png\" rel=\"noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/qL2fH.png\" alt=\"enter image description here\"></a></p>\n", "creationdate": "2019-01-11T14:38:02.043000", "posts_rownum": "posts_256788"}, "posts_257513": {"id": 387743, "owneruserid": 209784, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Determining variance of UMVUE", "tags": "<mathematical-statistics><estimation><unbiased-estimator>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>Let <span class=\"math-container\">$X_1,...,X_n$</span> be iid with pdf given by <span class=\"math-container\">$f(x;\\theta)=\\frac{log\\theta}{\\theta^{x-1}}I(x>1)$</span>. My task is to determine if the <span class=\"math-container\">$\\mu=E[X]=1+\\frac{1}{log\\theta}$</span> can be estimated efficiently, i.e. if the UMVUE for <span class=\"math-container\">$\\mu$</span> achieves the Cramer-Rao lower bound. Here's my work:</p>\n\n<p>The pdf <span class=\"math-container\">$f(x;\\theta)$</span> is a member of the one-parameter exponential family, so <span class=\"math-container\">$T=T(X)=\\sum_{i=1}^nX_i$</span> is complete-sufficient for <span class=\"math-container\">$\\theta$</span>, i.e. for <span class=\"math-container\">$\\mu$</span>. Furthermore, <span class=\"math-container\">$g(T)=\\frac{T}{n}$</span> is unbiased for <span class=\"math-container\">$\\mu$</span>, so by Lehmann-Scheffe, <span class=\"math-container\">$g(X)=\\bar X$</span> is the UMVUE. </p>\n\n<p>To see if <span class=\"math-container\">$\\bar X$</span> attains the Cramer-Rao lower-bound, we must calculate its variance, where <span class=\"math-container\">$V[\\bar X]=\\frac{V[X]}{n}$</span>. Here is where I'm stuck. To get <span class=\"math-container\">$V[X]$</span>, how should I calculate <span class=\"math-container\">$E[X^2]$</span>? Should I simply use the integration method? I believe it would require integration by parts twice, and I end up with very strange expression. Is there some other route I could take? </p>\n", "creationdate": "2019-01-17T15:28:31.027000", "posts_rownum": "posts_257513"}, "posts_260772": {"id": 392478, "owneruserid": 1352, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 392475, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>The first thing to look at is what happened in months 10 and 11: where did the large increases come from? Has the product reached a plateau? If so, essentially forecast a flat line on the level of sales in months 11-17. Or is another increase of a similar magnitude likely? Or was this a one-time push that saturated the market, so that future sales will drop down to the level in months 1-9?</p>\n\n<p>Forecasting 36 months based on 18 months history is very hard.</p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p>with the best fitting curve (an exponential curve)</p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p>In-sample fit is not a good proxy for out-of-sample predictive accuracy. Fitting an exponential curve to 18 months of history and extrapolating 36 months out invites disaster. You should not be expending more than two parameters on only 18 observations.</p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p>the MSE, MAD and MAPE are too high</p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p>What is \"too high\"? Your series may simply be hard to forecast. <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/q/222179/1352\">How to know that your machine learning problem is hopeless?</a></p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p>and the residual plots suggest correlation. </p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p>Given the upward trend, this does not surprise me. The important thing is to understand where that trend came from, and whether the driver is likely to continue.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2019-02-14T12:53:29.463000", "posts_rownum": "posts_260772"}, "posts_265353": {"id": 399319, "owneruserid": 242367, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Find a vector that satisfies the following: i) it has a given correlation with a second vector and ii) it is orthogonal to a set of vectors", "tags": "<correlation><orthogonal>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I would like to generate a vector <span class=\"math-container\">$\\vec{u}$</span> of dimension <span class=\"math-container\">$n$</span>, so that i) it has a given correlation <span class=\"math-container\">$r$</span> with a second vector <span class=\"math-container\">$\\vec{v}$</span> and ii) it is orthogonal to a set of <span class=\"math-container\">$m$</span> vectors <span class=\"math-container\">$A = \\{\\vec{w}_1, \\vec{w}_2, \\dots, \\vec{w}_k\\}$</span>. I would like to do it in R. Any idea?</p>\n\n<p>thanks a lot!</p>\n\n<p>PS: Solving <span class=\"math-container\">$A \\times x = 0$</span> would fix ii). Also, satisfiying i) is relatively straightforward. However I have not been able to find a way to to ensure both i) and ii).</p>\n", "creationdate": "2019-03-25T14:37:00.407000", "posts_rownum": "posts_265353"}, "posts_266538": {"id": 401072, "owneruserid": 212689, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 401035, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>If you genuinely have a small population and you manage to sample more than 5% of it, you can apply the finite population correction, where you multiply your standard error by: <span class=\"math-container\">$FPC=\\sqrt{\\frac{N-n}{N-1}}$</span>, where N is your population size and n is your sample size.</p>\n<p>However, I would urge caution on a few points, as I'm not convinced that you will meet the assumptions required to use the finite population correction:</p>\n<ol>\n<li><p>You need a random sample of your population, will you achieve that?</p>\n</li>\n<li><p>1% of a large population is still a large number.</p>\n</li>\n<li><p>You presumably want to make inferences about people with the condition in future, e.g. those who have not been born yet. So your population may actually be larger than you think. Even though that doesn't help you with recruitment for your study!</p>\n</li>\n</ol>\n<p>The difference you are trying to detect is quite small (and potentially very small relative to the expected population variance, which you don't give) which is probably why the software estimates that you need a large sample size.</p>\n<p>Others may have helpful suggestions for how to mitigate the effects of your small sample size.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2019-04-03T22:56:10.780000", "posts_rownum": "posts_266538"}, "posts_297274": {"id": 447319, "owneruserid": 153364, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 447303, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>If I'm reading your question correctly you are simply asking about <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_comparisons_problem\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">multiple comparison</a> in statistics which is a well known phenomena. To remedy this, you can correct your significance using something like a <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bonferroni_correction\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Bonferroni-correction</a>, although many types of correction methods exist.</p>\n\n<p>Note that you also need to consider the implication of your analysis. Is it something that will dictate how your company or medical department operates? Then you should probably take it more seriously than if your study is simply to pave way and direct future research. Multiple comparison and how we address it, is in essence just a dance between type-1 and type-2 errors.</p>\n\n<p>EDIT: After reading your edit.</p>\n\n<blockquote>\n  <p>This may be my main point: does significance at the regression\n  coefficient level mean anything in this case?</p>\n</blockquote>\n\n<p>The coefficient tells you both the direction and size of the impact your covariates have on the dependent variable, with respect to the model as a whole. If the p-value of a covariate is significant, but the model contains enough individual covariates with no pre-determined hypothesis, that you suspect the unadjusted p-values may be erroneous, the coefficient and the CI may be inflated, even if truly significant. Another important part with respect to coefficients is how well you have controlled for confounders as these can dramatically change the coefficients in your model. <a href=\"https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23583358\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Related literature</a> on this topic.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2020-01-31T18:33:43.840000", "posts_rownum": "posts_297274"}, "posts_308620": {"id": 465408, "owneruserid": 203570, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 465399, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>Hi you can train in self supervised way your 4D time series. \nYou can use a convolutionnal network you will have 4 inputs channels.\nYou will use then a MSE loss between your input let's says last 2048 points and prediction set at the 256 points for example.\nIn order to achieve a good accuracy you can train a convolutionnal VAE autoencodeur and use the encoder in your convolutionnal network for prediction.\nLike :\nInput -> Encode -> feedForward -> prediction</p>\n", "creationdate": "2020-05-09T13:10:08.897000", "posts_rownum": "posts_308620"}, "posts_313635": {"id": 472618, "owneruserid": 1352, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 472610, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>The most reliable way of understanding the capabilities of a package is, as always its CRAN page. In the specific case of <a href=\"https://cran.r-project.org/package=fable\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">the <code>fable</code> package</a>, we find <a href=\"https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/fable/fable.pdf\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">its reference manual</a> and two different vignettes, <a href=\"https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/fable/vignettes/fable.html\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">one introduction</a> and <a href=\"https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/fable/vignettes/transformations.html\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">one vignette on forecasting with transformations</a>.</p>\n<p>The reference manual in particular looks helpful. For instance, I see no less than ten <code>fitted.*()</code> functions:</p>\n<pre><code>> library(dplyr)\n> ls(getNamespace("fable"), all.names=TRUE) %>%\n+ grep(pattern="fitted",value=TRUE)\n[1] "fitted.AR"         "fitted.ARIMA"      "fitted.croston"   \n[4] "fitted.ETS"        "fitted.model_mean" "fitted.NNETAR"    \n[7] "fitted.RW"         "fitted.TSLM"       "fitted.VAR"\n</code></pre>\n<p>True, not all of them are very different (<code>fitted.AR()</code> vs. <code>fitted.ARIMA()</code>), but there are quite a few more than you mention (e.g., <code>fitted.NNETAR()</code>, <code>fitted.fable_theta()</code> or <code>fitted.croston()</code>).</p>\n<p>Also note that <code>fable</code> is the successor package to <code>forecast</code>, so over time, it will likely accumulate more models.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2020-06-17T05:44:41.513000", "posts_rownum": "posts_313635"}, "posts_316866": {"id": 477352, "owneruserid": 69508, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 230752, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>This is only a partial answer because it doesn't meet the accuracy requirements, however I'll explain where the answer comes from. As has been pointed out by <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/users/919/whuber\">whuber♦</a> above in the comments and in this <a href=\"https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/26988/probability-of-finding-a-particular-sequence-of-base-pairs\">post</a>, the specific content of the strings influence the true probability of the event described in the OP.</p>\n<p>Instead of analytically working out these many details, one might try a simulated approach. The following is an implementation in Python of an algorithm that simply generates k-mers of length 9 and 500 sequences of length 1000, counts occurrences of the k-mer in the other sequences, and puts the resulting count into a list. There are improvements that can be made to this code to improve the time and space requirements, but I think this simpler example communicates the process adequately.</p>\n<pre class=\"lang-py prettyprint-override\"><code>from random import choice\nimport numpy as np\n\ndef randseq(n):\n    return ''.join([choice(['A', 'T', 'C', 'G']) for i in range(n)])\n\ncounts = []\ni = 0\nwhile len(counts) < 5 or 3 * np.std(counts) / np.sqrt(i) > 0.0001:\n    i += 1\n    kmer = randseq(9)\n    kcount = 0\n    for j in range(500):\n        seq = randseq(1000)\n        if kmer in seq:\n            kcount += seq.count(kmer)\n    counts.append(kcount)\n    print(i, kcount, np.mean(counts), 3 * np.std(counts) / np.sqrt(i))\n</code></pre>\n<p>Using the above, I found that a sample of <span class=\"math-container\">$n=14199$</span> iterations of the 'experiment' yielded a mean of <span class=\"math-container\">$1.8833016409606311 \\pm 0.03492470125969519$</span> (3 times standard error). I stopped the calculations at this point because I realized that the mean would converge very slowly. The standard error of the mean is <span class=\"math-container\">$$s_{\\bar{x}} = \\frac{1}{\\sqrt{n}} \\sqrt{\\frac{(\\sum x_i - \\bar{x})^2}{n}} = \\frac{s_x}{\\sqrt{n}}$$</span></p>\n<p>where <span class=\"math-container\">$n$</span> is the sample size, <span class=\"math-container\">$x_i$</span> is an instance of the random variable representing the number of occurrences of the k-mer in the other sequences, and <span class=\"math-container\">$\\bar{x}$</span> is the estimate of the mean of this random variable.</p>\n<p>Since the mean and standard deviation are consistent estimators, we need only have a sufficiently large <span class=\"math-container\">$n$</span> to reach an arbitrary precision in <span class=\"math-container\">$\\bar{x}$</span> as calculated in terms of <span class=\"math-container\">$s_{\\bar{x}}$</span>. Thinking in terms of confidence intervals, perhaps we'd be satisfied with <span class=\"math-container\">$3 s_{\\bar{x}} = 10^{-4}$</span> being a way of declaring whether we've met the accuracy requirement, giving us:</p>\n<p><span class=\"math-container\">$$\\frac{s_x}{\\sqrt{n}} = \\frac{10^{-4}}{3}$$</span></p>\n<p>Given that my data had <span class=\"math-container\">$s_x = 1.387203975627196$</span> at <span class=\"math-container\">$n=14199$</span>, we'll use that value for a ball-park estimate. Substituting for <span class=\"math-container\">$s_x$</span>, and solving for <span class=\"math-container\">$n$</span>, I would expect that the required sample size using this approach would be <span class=\"math-container\">$n=1731901383$</span>. My approach here doesn't work to answer the question in a reasonable amount of time, but would <em>eventually</em> yield the correct answer.</p>\n<h3 id=\"update-8aqg\">Update</h3>\n<p>I re-ran the simulations and obtained a closer <span class=\"math-container\">$3 \\sigma$</span> estimate of <span class=\"math-container\">$\\bar{x} = 1.8897422883888795 \\pm 0.0043822154484445775$</span> where <span class=\"math-container\">$n=886650$</span>.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2020-07-15T19:31:39.497000", "posts_rownum": "posts_316866"}, "posts_317062": {"id": 477629, "owneruserid": 163146, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 477627, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>Basically, you reduce the input (dimension) by reducing the neurons per layer. This is the encoder part.\nAfterwards, based on that very low dimensional representation, the entire data is broken down to only important features.\nThis is what you finally wanna' have: A meaningful, low dimensional data representation.\nTo train and validate this encoder function, you decode this data by mostly using the same topology in a reversed manner.\nNow there are two options:</p>\n<ol>\n<li>Either you use the encoder + decoder: So you wanna' be able to restore all your data again only based on these few features. This would be something like a nonlinear PCA.</li>\n<li>Or you detach the encoder part and use it for new data.</li>\n</ol>\n<p>A good example, e.g., is the use for mobile communication which breaks down/encodes the data so that only a significant part of your speech remains, then this data is transfered and at the receiver side it is decoded.\nDespite from that concept the handling and so on is quite the same like for every neural network (train, validate, minimize error function and so on..).</p>\n<p><a href=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/ScCqO.png\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\"><img src=\"https://i.stack.imgur.com/ScCqO.png\" alt=\"AE\" /></a></p>\n<p><a href=\"https://lilianweng.github.io/lil-log/2018/08/12/from-autoencoder-to-beta-vae.html\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Image source</a></p>\n", "creationdate": "2020-07-17T11:07:59.030000", "posts_rownum": "posts_317062"}, "posts_317063": {"id": 477630, "owneruserid": 291597, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Fitting Joint Model with GLMM", "tags": "<r><mixed-model><survival><glmm>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I'm looking to fit a joint survival model (<a href=\"https://www.r-bloggers.com/an-introduction-to-joint-modeling-in-r/\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">example</a>). For those who are unfamiliar, joint survival models are Cox proportional hazard models where the covariates are allowed to be time-varying and are actually predictions from a mixed effects model. Typically these are fit by fitting an linear mixed effects model and survival model separately, and then putting the outputs into a joint modeling function. Example using <code>library(JM)</code> taken from <a href=\"https://aurora-mareviv.github.io/talesofr/2018/02/intro-joint-modeling-r/\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">this online example</a>:</p>\n<pre><code>library(JM)\n# Animation example \n# Mixed-effects model fit\nlmeFit.p1 <- lme(log(pro) ~ time + time:treat, data = prothro,\n    random = ~ time | id)  \n\n# Cox survival model fit\nsurvFit.p1 <- coxph(Surv(Time, death) ~ treat, data = prothros, x = TRUE)  \n\n# Joint model\njointFit.p1 <- jointModel(lmeFit.p1, survFit.p1, timeVar = "time",\n    method = "piecewise-PH-aGH")\n</code></pre>\n<p>However, in the case of my particular research question, my covariates are not normally distributed (they are rates, and are therefore Poisson distributed). I assume that this means that I'll need to be using a GLMM to estimate the time-varying predictors/covariates instead of a simple LMM.</p>\n<p>I'll be running my analyses in <code>R</code>, so am looking for packages that will accommodate GLMMs in the mixed model, but everything that I seem to find online only uses a <a href=\"https://www.annalsthoracicsurgery.org/article/S0003-4975(12)00409-2/pdf\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">linear mixed effect model</a> (e.g. from <code>lme</code>).</p>\n<p>Does anyone have any recommendations for extending the joint model to include GLMMs and/or any package recommendations to do so? I know that there are lots of GLMM packages out there that fit GLMMs, but is there anything that is analogous to the above code but using GLMMs instead of LMMs?</p>\n<p>As an aside, I also am looking into if transformations of the covariate is appropriate. However, I'm hoping to not lose interpretability on this particular covariate.</p>\n<p>Thank you!</p>\n", "creationdate": "2020-07-17T11:08:16.017000", "posts_rownum": "posts_317063"}, "posts_320522": {"id": 483263, "owneruserid": 294173, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "How to decide if categorical variable is significant in cox regression, SPSS", "tags": "<multiple-regression><survival><spss><cox-model>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I performed univariate analysis to identify predictors of survival in a cohort. not an equality, meaning the generalization of Lagrange multipliers is needed—the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions. The PMF is correct, because:</p>\n<ul>\n<li>all probabilities sum to 1</li>\n<li><span class=\"math-container\">$E[Z]$</span> gives the result I expected</li>\n<li>I generalized the PMF to <span class=\"math-container\">$n$</span> random variables with a nonlinear transformation and the expected value is still correct (I checked it by sampling 1 million times)</li>\n</ul>\n", "creationdate": "2020-10-12T23:48:26.663000", "posts_rownum": "posts_326368"}, "posts_327392": {"id": 493123, "owneruserid": 143489, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 492836, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>You are interested in the distribution of number of successes, that is how many dice out of an initial <span class=\"math-container\">$x$</span> will be left in the game after three rolls, given the rules. You estimated <span class=\"math-container\">$E[X]=np=20 \\cdot 0.11=2.2$</span>, this is the expected number of dies that remain in the game at the end. The variance is <span class=\"math-container\">$Var[X]=np(1-p)=20 \\cdot 0.11(1-0.11)=1.958$</span>.</p>\n<p>Your question, at the least the last one, is how many dice would you have to roll, such that you decrease the variance enough that 90 % of outcomes are within one standard deviation of the expected value. So if the expected value is 2.2, 90 % of outcomes would have to be between 1 and 3.</p>\n<p>This cannot be done. In fact, what you will find is that, by increasing the number of dice, while keeping the probability the same, the variance actually increases (so you would have to decrease the number of dice to decrease the variance). I think you got this idea from the distribution of the mean, where increasing the sample size decreases the variance of the distribution, that is the distribution gets narrower.</p>\n<p>In your case the only way you can decrease the variance is by changing the probability of success (which is related to changing the number of rolls, which is the question in your title but not in the actual text). This is actually a rule which is sometimes used when estimating the sample size, the variance is greatest at probability 0.5, and then decreases as you move towards the extremes 0 and 1.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2020-10-22T06:14:59.507000", "posts_rownum": "posts_327392"}, "posts_330803": {"id": 498103, "owneruserid": 1352, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 498101, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>The most balanced partition would be the one that has equal mass in all bins. So we should compare each partition to the equal-mass one.</p>\n<p>The most natural comparison metric would be the <a href=\"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth_mover%27s_distance\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">Earth Mover's Distance</a> (EMD), which calculates how much mass needs to be shifted how far to turn one distribution to another one. In your case, Partition 1 will have a smaller EMD to the uniform partition than Partition 2.</p>\n<p>The EMD is also known as the <a href=\"/questions/tagged/wasserstein\" class=\"post-tag\" title=\"show questions tagged 'wasserstein'\" rel=\"tag\">wasserstein</a> metric. You may want to look through the tag.</p>\n", "creationdate": "2020-11-26T06:50:22.050000", "posts_rownum": "posts_330803"}, "posts_331210": {"id": 498679, "owneruserid": 221384, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 498646, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>Note: This is just a comment but to quote a long code, I put it here.</p>\n<blockquote>\n<pre><code>for (ite in 2:NSim){\n#Full conditional for pi\n\n pi[ite]=rbeta(1, sum(delta[ite-1,])+0.5, sum(1-delta[ite-1,])+0.5)\n\n #Full conditional for delta\n for(j in 1:4){\n  p1=pi[ite]*exp(-beta[ite-1,j]^2/(20))\n  p0=((1-pi[ite])*10^3)*exp(-500*beta[ite-1,j]^2)\n  cat('\\n',ite,j,(p1/(p0+p1)))\n  delta[ite,j]=rbinom(1, 1,prob=(p1/(p0+p1)))\n  }\n</code></pre>\n</blockquote>\n<p>The error says that maybe <span class=\"math-container\">$p1$</span> and <span class=\"math-container\">$p0$</span> are NAs. The forward stepwise procedure will assign it a positive coefficient if and only if the following two conditions are true:\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$X_3^Ty/||X_3||_2 \\geq \\pm X_1^Ty/||X_1||_2$$</span>\nand\n<span class=\"math-container\">$$X_3^Ty/||X_3||_2 \\geq \\pm X_2^Ty/||X_2||_2$$</span>\nwhere <span class=\"math-container\">$X_j$</span> is the <span class=\"math-container\">$j$</span>th column vector of the design matrix, <span class=\"math-container\">$X \\in \\mathbb{R}^{N \\times p}$</span>, and <span class=\"math-container\">$y\\in \\mathbb{R}^n$</span> is the response vector.</p>\n<p><strong>My question is: how does "the 3rd variable minimizes the residual sum error" translate to the above two conditions?</strong></p>\n<p>From my understanding, the procedure would select the third variable <span class=\"math-container\">$X_3$</span> if <span class=\"math-container\">$\\sum_{i=1}^N (y_i - \\hat{\\beta}_3X_{3i})^2$</span> is smaller than  <span class=\"math-container\">$\\sum_{i=1}^N (y_i - \\hat{\\beta}_1X_{1i})^2$</span> and <span class=\"math-container\">$\\sum_{i=1}^N (y_i - \\hat{\\beta}_2X_{2i})^2,$</span> where <span class=\"math-container\">$\\hat{\\beta}_j = \\left(X_j^TX_j\\right)^{-1}X_j^Ty$</span> is the OLS estimate for the <span class=\"math-container\">$j$</span>th variable. X_{3i}y_i}{\\sqrt{\\sum_{i=1}^N X_{3i}^2}}\\geq \\pm \\frac{\\sum_{i=1}^N X_{1i}y_i}{\\sqrt{\\sum_{i=1}^N X_{1i}^2}}$</span> and <span class=\"math-container\">$\\frac{-\\sum_{i=1}^N "body": "<p>Suppose we know that random vectors <span class=\"math-container\">$x, y$</span> have joint density <span class=\"math-container\">$p(x, y) \\propto \\exp(-U(x_1, \\ldots, x_m, y_1, \\ldots, y_n))$</span>, and we want to draw a random sample from the marginal <span class=\"math-container\">$p(x)$</span> (i.e. we want a random sample of <span class=\"math-container\">$x$</span> but are not interested in <span class=\"math-container\">$y$</span>.)</p>\n<p>Naively, we can do an MCMC on the jointly density <span class=\"math-container\">$p(x, y)$</span>, getting a joint vector <span class=\"math-container\">$(x, y)$</span> and taking the <span class=\"math-container\">$x$</span> part as the sample.  But when <span class=\"math-container\">$n \\gg m$</span>, I speculate that this is not very efficient since we also draw a 'useless' sample of <span class=\"math-container\">$y$</span>, which we do not want. (e.g. papers like <a href=\"https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.7392\" rel=\"nofollow noreferrer\">this</a> indicate that the complexity of MCMC sampling scales polynomially with dimension)</p>\n<p>Question: Are there better techniques to sample from <span class=\"math-container\">$p(x)$</span> when <span class=\"math-container\">$n \\gg m$</span>?</p>\n", "creationdate": "2021-05-04T07:20:22.743000", "posts_rownum": "posts_346193"}, "posts_359760": {"id": 547886, "owneruserid": 337591, "posttypeid": 1, "acceptedanswerid": 548659, "parentid": null, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": "Dimensions in the PAM method", "tags": "<clustering>", "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "<p>I am just starting my adventure with data analysis. $\newcommand{\nd}{\frac{n}{2}}$For an $n$-sample following a Normal$(\mu=\theta,\sigma^2=\theta)$, how do we find the mle?

I can find the root of the score function $$ \theta=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{1-4\frac{s}{n}}}{2},s=\sum x_i^2, $$ but I don't see which one is the maximum.
I tried to substitute in the second derivative of the log-likelihood, without success.

For the likelihood, with $x=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$, $$ f(x) = (2\pi)^{-n/2} \theta^{-n/2} \exp\left( -\frac{1}{2\theta}\sum(x_i-\theta)^2\right), $$ then, with $s=\sum x_i^2$ and $t=\sum x_i$, $$ \ln f(x) = -\nd \ln(2\pi) -\nd\ln\theta-\frac{s}{2\theta}-t+\nd\theta, $$ so that $$ \partial_\theta \ln f(x) = -\nd\frac{1}{\theta}+\frac{s}{2\theta^2}+\nd, $$ and the roots are given by $$ \theta^2-\theta+\frac{s}{n}=0. $$ Also, $$ \partial_{\theta,\theta} \ln f(x) = \nd \frac{1}{\theta^2} - \frac{s}{\theta^3}. $$

How do you take the derivative of the function

$$s(\beta)=\displaystyle\sum\frac{Y_i}{X_i^\intercal\beta}X_i-\sum\frac{1-Y_i}{1-X_i^\intercal\beta}X_i?$$

Attempt:

$$H(\beta)=\frac\partial{\partial\beta}s(\beta)=\frac \partial {\partial \beta} \sum\left(\frac{Y_i}{X_i^\intercal\beta}X_i-\frac{1-Y_i}{1-X_i^\intercal\beta}X_i\right)=\\[2em]\sum\left(-\frac{Y_i}{(X_i^\intercal\beta)^2}X_iX_i^\intercal-\frac{1-Y_i}{(1-X_i^\intercal\beta)^2}X_iX_i^\intercal\right)$$

as well as calculate $EH(\beta)$?

I need this because I'm trying to calculate asymptotic variance of a maximum likelihood estimator $-I(\beta)^{-1}=-E(H(\beta))^{-1}$.

By the way, $E(Y_i|X_i)=X_i^\intercal\beta$ here if you want to take the solution all the way.

Assume that I have a rating system with $R$ rating classes, the classes have a probability of default $p_{i0}, i=1,2..,R$. The probability of default is the probability that a company in that class has a payment problem within one year.

I have a set of companies that I have to partition over these classes, using one or other model.

Let's say that I classified $N$ companies last year and each rating class contains $N_i$ companies where $\sum_{i=1}^R N_i=N$. Today, one year later, I count the observed number of defaults in each class and I find $d_i$.

I want to test whether my system is well calibrated, i.e. whether these observed numbers of defaults are in line with my a priori fixed probabilities $p_{i0}$.

I define my test statistic as $X^2=\sum_{I=1}^R \frac{(d_i-N_ip_{i0})^2}{N_i p_{i0}}$. If the expected cell counts $N_ip_{i0}$ are not too low and if the defaults in different rating classes are independent, then this test statistic is $\chi^2$, but what is the number of degrees of freedom , is it $R$ (because I have a sum of $R$ squared standard normal random variables that are independent) or is it $R-1$ as in pearson's $\chi^2$ ? If the latter is the case; where do I loose one degree of freedom ( a reference is fine also).

This is not a simple calculation in general, though the probability will be almost 1 if $n$ is any substantial size.

\n\n

To take your example of five people and 10 bars, there are $10^5$, i.e 100,000 possible equally-likely distributions. All of these will have at least one person alone, except the 10 cases where all five are in a single bar or the 900 cases where three are in a particular bar and two in another. That leaves 99090 distributions which satisfy your condition, more than 99%.

\n\n

Note that 99090 is not divisible by $\\binom{5 + 10 - 1}{5} = 2002$.

\n\n

For $n=1$ to $6$, the fractions seem to be $\\frac{2}{2},$ $\\frac{12}{16},$ $\\frac{210}{216},$ $\\frac{3920}{4096},$ $\\frac{99090}{100000}$ and $\\frac{2962872}{2985984}$, where the denominator in each case is $(2n)^n$. I would expect the probabilities then to keep rising as $n$ increases beyond 6.

The only standardizations that ensure the same limits are those based on the minimum and maximum such as (value $-$ minimum) / (maximum $-$ minimum) but these would usually be considered far from robust, if robust here means resistant to outliers, which is far from the only sense.

(value $-$ mean) / SD is very commonly used, but again that is not robust in the usual sense. (value $-$ median) / IQR is more robust.

You may be working with some other definition of robust, in which case you would need to spell it out here.

Your example of a hypothesis, "the distribution of prices had a different shape in the past", is rather general.

On a variety of grounds, I suspect that your problem would be simpler if you used a quite different approach and looked at logarithm of price. That should pull in outliers. That's not completely arbitrary because it is so common to talk of prices in general rising (sometimes falling) by some percentage, which corresponds to a shift of log price by the corresponding constant. Much here depends on whether you, and especially your likely readership, are comfortable with thinking on a logarithmic scale.

An alternative used by Howard Wainer for car prices is the reciprocal. An accessible summary of his article can be found at http://mahalanobis.twoday.net/stories/908248/

I'd expect that looking at a variety of graphs (histograms or even better quantile plots) would help to see what kinds of changes there have been to the distribution over time.

I don't have a proof of this, but I think this relates to the link function in the context of a generalized linear model. A model with normal errors and identity link (ie. an OLS regression) will have the property you describe. A model with a non-linear link function (like a logistic regression) will have differences in regression coefficients for rv1 between Y~rv1 + rv2 and Y~rv1 because you are averaging over a non-linear function.

Consider the linear mixed effects model $Y=X\beta+Zu+\epsilon$.

Where $u \stackrel{d}{\sim} N(0,D)$ and $\epsilon \stackrel{d}{\sim} N(0,R)$.  Furthermore:

$Var(Y|X,Z,\beta,u)=R$

$Var(Y|X,\beta)=Z'DZ+R=V$

Basically my question is: How exactly is $D$ estimated from the data for the various parameterizations?

**EDIT:**
From the book Variance Components (Searle, Casella, McCulloch 2006) I've managed to gleam the following:

If $D=\sigma^2_uI_q$ then then the variance components are updated and calculated as follows:

$\sigma_e^{2(k+1)} = Y'(Y-X{\hat{\beta}}^{(k)}-{Z}\hat{{u}}^{(k)})/n$

Where $\hat{\beta}^{(k)}$ and $\hat{{u}}^{(k)}$ are the $k$th updates respectively.

I'm guessing in the fully parameterized case, a Cholesky decomposition is used to ensure positive definiteness and symmetry.", "comment": "added 2 characters in body", "creationdate": "2011-11-30T05:07:53.340000", "posthistory_rownum": "posthistory_51992"}, "posthistory_277900": {"id": 383903, "postid": 114520, "userid": 845, "posthistorytypeid": 5, "userdisplayname": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "revisionguid": "e457494d-c0d9-4216-8220-f2272c5da00d", "text": "I'm wondering what the best ways to compare (possibly ranked) lists when we know what the true ranking is and also the variable that decides the ranking.

Historical note: [histograms != bar plots](http://www.worsleyschool.net/science/files/bargraphs/page.html)", "comment": "Changed to reflect edited question", "creationdate": "2011-01-12T02:02:07.317000", "posthistory_rownum": "posthistory_15483"}, "posthistory_589757": {"id": 914473, "postid": 256860, "userid": 845, "posthistorytypeid": 5, "userdisplayname": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 3.0", "revisionguid": "d5348199-fd5e-4822-a66e-06ede320b1b2", "text": "I'm wondering what the best way to generate prediction intervals from a linear model when there is known heteroscedastic AND the heteroscedasticity is predictable.

    gls_1 <- gls(

The data looks like this:

    # Construct data
    code_table_df <- data.frame(

        code = rep(rep(1:4), 2),
        value = c(61, 14, 15, 13, 50, 21,  3, 11)
    )
    
    # Create table
    code_table <- xtabs(value ~ YEAR + code, data = code_table_df)
    code_table
    
          code
    YEAR    1  2  3  4
      2019 61 14 15 13
      2020 50 21  3 11

[![Plot of proportions of each code for each year][1]][1]

A regular Z test of proportions is not appropriate here as I do not want to test if the proportions for codes 1-4 are equal within YEAR. Nor do I want to test if the proportions of YEAR are equal within code.

What I want to check is, are the proportions of the individual codes changing accross years? That is, for codes 1-4, have the proportions changed between 2019 and 2020? Or, in the plot above, is the there a statistically significant difference in height between the dark grey and light grey bar, for each code. For code 3, this would be testing $p_{3,2019}=15/(61+14+15+13)=0.146$ is not equal to $p_{3,2020}=3/(50+21+3+11)=0.035$.


The first thought I had was to use the $\chi^2$ test to test for association between the 2 features, YEAR and code. This gives me

    > chisq.test(code_table)
    
    	Pearson's Chi-squared test
    
    data:  code_table
    X-squared = 9.016, df = 3, p-value = 0.02908

This indicates there is some evidence for association between the 2 features. 

I could also do a proportion test (`prop.test()` in R) for each level of code, but is there a test that allows me to estimate the differences in proportions year on year for all codes with confidence intervals and also adjust/correct for the fact im performing multiple tests? 

  [1]: https://i.stack.imgur.com/C8jEK.png

"d7a7bcab-4e27-43ad-80f8-824049024573", "text": "Say I have 5 time series that may or may not be correlated with each other. I also suspect they individually may be mean reverting. I'd like to 

1) be able to test the hypothesis they are individually mean reverting 

2) generate/simulate future hypothetical trajectories based on estimates obtained (taking observed correlations in to account)

3) obtain analytic prediction intervals if possible

For (1) Is the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test appropriate to be run across the time series individually?

For (2) I figure a multivariate Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process might be appropriate. ", "creationdate": "2011-02-14T07:39:27.737000", "posts_rownum": "posts_6726"}, "posts_11058": {"id": 11969, "owneruserid": 5025, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 2, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "

A related question can be found here about the normal assumption of the error (or more generally of the data if we do not have prior knowledge about the data).

Basically,

  1. It is mathematically convenient to use normal distribution. (It's related to Least Squares fitting and easy to solve with pseudoinverse)
  2. Due to Central Limit Theorem, we may assume that there are lots of underlying facts affecting the process and the sum of these individual effects will tend to behave like normal distribution. In practice, it seems to be so.

An important note from there is that, as Terence Tao states here, "Roughly speaking, this theorem asserts that if one takes a statistic that is a combination of many independent and randomly fluctuating components, with no one component having a decisive influence on the whole, then that statistic will be approximately distributed according to a law called the normal distribution".

To make this clear, let me write a Python code snippet

# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
"""
Illustration of the central limit theorem

@author: İsmail Arı, http://ismailari.com
@date: 31.03.2011
"""
 
import scipy, scipy.stats
import numpy as np
import pylab
 
#===============================================================
# Uncomment one of the distributions below and observe the result
#===============================================================
x = scipy.linspace(0,10,11)
#y = scipy.stats.binom.pmf(x,10,0.2) # binom
#y = scipy.stats.expon.pdf(x,scale=4) # exp
#y = scipy.stats.gamma.pdf(x,2) # gamma
#y = np.ones(np.size(x)) # uniform
y = scipy.random.random(np.size(x)) # random
 
y = y / sum(y);

N = 3
ax = pylab.subplot(N+1,1,1)
pylab.plot(x,y)

# Plotting details 
ax.set_xticks([10])
ax.axis([0, 2**N * 10, 0, np.max(y)*1.1])
ax.set_yticks([round(np.max(y),2)])
 
#===============================================================
# Plots
#===============================================================
for i in np.arange(N)+1:
    y = np.convolve(y,y)
    y = y / sum(y);    
 
    x = np.linspace(2*np.min(x), 2*np.max(x), len(y))
    ax = pylab.subplot(N+1,1,i+1)
    pylab.plot(x,y)
    ax.axis([0, 2**N * 10, 0, np.max(y)*1.1])
    ax.set_xticks([2**i * 10])
    ax.set_yticks([round(np.max(y),3)])
 
pylab.show()

As can be seen from the figures, the resulting distribution (sum) tends towards a normal distribution regardless of the individual distribution types. So, if we do not have enough information about the underlying effects in the data, normality assumption is reasonable.

", "creationdate": "2010-07-19T19:26:13.693000", "posts_rownum": "posts_23"}, "posts_144": {"id": 154, "owneruserid": 108, "posttypeid": 2, "acceptedanswerid": null, "parentid": 1, "ownerdisplayname": null, "title": null, "tags": null, "contentlicense": "CC BY-SA 4.0", "body": "

I am currently researching the trial roulette method for my masters thesis as an elicitation technique. This is a graphical method that allows an expert to represent her subjective probability distribution for an uncertain quantity.

Experts are given counters (or what one can think of as casino chips) representing equal densities whose total would sum up to 1 - for example 20 chips of probability = 0.05 each. They are then instructed to arrange them on a pre-printed grid, with bins representing result intervals. Each column would represent their belief of the probability of getting the corresponding bin result.

Example: A student is asked to predict the mark in a future exam. The figure below shows a completed grid for the elicitation of a subjective probability distribution. The horizontal axis of the grid shows the possible bins (or mark intervals) that the student was asked to consider. The numbers in top row record the number of chips per bin. The completed grid (using a total of 20 chips) shows that the student believes there is a 30% chance that the mark will be between 60 and 64.9.

Some reasons in favour of using this technique are:

  1. Many questions about the shape of the expert's subjective probability distribution can be answered without the need to pose a long series of questions to the expert - the statistician can simply read off density above or below any given point, or that between any two points.

  2. During the elicitation process, the experts can move around the chips if unsatisfied with the way they placed them initially - thus they can be sure of the final result to be submitted.

  3. It forces the expert to be coherent in the set of probabilities that are provided. If all the chips are used, the probabilities must sum to one.

  4. Graphical methods seem to provide more accurate results, especially for participants with modest levels of statistical sophistication.

I'd recommend letting the subject expert specify the mean or mode of the prior but I'd feel free to adjust what they give as a scale. Most people are not very good at quantifying variance.

And I would definitely not let the expert determine the distribution family, in particular the tail thickness. For example, suppose you need a symmetric distribution for a prior. Other answers have covered what is normality and suggested normality test methods. Christian highlighted that in practice perfect normality barely exists.

I highlight that observed deviation from normality does not necessarily mean that methods assuming normality may not be used, and normality test may not be very useful.

  1. Deviation from normality may be caused by outliers that are due to errors in data collection. In many cases checking the data collection logs you can correct these figures and normality often improves.
  2. For large samples a normality test will be able to detect a negligible deviation from normality.
  3. Methods assuming normality may be robust to non-normality and give results of acceptable accuracy. The t-test is known to be robust in this sense, while the F test is not source. Concerning a specific method it's best to check the literature about robustness.
